lessons.title: Your first line of output
lessons.subtitle: Making the computer say something
lessons.concept:
A program is a list of instructions run top to bottom. The most useful first instruction is one that shows you something, because otherwise you cannot tell whether anything happened at all.

In Python that instruction is `print(...)`. Whatever sits between the parentheses is displayed. Text must be wrapped in quotes so Python knows it is literal text rather than the name of something — a piece of text like this is called a **string**.

That is a complete program. No setup, no boilerplate, no class to declare.
lessons.example_code:
print("Hello, world!")
print("Two lines, two prints.")
lessons.example_note: Each print() puts its text on its own line. Execution order is strictly top to bottom.
lessons.task: Print exactly `Hello, world!` — capital H, comma, exclamation mark.
lessons.solution_code: print("Hello, world!")
hints: Use print() with the text inside double quotes. The quotes are not part of the output.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Several lines in a row
lessons.subtitle: Statements run in order
lessons.concept:
Python executes one statement per line, in the order they appear. Three `print` calls produce three lines, always in the same order.

This sounds obvious, but it is the foundation of everything: a program is a sequence, and the sequence is exactly what you wrote.
lessons.example_code:
print("first")
print("second")
print("third")
lessons.example_note: Swap two of those lines and the output order changes to match. Nothing is reordered behind your back.
lessons.task:
Print these three lines in order:

`ready`
`steady`
`go`
lessons.solution_code:
print("ready")
print("steady")
print("go")
hints: Three separate print() calls, one per line.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Notes the computer ignores
lessons.subtitle: Writing comments
lessons.concept:
A **comment** is a note for humans. Python sees a `#` and ignores the rest of that line entirely.

Good comments explain *why* code does something — the code already says *what*. A comment can sit on its own line or trail after a statement.
lessons.example_code:
# This whole line is ignored
print("visible")   # so is everything after the hash
# print("this never runs")
lessons.example_note: Commenting out a line is a quick way to disable it without deleting it.
lessons.task: Print `code speaks` on one line and `comments explain` on the next. Include at least one comment in your file.
lessons.solution_code:

print("code speaks")
print("comments explain")
hints: Anything after # on a line is ignored, so it cannot affect your output.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Several values in one call
lessons.subtitle: Comma-separated arguments
lessons.concept:
You can pass `print` several values at once by separating them with commas. Python inserts a single space between each and prints them on one line.

This works for any mix of types — numbers do not need quotes, and you do not have to convert them yourself.
lessons.example_code:
print("one", "two", "three")
print("total:", 42)
print("x", 1, "y", 2)
lessons.example_note: Output: `one two three`, then `total: 42`, then `x 1 y 2`. The spaces come from the commas.

lessons.solution_code: print("score:", 95, "grade:", "A")
hints: Each comma adds exactly one space, so do not add spaces inside the strings as well.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Characters you cannot type directly
lessons.subtitle: Escape sequences
lessons.concept:
Some characters are awkward to put in a string: a newline, a tab, a quote of the same kind that surrounds the string. Python solves this with **escape sequences**, all starting with a backslash.

- `\n` newline
- `\t` tab
- `\\` a literal backslash
- `\"` a literal double quote

One string containing `\n` can therefore produce several lines from a single print.
lessons.example_code:
print("line one\nline two")
print("name\tyear")
print("She said \"hi\"")
print("C:\\Users")
lessons.example_note: The backslash disappears from the output — it is an instruction to the parser, not a character.
lessons.task:
With a single print call, produce these two lines separated by a tab in each:

`lang	year`
`Python	1991`
lessons.solution_code: print("lang\tyear\nPython\t1991")
hints: Put \t between the columns and \n between the two lines, all inside one string.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Controlling the joins
lessons.subtitle: sep and end
lessons.concept:
Two optional settings change how `print` assembles its output.

`sep=` replaces the space placed between arguments. `end=` replaces the newline placed at the end — setting `end=""` keeps the cursor on the same line so the next print continues it.

These are **keyword arguments**: they are named, so their position does not matter.
lessons.example_code:
print("2026", "08", "01", sep="-")
print("no newline...", end="")
print("same line")
print("a", "b", sep="", end="!\n")
lessons.example_note: Output: `2026-08-01`, then `no newline...same line`, then `ab!`.
lessons.task:
Using sep, print the three parts joined by slashes:

`usr/local/bin`
lessons.solution_code: print("usr", "local", "bin", sep="/")
hints: Pass sep="/" after the three strings.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Printing computed values
lessons.subtitle: Expressions inside print
lessons.concept:
Anything you put inside `print` is **evaluated first**, then displayed. `print(2 + 3)` shows `5`, not `2 + 3`, because Python works out the value before printing it.

This is the difference between a **literal** (a value written out) and an **expression** (something that computes a value).
lessons.example_code:
print(2 + 3)
print(10 * 4)
print("2 + 3")
print("answer:", 6 * 7)
lessons.example_note: The third line prints the characters 2 + 3 because quotes make it text, not arithmetic.
lessons.task: Print the results of these three calculations, one per line: 17 plus 25, 8 times 9, and 100 minus 37.
lessons.solution_code:

print(8 * 9)
print(100 - 37)
hints: No quotes — quotes would turn the sum into text and print it literally.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

questions.q: What does print("2" + "3") display?

lessons.title: Naming values
lessons.subtitle: Assignment with =
lessons.concept:
A **variable** is a name attached to a value. You create one with `=`, which here does not mean "equals" — it means "store the value on the right under the name on the left".

Once a value has a name you can reuse it anywhere and change it in one place. Python works out the type on its own, so there is no type keyword to write.

Names are lowercase with underscores: `user_name`, `total_cost`.
lessons.example_code:
language = "Python"
year = 1991

print(language, year)

year = year + 1
print("next:", year)
lessons.example_note: `year = year + 1` reads the old value, adds one, and stores the result back under the same name.
lessons.task:
Create `name` holding `Ada` and `age` holding `36`, then print exactly:

`Ada is 36 years old`
lessons.solution_code:
name = "Ada"
age = 36
print(name, "is", age, "years old")
hints: Strings need quotes; numbers do not. The commas in print supply the spaces.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: What kind of value is this?
lessons.subtitle: int, float, str, bool
lessons.concept:
Every value has a **type**. The four you meet first:

- `int` — a whole number, like `42`
- `float` — a number with a decimal point, like `3.5`
- `str` — text in quotes
- `bool` — exactly `True` or `False`

`type(x)` reports the type of a value. Types matter because they decide what operations are allowed: `+` adds numbers but joins strings.
lessons.example_code:
print(type(42))
print(type(3.5))
print(type("hi"))
print(type(True))
lessons.example_note: The output looks like <class 'int'> — Python is telling you the value belongs to the int class.

Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Changing what a name refers to
lessons.subtitle: Rebinding and swapping
lessons.concept:
A variable can be pointed at a new value at any time, and the new value need not be the same type as the old one.

Python also allows **multiple assignment**: `a, b = 1, 2` assigns both at once. That makes swapping two variables a single line: `a, b = b, a`, with no temporary variable needed.
lessons.example_code:
x = 10
x = "now a string"
print(x)

a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
lessons.example_note: In `a, b = b, a` the right-hand side is fully evaluated first, which is why the swap works.

lessons.title: Converting between types
lessons.subtitle: int(), float(), str()
lessons.concept:
Types can be converted explicitly. `int("42")` turns text into a number, `str(42)` turns a number into text, and `float("3.5")` produces a float.

This matters because Python refuses to guess. `"5" + 5` is an error, not `10` or `"55"` — you must say which you meant.

`int()` on a float truncates toward zero: `int(3.9)` is `3`, not `4`.
lessons.example_code:
text = "42"
number = int(text)
print(number + 8)

print(str(99) + " bottles")
print(int(3.9), float(7))
lessons.example_note: int(3.9) gives 3 because it truncates rather than rounds. Use round(3.9) for 4.

lessons.title: Naming things well
lessons.subtitle: Conventions and readability
lessons.concept:
Python names are case sensitive and cannot start with a digit or contain spaces. Beyond the rules there are strong conventions:

- variables and functions: `lower_snake_case`
- constants that never change: `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`
- avoid single letters except for counters and coordinates

Good names remove the need for comments. `d = 86400` needs explaining; `SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86400` does not.
lessons.example_code:
SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86400
days_elapsed = 3

total_seconds = SECONDS_PER_DAY * days_elapsed
print("total:", total_seconds)
lessons.example_note: Python does not enforce constants — the capitals are a message to other programmers, not to the interpreter.

lessons.solution_code:

print("worked:", MINUTES_PER_HOUR * hours_worked, "minutes")
hints: Multiply the two names rather than typing 420 directly.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Several values, one calculation
lessons.subtitle: Chaining variables together
lessons.concept:
Variables become powerful when one is defined in terms of others. Change the input at the top and every derived value updates, because each line is recomputed when it runs.

The order matters: a name must already exist before it is used. Python reads top to bottom and will complain if you reference something that has not been assigned yet.
lessons.example_code:
price = 4.5
quantity = 3
subtotal = price * quantity
tax = subtotal * 0.2
total = subtotal + tax

lessons.title: Checkpoint: values

lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What is the type of 3.0?
questions.explain: Any literal with a decimal point is a float, even when the fractional part is zero.

questions.q: What does int("7") + 3 give?
questions.explain: int("7") converts the text to the number 7, so the addition is arithmetic and gives 10.

questions.q: What does "5" + 5 do?
questions.explain: Python refuses to guess whether you meant addition or joining, so mixing str and int with + is an error.

questions.q: After a, b = 1, 2 then a, b = b, a, what is a?
questions.explain: The right-hand side is evaluated first, producing (2, 1), which is then unpacked — so a becomes 2.

questions.q: What is int(3.9)?

lessons.title: The arithmetic operators
lessons.subtitle: Seven ways to combine numbers
lessons.concept:
Python has seven arithmetic operators. Most behave as you expect; three are worth memorising.

- `+ - *` as usual
- `/` **always** produces a float, so `6 / 3` gives `2.0`
- `//` floor division, discarding the remainder
- `%` the remainder itself
- `**` exponentiation, so `2 ** 10` is `1024`

`//` and `%` are a pair: for `17` and `5`, `17 // 5` is `3` and `17 % 5` is `2`, because 17 = 5×3 + 2.
lessons.example_code:
a, b = 17, 5
print(a + b, a - b, a * b)
print(a / b)
print(a // b)
print(a % b)
print(a ** 2)
lessons.example_note: The remainder operator is the standard test for divisibility: n % 2 == 0 means n is even.

hints: Use // for the whole share, % for the leftover, and plain / for the exact value.

lessons.title: Which operation happens first
lessons.subtitle: Precedence and parentheses
lessons.concept:
Operators have a fixed **precedence**. From strongest to weakest: `**`, then unary `-`, then `* / // %`, then `+ -`.

So `2 + 3 * 4` is `14`, not `20`. Parentheses override everything and cost nothing — when in doubt, add them.

One quirk worth knowing: `**` is right-associative, so `2 ** 3 ** 2` is `2 ** 9`, which is `512`.
lessons.example_note: -3 ** 2 is -9 because ** binds tighter than the minus sign. (-3) ** 2 is 9.

lessons.title: Updating a value in place
lessons.subtitle: The += family
lessons.concept:
Adding to a variable is so common that Python has a shorthand: `total += 5` means `total = total + 5`.

Every arithmetic operator has an augmented form: `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `//=`, `%=`, `**=`. They work on strings too, where `+=` appends.

The shorthand is not just less typing — it makes the intent ("update this") clearer than repeating the name.
lessons.example_code:
total = 10
total += 5
total *= 2
total -= 4
print(total)

text = "ab"
text += "cd"
print(text)
lessons.example_note: The updates apply in order: 10 becomes 15, then 30, then 26.

lessons.title: Comparing values
lessons.subtitle: The six comparison operators
lessons.concept:
Comparisons produce a **bool**: either `True` or `False`.

`==` equal, `!=` not equal, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`.

A common beginner error is writing `=` when comparing. `=` assigns, `==` compares — they are unrelated.

Python also allows **chained comparisons**: `0 < x < 10` reads exactly like the mathematics and means both conditions must hold.
lessons.example_code:
x = 7
print(x == 7)
print(x != 7)
print(x < 10, x > 10)
print(0 < x < 10)
print("apple" < "banana")
lessons.example_note: Strings compare alphabetically, which is why "apple" < "banana" is True.

lessons.title: Combining conditions
lessons.subtitle: and, or, not
lessons.concept:
`and` is True only when both sides are True. `or` is True when at least one side is. `not` flips a boolean.

Both `and` and `or` **short-circuit**: `and` stops at the first False and `or` stops at the first True, without evaluating the rest. That is useful when the second part would fail otherwise.

Precedence runs `not`, then `and`, then `or`, so `a or b and c` means `a or (b and c)`.
lessons.example_code:
age = 25
member = False

print(age > 18 and age < 65)
print(member or age > 21)
print(not member)
print(not (age > 18 and member))
lessons.example_note: Parenthesise freely — the precedence rules are correct but rarely obvious to a reader.

lessons.title: Values that behave like booleans
lessons.subtitle: Truthy and falsy
lessons.concept:
Every Python value can be used where a boolean is expected. The **falsy** values are few and worth memorising:

`False`, `0`, `0.0`, `""` (empty string), `[]` (empty list), `{}` (empty dict), and `None`.

Everything else is **truthy**. `bool(x)` shows which a value is. This is why `if items:` is the idiomatic way to ask "is this list non-empty".
lessons.example_code:
print(bool(0), bool(1), bool(-1))
print(bool(""), bool("a"), bool(" "))
print(bool([]), bool([0]))
print(bool(None))
lessons.example_note: bool(" ") is True — a space is a character, so the string is not empty.

lessons.title: Two more operator pairs
lessons.subtitle: in, not in, is, is not
lessons.concept:
`in` tests **membership**: whether a value appears inside a string, list or other collection. `not in` is its negation.

`is` tests **identity**: whether two names refer to the very same object, which is different from being equal. Use `is` only with `None`, `True` and `False`; use `==` for values.

The rule of thumb: `x == 5` asks "does it equal five", `x is None` asks "is it the None object".

print("dog" in "cat")
print(3 in [1, 2, 3])
print("x" not in "cat")

print(value is None)
lessons.example_note: Membership on a string checks for a substring, so "at" in "cat" is also True.

questions.q: What is 2 + 3 * 4?

questions.q: What is 7 // 2?

questions.explain: and evaluates left to right and stops at the first falsy operand, so the right side is never reached when n is 0.

lessons.title: Running code only sometimes
lessons.subtitle: The if statement
lessons.concept:
An `if` statement runs a block of code only when its condition is True.

The critical Python detail is that the block is defined by **indentation**, not by braces or keywords. Four spaces is the universal convention. The colon at the end of the `if` line opens the block, and the block ends when the indentation returns to the previous level.

This is not cosmetic — indentation is real syntax in Python, and getting it wrong is a genuine error.
lessons.example_code:
temp = 31

if temp > 30:
    print("hot")
    print("stay hydrated")

print("always runs")
lessons.example_note: Both indented lines belong to the if. The last line is not indented, so it always runs.
lessons.task: With `n = 17`, print `positive` if n is above zero, then print `done` unconditionally.
lessons.solution_code:

print("done")
hints: Indent the body by four spaces and leave the final print at the outer level.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Two paths
lessons.subtitle: else
lessons.concept:
`else` supplies the block to run when the condition was False. Exactly one of the two blocks runs — never both, never neither.

The `else` keyword lines up with its `if` at the same indentation, and takes its own colon.
lessons.example_note: else has no condition of its own — it simply catches everything the if did not.

lessons.title: Many paths
lessons.subtitle: elif chains
lessons.concept:
`elif` (short for "else if") tests another condition when the previous ones failed. A chain can have as many `elif` branches as you like, with an optional `else` at the end.

Conditions are checked **in order**, and the first match wins — the rest are skipped entirely. That means order matters: put the most specific or highest thresholds first, or a broad condition will swallow the cases below it.
lessons.example_note: Because 74 fails the first two tests and passes the third, it prints C. Reversing the order would print C for everything above 70, including 95.
lessons.task: With `temp = 5`, print `freezing` under 0, `cold` under 10, `mild` under 25, otherwise `hot`.
hints: Order the thresholds from lowest to highest so each elif only sees what fell through.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Conditions inside conditions
lessons.subtitle: Nesting and flattening
lessons.concept:
An `if` can contain another `if`. Each level adds four more spaces of indentation.

Nesting is sometimes the clearest way to express a decision, but deep nesting quickly becomes hard to read. Often the same logic can be **flattened** by combining conditions with `and`, which is usually preferable.
lessons.example_note: Two levels of nesting is usually fine; four is a sign the logic wants restructuring.

lessons.title: A choice inside an expression
lessons.subtitle: The ternary form
lessons.concept:
When you only need to pick between two **values**, Python offers a one-line conditional expression:

`value = a if condition else b`

It reads almost like English: "a if the condition holds, otherwise b". Unlike a statement it produces a value, so it can go directly inside a call or an assignment.

Use it for simple choices; a full `if` statement is clearer for anything with multiple steps.
lessons.example_code:
n = 7
label = "even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd"
print(label)

print("high" if n > 5 else "low")

age = 20
price = 5 if age < 18 else 10
print(price)
lessons.example_note: The condition sits in the middle, which is unusual but becomes natural quickly.

lessons.title: Branching on a value
lessons.subtitle: Multi-way branching with elif
lessons.concept:
When you need to test one value against many possible options, a chain of `if`/`elif`/`else` is the classic Python approach. Each `elif` tests another condition, and the final `else` is the catch-all.

You can combine several values in one branch with `or`. This makes it visually obvious that every branch is testing the same subject.
lessons.example_note: The else branch is the catch-all that always matches, so it belongs last.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: conditionals
lessons.subtitle: Check what stuck before moving on
lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: How does Python know which lines belong to an if block?
questions.explain: Indentation is genuine syntax in Python. Consistently indented lines under the colon form the block.

questions.q: In an if/elif/elif/else chain, how many branches run?
questions.explain: Conditions are tested in order and the first match wins; every other branch is skipped.

questions.q: What does x = "a" if n > 0 else "b" do?
questions.explain: This is a conditional expression: it produces a value rather than executing statements.

questions.q: Why must the FizzBuzz check for divisibility by both 3 and 5 come first?
options: Otherwise the single-divisor branches match first and the combined case never runs
questions.explain: A number divisible by 15 also satisfies the divisible-by-3 test, so if that branch comes first the combined case is unreachable.

questions.q: What does the else branch do in an if/elif chain?
options: It runs only when no if or elif matched
It runs before the elif branches
It is required in every chain
questions.explain: The else branch is the catch-all that runs when none of the preceding conditions were true, so it belongs last.

lessons.title: Repeating a fixed number of times
lessons.subtitle: for and range
lessons.concept:
A `for` loop runs its body once for each item in a sequence. The simplest source of items is `range`.

- `range(n)` counts `0` up to but **not including** n
- `range(a, b)` starts at a and stops before b
- `range(a, b, step)` moves by step, which may be negative

The exclusive end feels odd at first but means `range(len(x))` covers exactly the valid indices.
lessons.example_note: The last loop prints 10, 7, 4, 1 — it stops as soon as continuing would pass the end.
lessons.task: Print the first five multiples of 3 (3, 6, 9, 12, 15), one per line, then `sum: 45`.
lessons.solution_code:
total = 0

for i in range(1, 6):
    value = i * 3
    print(value)
    total += value

print("sum:", total)
hints: Accumulate into a variable declared before the loop, then print it after.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Looping over things directly
lessons.subtitle: Strings and lists
lessons.concept:
A `for` loop works on anything **iterable**, not just ranges. Looping over a string yields each character; looping over a list yields each element.

This is the idiomatic Python style. Writing `for i in range(len(items))` and then indexing is almost always the clumsier option — loop over the items themselves when you need the values.
lessons.example_note: The loop variable is rebound on each pass and remains available after the loop ends.
lessons.task: Given `word = "loop"`, print each character on its own line, then print the number of characters.
lessons.solution_code:
word = "loop"

for ch in word:
    print(ch)

print(len(word))
hints: Iterate the string directly rather than over a range of indices.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Looping until something changes
lessons.subtitle: while
lessons.concept:
A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition stays True. It is the right tool when you do not know in advance how many passes are needed.

The danger is the infinite loop: **something inside the body must eventually make the condition False**. Forgetting to update the variable is the single most common cause.

Use `for` when counting a known number of times; use `while` when looping until a state is reached.
lessons.example_code:
n = 100
steps = 0

while n > 1:
    n //= 2
    steps += 1

print("halvings:", steps)
lessons.example_note: n shrinks every pass, guaranteeing the condition eventually fails. Without that line it would run forever.
lessons.task: Starting from 1, repeatedly double a value while it stays below 100, printing each value including the first. Then print how many doublings happened.
lessons.solution_code:
value = 1
count = 0

while value < 100:
    print(value)
    value *= 2
    count += 1

print("doublings:", count)
hints: Print before doubling so the initial 1 appears.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Leaving early and skipping ahead
lessons.subtitle: break and continue
lessons.concept:
`break` exits the loop immediately, skipping any remaining passes. `continue` abandons only the current pass and jumps to the next one.

`break` is how you implement a search: stop as soon as you find what you wanted, rather than scanning the rest pointlessly.

Both affect only the innermost loop they appear in.
lessons.example_note: The second loop prints only the odd numbers, because continue skips the rest of the body for even ones.
lessons.task: Loop from 1 to 30. Skip every multiple of 3 with continue, and stop entirely with break once the value exceeds 12. Print each value that survives.
hints: Test the break condition before the continue condition.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: A loop inside a loop
lessons.subtitle: Nesting
lessons.concept:
Placing one loop inside another runs the inner loop completely for **every single pass** of the outer loop. Two loops of ten passes each therefore execute the inner body a hundred times.

This is the natural shape for grids, tables and pairs. It is also where performance disappears quickly, since the work multiplies rather than adds.
lessons.example_note: The bare print() after the inner loop ends the row. Without it, everything would land on one line.
lessons.task: Print a 3 by 4 grid of hash characters — three rows, each containing four hashes with no spaces.
hints: Use end="" inside the inner loop and an empty print() to break the line.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: The loop that knows it finished
lessons.subtitle: for...else
lessons.concept:
Python loops accept an `else` clause, which runs **only if the loop completed without hitting a break**.

This is unusual and unique to Python. It is exactly what a search needs: the `else` is the "not found" case, and it removes the need for a separate flag variable.

Read it as "for ... else nothing broke out".
lessons.example_note: Because no break happened, the else runs and prints "not found".

hints: The else aligns with the for, not with the if.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: loops
lessons.subtitle: Check what stuck before moving on
lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What does range(2, 5) produce?
questions.explain: range includes the start and excludes the end, so it yields 2, 3 and 4.

questions.q: What is the most common cause of an infinite while loop?
options: Forgetting to change the variable the condition tests
questions.explain: If nothing in the body moves the condition toward False, it never becomes False.

questions.q: What does continue do?
options: Skips the rest of the current pass and moves to the next
Restarts the loop from the beginning
questions.explain: continue abandons only the current iteration; break is what exits the loop entirely.

questions.q: When does a for...else clause run?
options: Only when the loop body never executed
Only when the loop finished without hitting a break
questions.explain: The else is the "no break happened" case, which makes it ideal for the not-found branch of a search.

questions.q: How many times does the inner body run for two nested loops of 5 and 4 passes?
questions.explain: The inner loop runs completely for every outer pass, so the work multiplies: 5 x 4 = 20.

lessons.title: Reaching individual characters
lessons.subtitle: Indexing and negative indexes
lessons.concept:
A string is an ordered sequence of characters, and `text[i]` reaches the one at position `i`. Counting starts at **zero**, so the first character is `text[0]`.

Negative indexes count from the end: `text[-1]` is the last character, `text[-2]` the one before it. That saves computing `len(text) - 1` constantly.

Asking for an index that does not exist raises an `IndexError` rather than returning something empty.
lessons.example_code:
word = "python"

print(word[0])
print(word[3])
print(word[-1])
print(word[-2])
print(len(word))
lessons.example_note: Valid indexes for a six-character string run 0 to 5, or -1 to -6.
lessons.task: Given `word = "keyboard"`, print its first character, its last character, its fourth character and its length.
lessons.solution_code:

print(word[0])
print(word[-1])
print(word[3])
print(len(word))
hints: The fourth character is at index 3, because counting starts at zero.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Taking a section
lessons.subtitle: Slices
lessons.concept:
`text[start:end]` returns a new string from `start` up to but **not including** `end`. Omitting either side means "from the beginning" or "to the end".

A third value gives the step: `text[::2]` takes every second character, and `text[::-1]` reverses the string — the standard Python idiom for reversal.

Slices never raise an error for out-of-range values; they simply return as much as exists.
lessons.example_code:
text = "programming"

print(text[0:4])
print(text[4:])
print(text[:3])
print(text[-4:])
print(text[::2])
print(text[::-1])
lessons.example_note: text[:n] and text[n:] always split the string into two parts that rejoin perfectly.
lessons.task: Given `text = "abcdefgh"`, print the first three characters, the last three, everything except the first and last, and the whole string reversed.
lessons.solution_code:

print(text[:3])

print(text[1:-1])
print(text[::-1])
hints: text[1:-1] drops one character from each end.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Asking a string to do things
lessons.subtitle: Case, trimming and testing
lessons.concept:
Strings carry **methods** — functions attached to the value, called with a dot.

- `.upper()`, `.lower()`, `.title()`, `.capitalize()` change case
- `.strip()`, `.lstrip()`, `.rstrip()` remove surrounding whitespace
- `.startswith()`, `.endswith()`, `.count()`, `.find()` inspect content
- `.isdigit()`, `.isalpha()`, `.isspace()` test the characters

Strings are **immutable**, so every one of these returns a *new* string rather than changing the original.
lessons.example_code:
raw = "  Hello World  "

print(raw.strip())
print(raw.strip().upper())
print(raw.strip().lower())
print("hello".capitalize())
print("hello world".title())
print("banana".count("a"))
print("hello".find("ll"))
lessons.example_note: .find() returns the index of the first match, or -1 when there is none.

lessons.solution_code:

lessons.title: Building text from values
lessons.subtitle: f-strings
lessons.concept:
An **f-string** substitutes values directly into text. Put `f` before the quote and place any expression inside `{}`.

A colon inside the braces introduces a **format spec**:
- `{v:.2f}` two decimal places
- `{v:>8}` right-align in 8 columns, `{v:<8}` left-align, `{v:^8}` centre
- `{v:,}` thousands separators
- `{v=}` prints both the expression and its value, which is superb for debugging
lessons.example_code:
name = "Ada"
score = 91.5678

print(f"{name} scored {score:.1f}")
print(f"|{name:<10}|{name:>10}|{name:^10}|")
print(f"{1234567:,}")
print(f"{score=}")
lessons.example_note: Anything valid as an expression works inside the braces, including method calls and arithmetic.
lessons.task: Given `item = "coffee"` and `price = 3.5`, print `coffee costs $3.50` using an f-string with two decimal places.
lessons.solution_code:

hints: The dollar sign is literal text; the format spec is :.2f.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Between text and lists
lessons.subtitle: split and join
lessons.concept:
`.split(sep)` breaks a string into a list. With no argument it splits on any run of whitespace, which is what you want for words.

`sep.join(list)` is the inverse: it glues a list of strings together with `sep` between them. Note the direction — the separator is the thing you call `.join` on.

Every element must already be a string; join will not convert numbers for you.
lessons.example_code:
sentence = "the quick brown fox"
words = sentence.split()
print(words)
print(len(words))

print("-".join(words))
print(" ".join(["a", "b", "c"]))

print("2026-08-01".split("-"))
lessons.example_note: "".join(parts) concatenates with nothing between, which is the fastest way to build a string from pieces.
lessons.task: Given `csv = "red,green,blue"`, split it into a list, print the list, print how many parts there are, and print them rejoined with `" | "`.
lessons.solution_code:

print(parts)

hints: Pass the comma explicitly to split, since the default splits on whitespace.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Substituting content
lessons.subtitle: replace and immutability
lessons.concept:
`.replace(old, new)` returns a new string with every occurrence swapped. An optional third argument limits how many are replaced.

Because strings are immutable, `text.replace(...)` on its own changes nothing — you must assign the result. This catches almost everyone once.

The same applies to every string method: they all return new values.
lessons.example_code:
text = "one two one two"

print(text.replace("one", "1"))
print(text.replace("one", "1", 1))
print(text)

text = text.replace("two", "2")
print(text)
lessons.example_note: The third print shows the original unchanged — proof that replace did not modify it in place.

lessons.title: Many values under one name
lessons.subtitle: Creating and indexing lists
lessons.concept:
A **list** holds an ordered sequence of values in a single variable, written with square brackets. The values can be any type, and they can be mixed.

Indexing works exactly as it does for strings: `items[0]` is the first, `items[-1]` is the last, and `len(items)` gives the count.

Unlike a string, a list is **mutable** — `items[0] = "new"` replaces an element in place, changing the list itself rather than producing a copy.
lessons.example_code:
langs = ["python", "c", "rust"]

print(langs)
print(langs[0])
print(langs[-1])
print(len(langs))

langs[1] = "cpp"
print(langs)
lessons.example_note: Printing a list shows its bracket form, with strings in quotes — useful for seeing exactly what it holds.
lessons.task: Create a list of the four seasons, print the whole list, the first season, the last season, and how many there are.

lessons.title: Growing and shrinking a list
lessons.subtitle: append, insert, remove, pop
lessons.concept:
Lists change size on demand.

- `.append(x)` adds one item to the end
- `.insert(i, x)` inserts at a position, shifting the rest along
- `.extend(other)` adds every item from another list
- `.remove(x)` deletes the first occurrence **by value**
- `.pop()` removes and returns the last item; `.pop(i)` removes at an index
- `.clear()` empties it

The distinction between `remove` (by value) and `pop` (by index) is worth fixing in your memory now.
lessons.example_code:
items = ["a", "b"]
items.append("c")
items.insert(0, "start")
items.extend(["d", "e"])
print(items)

last = items.pop()
items.remove("b")
print(items, "removed:", last)
lessons.example_note: append takes one item; extend takes a list. append([1,2]) would nest a list inside your list.

lessons.title: Sections of a list
lessons.subtitle: Slices and copies
lessons.concept:
Lists slice exactly like strings: `items[a:b]` returns a **new list** from a up to but not including b, and the step form `items[::2]` works too.

This matters for copying. `b = a` gives two names for the *same* list, so changing one changes the other. `b = a[:]` (or `a.copy()`) makes a genuine copy that can be modified independently.

That single distinction is the source of a great many confusing bugs.
lessons.example_code:
nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

print(nums[2:5])
print(nums[:3])
print(nums[::2])
print(nums[::-1])

alias = nums
copy = nums[:]
alias.append(99)
print(len(nums), len(copy))
lessons.example_note: nums grew to 7 because alias is the same list; copy stayed at 6 because it is separate.

hints: The same slice syntax you learned for strings applies unchanged.

lessons.title: Putting a list in order
lessons.subtitle: sort, sorted and reverse
lessons.concept:
There are two ways to order a list, and the difference matters.

`items.sort()` rearranges the list **in place** and returns `None`. `sorted(items)` leaves the original alone and returns a **new** sorted list.

Both accept `reverse=True` for descending order, and `key=` to sort by a computed value — `key=len` sorts strings by length, for instance.

A classic error is writing `items = items.sort()`, which sets items to None.
lessons.example_code:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
print(sorted(nums))
print(nums)

nums.sort()
print(nums)

words = ["pear", "fig", "banana"]
print(sorted(words, key=len))
print(sorted(words, reverse=True))
lessons.example_note: Use sorted() when you still need the original order; use .sort() when you do not.

lessons.solution_code:

hints: sorted() returns a value; .sort() mutates and returns nothing.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Summarising a list
lessons.subtitle: len, sum, min, max and friends
lessons.concept:
Several built-in functions take a list and reduce it to one value: `len`, `sum`, `min`, `max`. There is no need to write a loop for these.

Other useful operations:
- `items.count(x)` how many times x appears
- `items.index(x)` where x first appears
- `x in items` membership
- `any(items)` / `all(items)` whether any or every value is truthy

`sum` only works on numbers; `min` and `max` also work on strings, comparing alphabetically.
lessons.example_code:
nums = [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]

print(len(nums), sum(nums))
print(min(nums), max(nums))
print(sum(nums) / len(nums))
print(nums.index(15), nums.count(8))
print(any(n > 40 for n in nums), all(n > 0 for n in nums))
lessons.example_note: sum(nums) / len(nums) is the standard way to compute a mean.
lessons.task: Given `scores = [67, 91, 42, 78, 57]`, print the count, the highest, the lowest, the total and the average.
lessons.solution_code:
scores = [67, 91, 42, 78, 57]

print("count:", len(scores))
print("max:", max(scores))
print("min:", min(scores))
print("total:", sum(scores))
print("average:", sum(scores) / len(scores))
hints: All five come from built-in functions — no loops needed.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Lists that cannot change
lessons.subtitle: Tuples and unpacking
lessons.concept:
A **tuple** is an ordered sequence like a list, but **immutable** — written with parentheses instead of brackets. Once created, its contents are fixed.

Use a tuple when the collection represents one thing with fixed parts: a coordinate, an RGB colour, a database row. Use a list when the collection is a variable-length series of similar items.

Tuples support **unpacking**: `x, y = point` pulls the parts into separate names, which is how functions return several values.
lessons.example_code:
point = (3, 7)
print(point, point[0], len(point))

x, y = point
print("x =", x, "y =", y)

first, *rest = (1, 2, 3, 4)
print(first, rest)
lessons.example_note: The starred name collects everything remaining into a list — handy when you only care about the first item.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: lists

lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What does items.sort() return?
questions.explain: sort() mutates the list and returns None. Use sorted(items) when you want a new list back.

questions.q: After b = a where a is a list, what happens if you append to b?
options: Both a and b change — they are the same list
questions.explain: Assignment copies the reference, not the list. Use a[:] or a.copy() for an independent copy.

questions.q: What is the difference between remove and pop?
options: remove takes a value, pop takes an index
remove takes an index, pop takes a value
questions.explain: remove(x) deletes the first element equal to x; pop(i) deletes the element at index i and returns it.

questions.q: Why can a tuple not be modified?
options: It is stored as a string
questions.explain: Immutability is the defining feature of a tuple, which is what makes it suitable for fixed records.

questions.q: What does items[-2:] give?
questions.explain: A negative start counts from the end, and an omitted stop means "to the end", so this is the final two elements.

lessons.title: Looking things up by name
lessons.subtitle: Creating and reading dictionaries
lessons.concept:
A **dictionary** stores pairs: each **key** maps to a **value**. Where a list is indexed by position, a dict is indexed by whatever key you chose — usually a string.

Write them with braces and colons, and read with `d[key]`. Assigning to a key that does not exist creates it; assigning to one that does replaces its value.

Since Python 3.7, dictionaries preserve insertion order, so iteration is predictable.
lessons.example_code:
ages = {"ada": 36, "alan": 41}

print(ages)
print(ages["ada"])
print(len(ages))

ages["grace"] = 45
ages["ada"] = 37
print(ages)
lessons.example_note: Keys must be immutable — strings, numbers and tuples work; lists cannot be keys.
lessons.task: Build a dictionary of three capital cities (France/Paris, Japan/Tokyo, Peru/Lima). Print the whole dict, the capital of Japan, and how many entries it has.
lessons.solution_code:
capitals = {"France": "Paris", "Japan": "Tokyo", "Peru": "Lima"}

print(capitals)
print(capitals["Japan"])
print(len(capitals))
hints: Look up with square brackets and the key.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Keys that might not be there
lessons.subtitle: get, in and setdefault
lessons.concept:
Reading a missing key with `d[key]` raises a `KeyError` and stops your program. Three safer options exist.

`d.get(key)` returns `None` instead of raising; `d.get(key, default)` returns your chosen fallback. `key in d` tests presence directly. `d.setdefault(key, default)` returns the existing value or inserts the default and returns that.

The `get` form with a default is the workhorse, and it is what makes counting so concise.
lessons.example_code:
stock = {"apple": 4}

print(stock.get("apple"))
print(stock.get("pear"))
print(stock.get("pear", 0))
print("apple" in stock, "pear" in stock)

stock.setdefault("pear", 0)
print(stock)
lessons.example_note: get never modifies the dict; setdefault does when the key is absent.
lessons.task: Given `stock = {"apple": 4, "banana": 12}`, print the count of apples, the count of cherries defaulting to 0, and whether `"banana"` is present.
lessons.solution_code:
stock = {"apple": 4, "banana": 12}

print(stock.get("apple"))
print(stock.get("cherry", 0))
print("banana" in stock)
hints: The second argument to get is the fallback value.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Walking through a dictionary
lessons.subtitle: keys, values and items
lessons.concept:
Looping over a dict directly yields its **keys**. Three methods make the intent explicit:

- `.keys()` the keys
- `.values()` the values
- `.items()` both, as `(key, value)` tuples

The `.items()` form combined with tuple unpacking is the standard way to process a dictionary: `for key, value in d.items():`.
lessons.example_note: Aggregate functions like sum, min and max work directly on .values().
lessons.task: Given `stock = {"apple": 4, "banana": 12, "cherry": 30}`, print each entry as `apple: 4`, then print the total quantity and the number of kinds.
hints: Unpack each item into two loop variables.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Counting with a dictionary
lessons.subtitle: The standard counting idiom
lessons.concept:
Counting occurrences is the single most common use of a dictionary. The idiom is:

`counts[key] = counts.get(key, 0) + 1`

Read it as "take the current count, defaulting to zero if unseen, and add one". No special case for the first occurrence is needed.

This pattern generalises to grouping, totalling and any other accumulation keyed by name.
lessons.example_note: max(counts, key=counts.get) finds the key with the highest value — the most frequent character.

lessons.title: Dictionaries inside dictionaries
lessons.subtitle: Nested structures
lessons.concept:
A dictionary value can itself be a dict or a list, which is how structured data is represented. Access chains left to right: `data["ada"]["score"]`.

This is exactly the shape of JSON, so once you can navigate nested dicts you can navigate almost any API response or configuration file.

When the structure gets deep, use `.get()` at each level to avoid a KeyError cascade.
lessons.example_note: Note the single quotes inside the f-string braces — the outer string already uses double quotes.

lessons.title: Collections without duplicates
lessons.subtitle: Sets and set algebra
lessons.concept:
A **set** holds unique, unordered values. Duplicates vanish automatically, which makes `set(items)` the quickest way to deduplicate a list.

Membership testing is extremely fast, faster than scanning a list.

Sets support the algebra you would expect:
- `a | b` union (everything in either)
- `a & b` intersection (in both)
- `a - b` difference (in a but not b)
- `a ^ b` symmetric difference (in one but not both)

An empty set must be written `set()` — `{}` creates an empty dict.
lessons.example_code:
nums = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]
unique = set(nums)
print(unique, len(unique))

a = {1, 2, 3}
b = {3, 4, 5}
print(a | b)
print(a & b)
print(a - b)
print(a ^ b)
lessons.example_note: Sets are unordered, so use sorted(a | b) whenever the printed order needs to be predictable.

hints: Wrap each result in sorted() so the output is deterministic.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: dicts and sets
lessons.subtitle: Check what stuck before moving on
lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What happens when you read d["missing"]?
questions.explain: Square-bracket access on an absent key raises KeyError. Use d.get(key, default) to avoid it.

questions.q: What does counts[k] = counts.get(k, 0) + 1 accomplish?
options: Counts occurrences, handling the first one automatically
questions.explain: get supplies 0 for an unseen key, so no special case is needed for the first occurrence.

questions.q: What does .items() yield?
questions.explain: items() yields both parts as tuples, which is why for k, v in d.items() unpacks so neatly.

questions.q: What is the fastest way to remove duplicates from a list?
questions.explain: A set stores only unique values, so converting and back is the concise and efficient approach.

questions.q: How do you create an empty set?
questions.explain: {} creates an empty dictionary, so the set constructor must be called explicitly.

lessons.title: Packaging code under a name
lessons.subtitle: def and calling
lessons.concept:
A **function** is a named block of code you can run on demand. `def` defines one, and the indented block below is its body.

Defining a function does not run it — nothing happens until you **call** it with parentheses. That separation is the point: the logic lives in one place and runs whenever needed.

A function whose body only prints is fine, but usually you want it to hand a value back.
lessons.example_code:
def greet():
    print("hello")
    print("world")

greet()
greet()
lessons.example_note: The two calls run the body twice. Without the calls, defining greet would produce no output at all.
lessons.task: Define a function `banner()` that prints a line of ten equals signs, then call it, print `MENU`, and call it again.
lessons.solution_code:

    print("==========")

banner()
print("MENU")
banner()
hints: Define first, then call. The parentheses are what run it.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Inputs and outputs
lessons.subtitle: Parameters and return
lessons.concept:
**Parameters** are named placeholders in the definition; **arguments** are the actual values passed at the call site.

`return` sends a value back and ends the function immediately. A function with no `return` gives back `None`.

The difference between printing and returning is fundamental: printing shows something to a human, returning hands a value to the rest of your program so it can be used further.
lessons.example_code:
def area(width, height):
    return width * height

def shout(text):
    return text.upper() + "!"

result = area(3, 4)
print(result)
print(area(10, 2) + area(1, 1))
print(shout("hello"))
lessons.example_note: Because area returns a number, its results can be added together. A printing version could not be used this way.

hints: Use return, not print, so the caller receives the value.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Optional and named arguments
lessons.subtitle: Defaults and keywords
lessons.concept:
A parameter can have a **default value**, making it optional: `def greet(name, greeting="Hello")`. Parameters with defaults must come after those without.

Arguments can also be passed **by name** at the call site, which makes the meaning obvious and lets you skip earlier optional parameters: `power(base=2, exponent=8)`.

One trap: never use a mutable default like `[]`, because the same list is reused across every call. Use `None` and create the list inside instead.
lessons.example_code:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello", punct="!"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}{punct}"

print(greet("Ada"))
print(greet("Alan", "Good morning"))
print(greet("Grace", punct="."))
print(greet(greeting="Hi", name="Cy"))
lessons.example_note: Keyword arguments can be given in any order, which is why the last call works.

lessons.title: Where names live
lessons.subtitle: Local and global scope
lessons.concept:
Variables created inside a function are **local** to it: they exist only while the call runs and are invisible outside.

A function can *read* names from the enclosing module, but assigning to one creates a new local variable instead of changing the outer one. That is deliberate — it stops functions from quietly corrupting shared state.

The cleaner design is almost always to take values in as parameters and hand results back with `return`, rather than reaching outside.
lessons.example_code:
count = 10

def show():
    print("can read:", count)

def attempt():
    count = 99
    print("local:", count)

show()
attempt()
print("outer still:", count)
lessons.example_note: attempt() created its own count. The module-level count was untouched.

lessons.title: Any number of arguments
lessons.subtitle: *args and **kwargs
lessons.concept:
`*args` collects any number of positional arguments into a **tuple**. `**kwargs` collects any number of named arguments into a **dict**.

The names are conventional, not required — the asterisks do the work.

The same syntax works in reverse at a call site: `f(*my_list)` spreads a list into separate arguments, and `f(**my_dict)` spreads a dict into keyword arguments.
lessons.example_note: total(*values) spreads the list, so it behaves like total(4, 5, 6) rather than passing one list.

lessons.title: Functions without names
lessons.subtitle: lambda expressions
lessons.concept:
A `lambda` is a small anonymous function written as a single expression: `lambda x: x * 2`. It has no name and no `return` — the expression *is* the result.

Lambdas exist for the moments when a function is needed as an argument and defining a full one would be noise. The classic use is the `key=` parameter of `sorted`.

If a lambda needs more than one expression, use `def`. Readability wins.
lessons.example_code:
double = lambda x: x * 2
print(double(5))

words = ["banana", "fig", "cherry"]
print(sorted(words, key=lambda w: len(w)))

pairs = [("ada", 91), ("bob", 78)]
print(sorted(pairs, key=lambda p: p[1]))
print(sorted(pairs, key=lambda p: -p[1]))
lessons.example_note: Negating the key is the concise way to sort descending by a numeric field.
lessons.task: Given `people = [("ada", 36), ("bob", 24), ("cy", 45)]`, print them sorted by age ascending, then sorted by name length, using lambdas.
lessons.solution_code:
people = [("ada", 36), ("bob", 24), ("cy", 45)]

print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1]))

lessons.title: Documenting and self-calling
lessons.subtitle: Docstrings and recursion
lessons.concept:
A **docstring** is a string literal on the first line of a function body. Tools and `help()` read it, so it is the conventional place to say what a function does.

A **recursive** function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. Every recursion needs a **base case** that returns without recursing, or it never stops.

Factorial is the classic example: `n! = n × (n-1)!`, with `0! = 1` as the base case.
lessons.example_note: Each call waits for the one it made. factorial(5) unwinds to 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: functions

lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What does a function return when it has no return statement?
questions.explain: Every Python function returns something; without an explicit return that value is None.

questions.q: What is the difference between printing and returning?
options: print shows a value to the user; return hands it back for further use
questions.explain: A returned value can be stored, combined or passed on. A printed value has already left the program.

questions.q: What does *args collect?
options: A tuple of extra positional arguments
questions.explain: The single asterisk gathers any number of positional arguments into a tuple; ** gathers named ones into a dict.

questions.q: What happens when a function assigns to a module-level name?
options: A new local variable is created instead
questions.explain: Assignment inside a function creates a local binding by default, which prevents accidental changes to shared state.

questions.q: What must every recursive function have?
options: A base case that returns without recursing
questions.explain: Without a base case the recursion never terminates and eventually exhausts the call stack.

lessons.title: Building a list in one line
lessons.subtitle: List comprehensions
lessons.concept:
A **list comprehension** builds a new list from an existing sequence in a single expression:

`[expression for item in sequence]`

Read it left to right: "give me this expression, for each item". It replaces the three-line create-empty-list-then-append pattern and reads much closer to the intent.

The expression can be anything: arithmetic, a method call, an f-string, even another comprehension.
lessons.example_code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]

print([n * n for n in nums])
print([n * 2 for n in nums])
print([str(n) for n in nums])
print([f"#{n}" for n in nums])
print([len(w) for w in ["hi", "hello"]])
lessons.example_note: The original list is never modified — a comprehension always produces a new one.
lessons.task: Given `nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`, use comprehensions to print the cubes, the values as strings, and each value doubled then decreased by one.
lessons.solution_code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

print([n ** 3 for n in nums])
print([str(n) for n in nums])
print([n * 2 - 1 for n in nums])
hints: The expression sits before the for keyword.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Keeping only some items
lessons.subtitle: Comprehensions with if
lessons.concept:
Adding `if condition` at the end filters the source: only items satisfying it reach the output.

`[expression for item in sequence if condition]`

There is a second, different placement: an `if/else` **before** the `for` transforms every item rather than filtering. `[x if x > 0 else 0 for x in nums]` keeps the length the same; `[x for x in nums if x > 0]` shortens it. Recognising which is which is the key skill here.
lessons.example_code:
nums = [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3]

print([n for n in nums if n > 0])
print([n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0])
print([n if n > 0 else 0 for n in nums])
print([w.upper() for w in ["hi", "a", "yes"] if len(w) > 1])
lessons.example_note: Filter form: if at the end, output may be shorter. Transform form: if/else at the front, output is the same length.
lessons.task: Given `words = ["python", "c", "rust", "go", "java"]`, print the uppercase forms of only the words longer than three letters, and then the count kept.
lessons.solution_code:
words = ["python", "c", "rust", "go", "java"]
long_words = [w.upper() for w in words if len(w) > 3]

print(long_words)
print("kept", len(long_words))
hints: Transform with .upper() and filter with if len(w) > 3.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Comprehensions for dicts and sets
lessons.subtitle: Other comprehension forms
lessons.concept:
The same syntax builds dictionaries and sets.

A **dict comprehension** uses `key: value` before the `for`: `{w: len(w) for w in words}`.

A **set comprehension** uses braces without a colon: `{w[0] for w in words}` — duplicates collapse automatically.

Watch the braces: `{}` with a colon is a dict, without is a set.
lessons.example_code:
words = ["apple", "fig", "cherry"]

print({w: len(w) for w in words})
print({w[0] for w in words})
print({n: n * n for n in range(1, 5)})

scores = {"ada": 91, "bob": 45}
print({k: v for k, v in scores.items() if v > 50})
lessons.example_note: The last example filters a dictionary by its values, keeping only the entries that pass.

lessons.title: Indexes and pairs
lessons.subtitle: enumerate and zip
lessons.concept:
Two built-ins remove the need for manual index bookkeeping.

`enumerate(items)` yields `(index, item)` pairs, with an optional `start=`. It is the correct answer whenever you find yourself writing `for i in range(len(items))`.

`zip(a, b)` yields tuples pairing corresponding elements, stopping at the shorter input. `zip(*pairs)` unzips back into separate sequences.
lessons.example_note: dict(zip(keys, values)) is the neatest way to build a dictionary from two parallel lists.
lessons.task: Given `items = ["bread", "milk", "eggs"]` and `prices = [2.5, 1.2, 3.0]`, print each as `1. bread 2.5` numbered from one, then print the total price.
lessons.solution_code:
items = ["bread", "milk", "eggs"]
prices = [2.5, 1.2, 3.0]

for i, (item, price) in enumerate(zip(items, prices), start=1):
    print(f"{i}. {item} {price}")

print("total:", sum(prices))
hints: Combining enumerate with zip needs parentheses around the inner pair.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Values produced on demand
lessons.subtitle: Generator expressions and yield
lessons.concept:
A **generator expression** looks like a list comprehension with parentheses: `(n * n for n in nums)`. It does not build a list — it produces values one at a time, as they are requested.

That makes it memory-efficient for large sequences, and it is why `sum(n * n for n in nums)` needs no brackets at all.

A **generator function** uses `yield` instead of `return`. Each `yield` hands back one value and pauses, resuming from that point on the next request.
lessons.example_code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]

squares = (n * n for n in nums)
print(sum(squares))

print(sum(n for n in range(1, 101)))
print(max(len(w) for w in ["hi", "hello"]))

def countdown(n):
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1

print(list(countdown(4)))
lessons.example_note: A generator is exhausted after one pass — summing squares twice would give 0 the second time.
lessons.task: Using generator expressions, print the sum of the squares from 1 to 10, the count of even numbers below 50, and the longest word length in a short list.
lessons.solution_code:
print(sum(n * n for n in range(1, 11)))
print(sum(1 for n in range(50) if n % 2 == 0))
print(max(len(w) for w in ["fig", "banana", "kiwi"]))
hints: sum(1 for ... if ...) is a compact way to count matches.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Questions about whole sequences
lessons.subtitle: any, all and sorted keys
lessons.concept:
`any(iterable)` is True when at least one item is truthy; `all(iterable)` is True when every item is. Combined with a generator expression they express conditions over whole collections in one readable line.

Both short-circuit: `any` stops at the first True, `all` at the first False.

`sorted` accepts a `key` function, and returning a **tuple** from it sorts by several fields at once — negate a numeric field to reverse just that one.
lessons.example_code:
nums = [4, 8, 15, 16]

print(any(n > 15 for n in nums))
print(all(n > 0 for n in nums))
print(any(n < 0 for n in nums))

people = [("bob", 30), ("ada", 30), ("cy", 25)]
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0])))
lessons.example_note: The tuple key sorts by age descending, then by name ascending within each age.
lessons.task: Given `nums = [3, 7, 11, 14]`, print whether any are even, whether all are positive, and whether all are odd.
lessons.solution_code:

print(all(n > 0 for n in nums))

questions.q: What does [n for n in nums if n > 0] produce?
options: Only the positive values — possibly shorter

questions.q: What does [n if n > 0 else 0 for n in nums] produce?

questions.q: What is the difference between (n for n in x) and [n for n in x]?
options: The first is a generator producing values on demand; the second builds a list immediately

lessons.title: Defining a new kind of thing
lessons.subtitle: class and instances
lessons.concept:
A **class** describes a kind of thing; an **instance** is one particular example of it. `class Dog:` defines the kind, `Dog()` creates an instance.

The `__init__` method runs automatically whenever a new instance is created. Its first parameter is always `self`, which refers to the instance being built. `self.name = name` stores a value **on that instance**, where it stays for as long as the object lives.

Those stored values are called **attributes**.
lessons.example_code:
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        self.name = name
        self.breed = breed

rex = Dog("Rex", "collie")
fido = Dog("Fido", "pug")

print(rex.name, rex.breed)
print(fido.name, fido.breed)
lessons.example_note: You never pass self yourself — Python supplies it automatically when you call through an instance.
lessons.task: Define a `Book` class storing `title` and `pages`. Create two books and print each as `Dune has 412 pages`.
lessons.solution_code:
class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, pages):
        self.title = title
        self.pages = pages

a = Book("Dune", 412)
b = Book("Anthem", 105)

print(f"{a.title} has {a.pages} pages")
print(f"{b.title} has {b.pages} pages")
lessons.expected_output:
Dune has 412 pages
Anthem has 105 pages
hints: Assign both parameters to self inside __init__.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Behaviour attached to data
lessons.subtitle: Instance methods
lessons.concept:
A **method** is a function defined inside a class. Its first parameter is `self`, giving it access to that instance’s attributes.

This is the whole idea of object-oriented programming: the data and the operations that make sense on that data live together. Instead of `is_long(book)` you write `book.is_long()`, and the method already knows which book it is talking about.

Methods can also modify attributes, changing the object’s state.
lessons.example_note: increment changes the instance; is_high only reports on it. Both reach the same self.count.

lessons.title: Deciding how an object prints
lessons.subtitle: __str__ and __repr__
lessons.concept:
Printing an object without help gives something useless like `<__main__.Book object at 0x7f...>`.

Defining `__str__` fixes that: it returns the string shown by `print()` and `str()`. `__repr__` is the developer-facing version, used in the interactive prompt and when printing a list of objects.

Methods with double underscores are called **dunder** methods. Python calls them for you at the right moments — you define them, you rarely call them directly.
lessons.example_note: Printing a list uses __repr__ for the elements, which is why both are worth defining.

lessons.title: Shared versus per-object data
lessons.subtitle: Class attributes
lessons.concept:
An attribute assigned directly in the class body is a **class attribute**: one copy shared by every instance. An attribute assigned via `self` in `__init__` is an **instance attribute**: each object gets its own.

Use class attributes for constants and shared counters, instance attributes for anything describing one particular object.

The common trap: a mutable class attribute like a list is shared, so appending through one instance affects all of them.
lessons.example_code:
class Dog:
    species = "Canis familiaris"
    count = 0

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        Dog.count += 1

a = Dog("Rex")
b = Dog("Fido")

print(a.species, b.species)
print(Dog.count)
print(a.name, b.name)
lessons.example_note: Dog.count is incremented on the class, so it counts every instance ever created.
lessons.task: Define a `Student` class with a class attribute `school = "Central High"` and a class-level `total` counter. Create three students and print the school, each name, and the total.

    school = "Central High"
    total = 0

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        Student.total += 1

names = ["ada", "bob", "cy"]
students = [Student(n) for n in names]

print(Student.school)
for s in students:
    print(s.name)
print("total:", Student.total)

Central High
ada
bob
cy
total: 3
hints: Increment the counter on the class, not on self.
Print exactly the lines shown — spacing and punctuation are compared character for character.

lessons.title: Building on an existing class
lessons.subtitle: Subclasses and super()
lessons.concept:
**Inheritance** lets a class reuse and extend another. `class Cat(Animal):` makes Cat a subclass: it gets everything Animal has, and may add or replace parts.

`super().__init__(...)` calls the parent’s initialiser, so shared setup is written once. Defining a method with the same name as the parent’s **overrides** it.

The test for inheritance is "is a": a Cat *is an* Animal. When the relationship is "has a" instead, store the other object as an attribute rather than inheriting.
lessons.example_note: describe is defined only on Animal, yet each subclass gets its own speak used inside it. That is polymorphism.

lessons.title: Controlling access to attributes
lessons.subtitle: Underscores and @property
lessons.concept:
Python has no truly private attributes; it uses convention. A single leading underscore (`_balance`) means "internal, please do not touch from outside".

`@property` turns a method into something that reads like an attribute: `account.balance` with no parentheses, but computed on demand. A matching `@name.setter` intercepts assignment, which is where validation belongs.

This gives you the freedom to start with a plain attribute and add logic later without changing any calling code.
lessons.example_note: The setter rejected the negative value, so the balance stayed at 250.

class Account:
    def __init__(self, balance=0):
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):

            print("insufficient")
            return
        self.balance -= amount

a.deposit(50)

a.withdraw(30)

a.withdraw(500)

lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What is self in a method?
options: A reference to the instance the method was called on
questions.explain: self is how a method reaches the particular object it was invoked on, and Python passes it automatically.

questions.q: When does __init__ run?
options: Every time a method is called
Automatically when a new instance is created
questions.explain: __init__ is the initialiser, run once per instance at creation time to set up its attributes.

questions.q: What is the difference between a class attribute and an instance attribute?
options: A class attribute is shared by all instances; an instance attribute belongs to one object
questions.explain: Class attributes live on the class itself and are shared; self.x creates per-object storage.

questions.q: What does super().__init__() do?
questions.explain: It delegates to the parent so shared setup lives in one place rather than being duplicated.

questions.q: What does @property achieve?
options: Lets a method be read like an attribute, with no parentheses
questions.explain: It exposes computed values with attribute syntax, so logic can be added later without changing calling code.

lessons.title: When things go wrong
lessons.subtitle: try, except, finally
lessons.concept:
An **exception** is raised when an operation cannot proceed — dividing by zero, converting `"abc"` to an int, reading a missing dict key. Left alone it stops the program.

`try` runs risky code; `except` catches a failure and decides what to do. Catch **specific** types (`ValueError`, `ZeroDivisionError`) rather than everything, so real bugs are not silently hidden.

`else` runs when no exception occurred, and `finally` always runs — ideal for cleanup.
lessons.example_note: `as err` captures the exception object so you can inspect its message.

hints: int("3.5") raises ValueError too, because the string is not a whole number.

lessons.title: Reporting problems yourself
lessons.subtitle: raise and custom exceptions
lessons.concept:
`raise` signals that a function cannot do what was asked. It is better than returning `None` or `-1`, because the caller cannot accidentally ignore it.

Choose the type that fits: `ValueError` for a bad value, `TypeError` for a wrong type. For domain-specific problems, define your own by subclassing `Exception` — the class body can be just `pass`.

A custom exception type lets callers catch exactly your error and nothing else.
lessons.example_note: Multiple except blocks let each failure be handled differently.

lessons.title: Using code written by others
lessons.subtitle: import and the standard library
lessons.concept:
Python ships with a large **standard library**. `import math` makes a module available as `math.sqrt(...)`; `from math import sqrt` brings a single name in directly.

Useful modules to know early:
- `math` for sqrt, floor, ceil, pi
- `random` for choice, randint, shuffle (seed it for reproducible output)
- `datetime` for dates and times
- `collections` for Counter and defaultdict

Always import at the top of the file.
lessons.example_code:
import math
from collections import Counter

print(math.sqrt(144))
print(math.floor(3.7), math.ceil(3.2))
print(round(math.pi, 4))

words = "a b a c b a".split()
print(Counter(words))
print(Counter(words).most_common(2))
lessons.example_note: Counter is a dict subclass built for exactly the counting pattern you wrote by hand earlier.

lessons.title: Wrapping a function in another
lessons.subtitle: Decorators
lessons.concept:
Functions are objects: they can be passed around and returned like any value. A **decorator** takes a function and returns a replacement that usually calls the original with extra behaviour around it.

The `@decorator` line above a `def` is shorthand for `f = decorator(f)`.

The inner wrapper takes `*args, **kwargs` so it works with any signature. This is the machinery behind `@property` and `@staticmethod`.
lessons.example_note: add is now the wrapper, which prints, calls the original, prints again, and passes the result through.

lessons.title: Classic algorithms
lessons.subtitle: Binary search and bubble sort
lessons.concept:
Two algorithms worth implementing once by hand.

**Binary search** finds a value in a *sorted* list by repeatedly halving the range. Twenty steps suffice for a million items, because each comparison discards half the remaining possibilities.

**Bubble sort** repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs. It is slow and nobody uses it in production, but writing it teaches how sorting works from the inside.

In real code use `in` and `sorted()`; the point here is understanding the cost of each.
lessons.example_note: Returning -1 for "not found" is a common convention, mirroring str.find.

lessons.title: Processing multi-line text
lessons.subtitle: Line-by-line parsing
lessons.concept:
Real data arrives as text: log files, CSV exports, configuration. The pattern is always the same — split into lines, split each line into fields, convert types, accumulate.

`text.strip().split("\n")` gives the lines; `line.split(",")` gives the fields. Skip blanks, and remember every field starts as a **string** even when it looks like a number.

A triple-quoted string is a convenient stand-in for a file while you are learning the shape of the code.
lessons.example_code:
data = """ada,91
bob,78
cy,95"""

total = 0
for line in data.strip().split("\n"):
    name, score = line.split(",")
    score = int(score)
    total += score
    print(f"{name}: {score}")

print("average:", total / 3)
lessons.example_note: Unpacking directly into name, score works because each line has exactly two fields.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: advanced Python

questions.q: Why catch a specific exception rather than using a bare except?
options: A bare except hides genuine bugs, including typos and interrupts
Bare except is a syntax error
questions.explain: Catching everything swallows unrelated errors, making failures invisible and debugging far harder.

questions.q: When does a finally block run?
options: Always, whether or not an exception occurred
questions.explain: finally always executes, which makes it the right place for cleanup that must not be skipped.

questions.q: What is @decorator shorthand for?
options: f = decorator(f) applied to the function below
questions.explain: The decorator receives the function and its return value replaces the original name.

questions.q: Why is binary search so much faster than scanning?
options: Each comparison discards half the remaining possibilities
questions.explain: Halving the search space each step gives logarithmic growth, so a million items need only about twenty comparisons.

questions.q: What must be true for binary search to work?
questions.explain: The algorithm relies on order to decide which half to discard, so an unsorted list gives wrong answers.

lessons.title: The shape of a C program
lessons.subtitle: main, printf and #include
lessons.concept:
C is **compiled**: a compiler translates your entire file into machine code before anything runs, and refuses to produce a program if the code is malformed. That feedback loop is slower than Python’s but catches whole categories of mistake before execution.

Every C program begins at a function called `main`. `int main(void)` means "takes no arguments, returns an integer" — that integer is the exit status, where `0` means success.

`printf` lives in the standard input/output library, so `#include <stdio.h>` must appear first. Without it the compiler does not know what printf is.

Two things Python did not need: every statement ends with a **semicolon**, and printf does **not** add a newline — you write `\n` yourself.
lessons.example_note: The braces mark the body of main. Omit the \n and the next output continues on the same line.
lessons.task: Print exactly `Hello, world!` followed by a newline.
hints: printf("Hello, world!\n"); — note the semicolon.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Several lines of output
lessons.subtitle: Statements and newlines
lessons.concept:
Statements execute in order, top to bottom. Since printf adds nothing of its own, the layout of your output is entirely determined by the `\n` characters you include.

This means three printf calls without newlines produce one line, and one printf with two newlines produces two lines. C does not care how your source is arranged — only what characters you actually emit.
lessons.example_note: The first two calls join into `one line` because neither ended with a newline until the second.

lessons.title: Notes for humans
lessons.subtitle: Both comment styles
lessons.concept:
C has two comment forms. `//` comments run to the end of the line. `/* ... */` comments can span multiple lines, and are the older style.

Block comments cannot be nested — the first `*/` closes the comment, which occasionally bites people trying to comment out a region that already contains one.
lessons.example_note: Comments are stripped before compilation, so they cannot affect behaviour.
