lessons.title: Special characters
lessons.subtitle: Escape sequences
lessons.concept:
Because printf takes a plain string, awkward characters need escaping:

- `\n` newline
- `\t` tab
- `\\` a literal backslash
- `\"` a literal double quote
- `%%` a literal percent sign (printf-specific)

That last one is unique to printf: `%` starts a format specifier, so printing a real percent sign requires doubling it.
lessons.example_note: The backslash and the doubled percent are instructions to the parser, so they never appear in the output.

lessons.title: Inserting values into text
lessons.subtitle: Format specifiers
lessons.concept:
printf’s real purpose is substitution. A **format specifier** in the string marks a slot, and the values follow as extra arguments:

- `%d` int
- `%f` double (`%.2f` for two decimals)
- `%c` a single char
- `%s` a string
- `%zu` a size_t

The specifiers must match the arguments **in order and in type**. A mismatch is undefined behaviour — you may get garbage rather than an error — which is why compiler warnings matter here.
lessons.example_note: Single quotes mean a char; double quotes mean a string. They are different types in C.

lessons.title: Lining columns up
lessons.subtitle: Field widths
lessons.concept:
A number between `%` and the type letter sets a **minimum field width**, padding with spaces. `%8d` right-aligns in eight columns; `%-8d` left-aligns. Combined with `%s` this produces neat tables without counting spaces by hand.

For floats, `%8.2f` means "eight columns wide, two decimal places".
lessons.example_note: The minus sign left-aligns. Without it, text is pushed to the right of the field.

lessons.title: What main gives back
lessons.subtitle: Exit status
lessons.concept:
`return 0;` at the end of main reports success to whatever launched the program. A non-zero value signals failure, and shell scripts use it to decide whether to continue.

Since C99 you may omit the return and 0 is assumed, but writing it is clearer.

The `void` in `int main(void)` explicitly says "no parameters". The alternative form `int main(int argc, char *argv[])` receives command-line arguments.

lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.

questions.q: Why is #include <stdio.h> required?
options: It tells the compiler what printf is
questions.explain: The header declares printf and friends. Without it the compiler has never heard of the function you are calling.

questions.q: What does return 0 from main mean?
questions.explain: Zero is the conventional success exit status; non-zero signals failure to whatever launched the program.

questions.q: Does printf add a newline?
questions.explain: Unlike Python’s print, printf emits exactly the characters you specify and nothing more.

questions.q: How do you print a literal percent sign with printf?
questions.explain: A single % begins a format specifier, so it must be doubled to produce one in the output.

questions.q: What does %-8s do?
questions.explain: The width sets a minimum field size and the minus sign switches the padding to the right, left-aligning the text.

lessons.title: Declaring variables
lessons.subtitle: Types are fixed
lessons.concept:
In C every variable’s type is decided at declaration and never changes. You write the type, then the name: `int count = 5;`

The types you need first:
- `int` — whole number, typically 32 bits
- `double` — floating point with good precision
- `char` — a single character, in single quotes

A declaration without an initialiser leaves **garbage** in the variable, not zero. Reading an uninitialised variable is undefined behaviour, so always initialise.
lessons.example_note: The type is permanent; the value is not. year can be reassigned but always holds an int.
lessons.task:
Declare `int items = 7;` and `double price = 2.5;`, compute the total as a double, and print:

`items: 7`
`price: 2.50`
`total: 17.50`
hints: int * double promotes to double, so declare total as double.

lessons.title: The integer division trap
lessons.subtitle: Casting between types
lessons.concept:
This catches everyone once. Dividing two `int`s performs **integer division**: the fractional part is discarded, not rounded. `7 / 2` is `3`, full stop.

To get a real answer, at least one operand must be floating point. The usual tool is a **cast**: `(double)a / b` treats a as a double for that expression, so the division happens in floating point.

`%` gives the remainder and works only on integers.
lessons.example_note: Casting either operand is enough — the other is promoted automatically.
lessons.task: With `int total = 47;` and `int people = 6;` print the whole share, the remainder, and the exact average to three decimals.
hints: The first line wants the truncating division; the third needs a cast.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: How much space a type takes
lessons.subtitle: sizeof and ranges
lessons.concept:
Every type occupies a fixed number of bytes, and `sizeof(type)` reports it. Typical values on a 64-bit system: `char` 1, `int` 4, `double` 8, pointers 8.

The C standard sets only **minimums**, so sizes can differ between platforms — which is exactly why `sizeof` exists rather than hard-coded numbers.

`sizeof` returns a `size_t`, printed with `%zu`. It becomes essential later for arrays and memory allocation.
lessons.example_note: sizeof is evaluated at compile time, so it costs nothing at run time.
lessons.task: Print the sizes of char, short, int and double, each on its own line as `int 4`.
hints: Use %zu for every sizeof result.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Values that must not change
lessons.subtitle: const and #define
lessons.concept:
Marking a variable `const` promises it will never be reassigned, and the compiler enforces it. That turns an accidental modification into a compile error rather than a mysterious bug.

`#define NAME value` is the older alternative: a preprocessor substitution performed before compilation. It has no type and no scope, so `const` is preferred in modern C.

By convention, both are named in capitals.
lessons.example_note: Attempting TAX_RATE = 0.3; would refuse to compile, which is the entire point.
lessons.task: Define `SECONDS_PER_DAY` as 86400 with #define, declare `const int days = 3;`, and print the total seconds.
hints: The #define goes above main, outside any function.

lessons.title: Characters are numbers
lessons.subtitle: char arithmetic and ASCII
lessons.concept:
A `char` is a one-byte integer holding a character **code**. `'A'` is 65 and `'a'` is 97 in ASCII, which means arithmetic on characters is meaningful.

`'a' - 32` gives `'A'`, and `ch - '0'` converts a digit character to its numeric value. `'A' + 1` is `'B'`.

Printing the same char with `%c` shows the letter and with `%d` shows the code — same value, different interpretation.
lessons.example_note: digit - '0' works because the digit codes are consecutive: '7' is exactly seven past '0'.
lessons.task: Given `char ch = 'd';` print the character, its code, its uppercase form, and the numeric value of the digit character `'9'`.
hints: Subtract 32 to convert lowercase to uppercase.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: When numbers run out of room
lessons.subtitle: Overflow and unsigned types
lessons.concept:
An `int` has a fixed range, roughly ±2.1 billion. Exceeding it is **overflow**, and for signed types it is undefined behaviour — the compiler is entitled to assume it never happens.

`unsigned int` cannot be negative and wraps around predictably instead. `long long` gives a much larger range when you need it.

The practical lesson: choose a type wide enough for the values you expect, and be wary of subtracting from unsigned values, because the result can never go below zero.
lessons.example_note: Subtracting one from an unsigned zero wraps to the maximum value — a classic loop bug.

hints: Include <limits.h> for the INT_MAX macros and use %u for unsigned.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: types
lessons.subtitle: Check what stuck before moving on
lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What is 7 / 2 when both are int?
questions.explain: Integer division truncates toward zero, discarding the fraction entirely.

questions.q: How do you get 3.5 from int a = 7, b = 2?
questions.explain: Casting one operand forces the division to happen in floating point; the other is promoted automatically.

questions.q: What is in an uninitialised local int?
options: Whatever garbage was in that memory
questions.explain: C does not zero local variables, so reading one before assignment is undefined behaviour.

questions.q: What does '7' - '0' give?
questions.explain: Digit character codes are consecutive, so subtracting '0' converts a digit character to its numeric value.

questions.q: Which specifier prints a sizeof result?
questions.explain: sizeof yields a size_t, whose matching specifier is %zu. Using %d is a type mismatch.

lessons.title: The arithmetic operators
lessons.subtitle: Five operators and their quirks
lessons.concept:
C has five arithmetic operators: `+ - * / %`.

There is no exponentiation operator — `pow()` from `<math.h>` covers that, or you multiply by hand.

`/` behaves differently depending on the operand types: integer division truncates, floating-point division does not. `%` requires integers and gives the remainder.

Unary minus negates. Note there is no separate integer-division operator as in Python; the types decide.
lessons.example_note: The same / symbol means two different operations depending on whether the operands are integers.
lessons.task: With `int a = 23` and `int b = 4`, print the sum, difference, product, quotient, remainder and exact division to two decimals — six lines.
hints: Only the last line needs a cast.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Adding one, two ways
lessons.subtitle: Prefix and postfix
lessons.concept:
`i++` and `++i` both add one to i, but they **evaluate** to different things. `i++` yields the old value then increments; `++i` increments then yields the new value.

As a standalone statement they are identical. Inside a larger expression they differ, which is why mixing them into complex expressions is discouraged.

`--` works the same way. The augmented operators `+= -= *= /= %=` cover the general case.
lessons.example_note: i++ printed 5 then left i at 6; ++j printed 6 immediately. Both variables end at 6.
lessons.task: Start `int n = 8;`. Print n, then n++ and n again, then ++n and n again — five lines total.
hints: Postfix reports the old value; prefix reports the new one.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Comparing values
lessons.subtitle: Relational operators and truth
lessons.concept:
The six comparisons are `== != < > <= >=`. Each produces `1` for true and `0` for false — C had no boolean type until C99, and even now `bool` is a thin layer over an integer.

That means **any non-zero value is true** and zero is false. `if (5)` is always taken.

The notorious pitfall: `=` assigns and `==` compares. `if (x = 5)` assigns 5 to x and is always true, which compiles happily. Enabling warnings catches it.
lessons.example_note: Comparisons print as 1 or 0 because that is literally what they evaluate to.
lessons.task: With `int n = 15;` print whether it equals 15, is under 10, is at least 15, and differs from 20 — four lines of 1 or 0.
hints: Print each comparison directly with %d.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Combining conditions
lessons.subtitle: &&, || and !
lessons.concept:
`&&` is logical and, `||` is logical or, `!` is negation. All treat any non-zero value as true and produce 1 or 0.

Both `&&` and `||` **short-circuit**: `&&` stops at the first false operand, `||` at the first true one. The remaining operands are not evaluated at all.

This is not merely an optimisation — it is a guarantee you can rely on. `if (n != 0 && 100 / n > 2)` is safe precisely because the division is skipped when n is zero.
lessons.example_note: The last line does not crash: && never evaluates the division because n != 0 is already false.
lessons.task: With `int temp = 22` and `int raining = 1`, print whether it is warm and dry, warm or dry, and not raining. Treat warm as above 20.
hints: Dry is simply !raining.

lessons.title: Working with individual bits
lessons.subtitle: Bitwise operators
lessons.concept:
C gives direct access to the bits of an integer:

- `&` and — 1 only where both bits are 1
- `|` or — 1 where either is
- `^` xor — 1 where exactly one is
- `~` not — flips every bit
- `<<` and `>>` shift left and right

Shifting left by n multiplies by 2ⁿ; shifting right divides. These are the tools for flags, masks and low-level protocol work.

Do not confuse `&` with `&&`: the first works bit by bit, the second on whole truth values.
lessons.example_note: 12 is 1100 and 10 is 1010 in binary, so & gives 1000 (8) and | gives 1110 (14).
lessons.task: With `int flags = 0b1010;` (or 10), print the result of anding with 12, oring with 5, xoring with 15, shifting left once and shifting right once.
hints: Each operator applies to the binary representation.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Which operation binds tighter
lessons.subtitle: Precedence and parentheses
lessons.concept:
C has fifteen precedence levels. The ones that matter daily, tightest first:

1. `++ -- !` and casts
2. `* / %`
3. `+ -`
4. `<< >>`
5. `< > <= >=`
6. `== !=`
7. `&`, then `^`, then `|`
8. `&&`, then `||`
9. `?:` and assignment

The surprise is that the bitwise operators bind **looser** than comparisons, so `a & 1 == 0` means `a & (1 == 0)` — almost never what you wanted. Parenthesise bitwise expressions.
lessons.example_note: The last two differ: without parentheses the comparison happens first, giving 8 & 0 which is 0.
hints: Division is left-associative, so 20 / 4 / 5 is (20 / 4) / 5.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: A choice inside an expression
lessons.subtitle: The conditional operator
lessons.concept:
The conditional operator `?:` is C’s only three-operand operator:

`condition ? value_if_true : value_if_false`

Unlike `if`, it is an **expression**, so it produces a value usable in an assignment or directly inside printf. It is the concise way to choose between two values.

Keep it simple. Nesting several is legal but rapidly unreadable — use `if` for anything with real branching.
lessons.example_note: Both branches must have compatible types, since the whole thing must have one type.

lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What does i++ evaluate to?
questions.explain: Postfix yields the value before the increment; ++i yields the value after it. Both leave i one larger.

questions.q: What does a comparison like x < 10 produce in C?
questions.explain: C comparisons are integer expressions producing 1 or 0, which is why they can be printed with %d.

questions.q: Why is 8 & 1 == 0 surprising?
options: The comparison binds tighter, so it means 8 & (1 == 0)
questions.explain: Bitwise operators sit below comparisons in precedence, so bitwise expressions almost always need parentheses.

questions.q: What is the difference between & and &&?
options: & works bit by bit; && works on whole truth values and short-circuits
questions.explain: & combines corresponding bits of both operands; && evaluates truth and may skip the right operand entirely.

questions.q: What does 1 << 10 equal?
questions.explain: Shifting left by n multiplies by 2 to the power n, and 2 to the power 10 is 1024.

lessons.title: Branching
lessons.subtitle: if and else
lessons.concept:
`if` takes a condition in **parentheses** and a block in **braces**. Indentation is purely cosmetic here — the braces define the block.

Omitting braces for a single statement is legal, but it is a well-known source of bugs: adding a second line later silently leaves it outside the if. Always use braces.

Since the condition is just an integer test, `if (count)` means "if count is non-zero".
lessons.example_note: if (count) is idiomatic C for "count is non-zero" — no comparison needed.
lessons.task: With `int n = 12;` print `even` or `odd`, then `big` or `small` treating over 10 as big.
hints: Use == not = in the comparison.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Many branches
lessons.subtitle: else if chains
lessons.concept:
C has no `elif` keyword — it simply allows another `if` directly after `else`, giving `else if`.

Conditions are tested **in order** and the first match wins. Order therefore matters: with descending thresholds, put the highest first, or a broader condition will capture everything below it.

The final `else` is optional but usually wise, since it documents the fallback case.
lessons.example_note: 74 fails the first two tests and passes the third. Reversing the order would print C for 95 as well.
lessons.task: With `int temp = 5;` print `freezing` below 0, `cold` below 10, `mild` below 25, otherwise `hot`.
hints: Ascending thresholds mean each else if only sees what fell through.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Matching one value against many
lessons.subtitle: switch, case and break
lessons.concept:
`switch` compares one integer or character against a list of `case` labels. It is often clearer than a long `else if` chain when every test compares the same variable.

The crucial detail is **fall-through**: without a `break`, execution continues into the next case. That is occasionally useful for grouping labels, and is otherwise a classic bug.

`default` handles anything unmatched. `switch` works only on integer types — not on strings or floats.
lessons.example_note: Case 6 has no body, so it falls through into case 7 — the intentional use of fall-through for grouping.
lessons.task: With `char grade = 'B';` use switch to print `excellent` for A, `good` for B, `pass` for C, otherwise `fail`.
hints: Character literals in single quotes work as case labels.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Conditions within conditions
lessons.subtitle: Nesting and flattening
lessons.concept:
An `if` may contain another. Each level adds indentation and one more thing for the reader to hold in mind.

Deep nesting is a smell. Two techniques flatten it: combine conditions with `&&`, or use an **early return** to handle the failure case first and let the main path continue unindented.

Early returns are particularly effective in functions with several validation checks.
lessons.example_note: The flattened version handles only the success case, which is often all you need.

lessons.title: A real boolean type
lessons.subtitle: stdbool.h
lessons.concept:
C99 added `<stdbool.h>`, which defines `bool`, `true` and `false`. Underneath it is still an integer, but the names document intent far better than `int flag = 1;`.

Use `bool` for anything genuinely two-valued. Print it with `%d` (giving 1 or 0) or convert it yourself with the conditional operator.

Modern C code uses `bool` throughout; older code you will read uses plain `int`.
lessons.example_note: A bool assigned any non-zero value becomes exactly 1, which makes comparisons predictable.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: conditionals
lessons.subtitle: Check what stuck before moving on
lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What is wrong with if (x = 5)?
options: It assigns 5 to x and is always true
questions.explain: A single = assigns and the expression evaluates to 5, which is non-zero and therefore always true.

questions.q: What happens in a switch case without break?
options: Execution falls through into the next case
questions.explain: Fall-through is the default behaviour, useful for grouping labels but a common source of bugs otherwise.

questions.q: What can a switch statement test?
questions.explain: switch requires an integral expression, so strings and floating-point values need if chains instead.

questions.q: What does if (count) mean when count is an int?
questions.explain: Any non-zero value is true in C, so this is the idiomatic test for a non-zero counter or a non-null pointer.

questions.q: Why should single-statement if bodies still use braces?
options: Adding a second line later would silently fall outside the if
questions.explain: Without braces only the first statement is conditional, which has caused real security bugs in shipped software.

lessons.title: The counting loop
lessons.subtitle: for in three parts
lessons.concept:
The C `for` loop packs three clauses into one line, separated by semicolons:

`for (init; condition; step)`

It initialises once, tests the condition **before** each pass, and runs the step **after** each pass. So a loop whose condition is false initially never executes its body at all.

Declaring the counter inside the parentheses (`int i = 0`) scopes it to the loop, which is the modern style and prevents accidental reuse afterwards.
lessons.example_note: The second loop prints 10 7 4 1 and stops when the condition fails.
lessons.task: Print the first five multiples of 3, one per line, then `sum: 45`.
hints: Declare the accumulator before the loop so it survives afterwards.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Looping until a condition fails
lessons.subtitle: while
lessons.concept:
`while (condition)` repeats as long as the condition holds. Use it when the number of passes is not known in advance.

Something inside the body **must** move the condition toward false, or the loop never ends. Forgetting the update is the classic infinite loop.

`while (1)` deliberately loops forever, relying on a `break` inside to escape — a common and perfectly idiomatic pattern for search and event loops.
lessons.example_note: n /= 2 shrinks n every pass, guaranteeing termination. Without it the loop would hang.
lessons.task: Starting at 1, double a value while it stays below 100, printing each value, then print how many doublings occurred.
hints: Print before doubling so the initial 1 appears.

lessons.title: A loop that always runs once
lessons.subtitle: do...while
lessons.concept:
`do { ... } while (condition);` tests the condition **after** the body, so the body always executes at least once.

That makes it right for menus and input validation — you must prompt before you can check the answer.

Note the trailing semicolon after the closing parenthesis; it is required, and forgetting it is a compile error.
lessons.example_note: The first loop ran even though 100 < 3 was false from the start — that is the whole point.

lessons.title: Leaving early and skipping
lessons.subtitle: break and continue
lessons.concept:
`break` exits the innermost loop immediately. `continue` abandons the current pass and jumps to the step clause, starting the next one.

`break` is how a search stops as soon as it succeeds, rather than pointlessly scanning the remainder.

Both affect only the innermost enclosing loop. Escaping two levels at once requires a flag or a `goto`, which is one of the few defensible uses of `goto` in C.
lessons.example_note: In a for loop, continue still runs the step clause, so the counter advances normally.

hints: Test the break condition before the continue condition.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Loops inside loops
lessons.subtitle: Nesting and grids
lessons.concept:
An inner loop runs **completely** for every single pass of the outer loop. Two loops of ten passes execute the inner body one hundred times, so the cost multiplies rather than adds.

This is the natural structure for grids, tables and comparing every pair. Use different counter names — reusing `i` for both is a guaranteed bug.

A `printf("\n")` after the inner loop ends each row.
lessons.example_note: The row newline belongs to the outer loop, after the inner one has finished.

lessons.title: Accumulating across passes
lessons.subtitle: Sums, counts and running extremes
lessons.concept:
Most loops exist to build one answer from many values. Three patterns cover the majority:

- **Accumulate**: `total += value;` with total initialised to 0 (or 1 for products)
- **Count**: `if (test) count++;`
- **Track an extreme**: initialise from the first element, then replace when a better one appears

For the extreme, initialising `max = 0` is a bug when the data may be negative. Start from the first actual value.
lessons.example_note: All three accumulators are updated in one pass — there is rarely a reason to loop three times.

lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: In for (init; cond; step), when is the condition tested?
options: Before each pass, including the first
questions.explain: The condition is checked before every pass, so a for loop whose condition starts false never runs its body.

questions.q: What is unique about do...while?
options: The body always runs at least once
questions.explain: The condition is tested after the body, which is why it suits prompt-then-validate patterns.

questions.q: In a for loop, does continue skip the step clause?
questions.explain: continue jumps to the step clause, so the counter advances normally and the loop still terminates.

questions.q: How many times does the inner body run for nested loops of 5 and 4?
questions.explain: The inner loop runs fully for every outer pass, so the counts multiply.

questions.q: Why is initialising max = 0 risky when finding a maximum?
options: All values may be negative, so the answer would wrongly be 0
questions.explain: Initialising from the first actual element avoids returning a value that was never in the data.

lessons.title: Writing your own functions
lessons.subtitle: Return types and parameters
lessons.concept:
A C function declares its return type, its name, and the type of every parameter:

`int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }`

A function returning nothing uses `void`. One taking no parameters uses `(void)`.

C reads the file top to bottom, so a function must be **known** before it is used. The simplest approach is to define helpers above `main`.
lessons.example_note: Because square returns a value, its results can be combined arithmetically.
lessons.task: Write `int max_of(int a, int b)` returning the larger value, then print `max_of(17, 42)` and `max_of(7, 3)` as `max: 42`.
hints: An if with a return, then a bare return handles the other case.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Declaring before defining
lessons.subtitle: Function prototypes
lessons.concept:
A **prototype** declares a function’s signature without its body, ending in a semicolon:

`int add(int a, int b);`

That lets you call the function before its definition appears, which frees you to put `main` at the top where readers expect it. In multi-file projects, prototypes live in header files.

Without a prototype or prior definition, the compiler cannot check your call, and modern C treats that as an error.
lessons.example_note: Parameter names in a prototype are optional — int triple(int); is equally valid — but naming them documents intent.
lessons.task: Using prototypes, declare `int cube(int)` and `void header(void)` above main, define them below, and print the cubes of 2, 3 and 4.
hints: The prototypes end with semicolons; the definitions follow main.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Functions get copies
lessons.subtitle: Pass by value
lessons.concept:
C passes arguments **by value**: the function receives a copy. Modifying a parameter inside the function has no effect on the caller’s variable.

This is why a naive `swap(int a, int b)` cannot work — it faithfully swaps its own two copies and then discards them.

The only way to let a function modify the caller’s data is to pass an **address**, which is the subject of the pointers module. Recognising the limitation now makes pointers feel like a solution rather than an arbitrary complication.
lessons.example_note: The function genuinely set its n to 999 — but that n was a copy that ceased to exist on return.
lessons.task: Write `void attempt(int n)` that sets n to 100 and prints it, then call it with a variable holding 7 and print that variable afterwards to show it is unchanged.
hints: The outer value stays 7 because the function only changed its copy.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Functions that call themselves
lessons.subtitle: Recursion
lessons.concept:
A **recursive** function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. Every recursion needs a **base case** that returns without recursing, or it exhausts the call stack and crashes.

Each call gets its own copy of the parameters and locals, stacked up until the base case is reached, then unwound.

Recursion is elegant for naturally recursive structures. For simple counting, a loop is usually faster and uses no stack.
lessons.example_note: factorial(6) expands to 6 x 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1, with each call waiting for the one it made.
lessons.task: Write a recursive `int power(int base, int exp)` without using pow, and print power(2, 10) and power(5, 3).
hints: Anything to the power zero is 1 — that is the base case.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Where variables live and how long
lessons.subtitle: Scope, lifetime and static
lessons.concept:
A variable declared inside a block exists only within that block — its **scope**. It is created on entry and destroyed on exit, which is its **lifetime**.

A `static` local variable is different: it is initialised once and **retains its value between calls**, while still being invisible outside the function. That makes it a private counter.

A variable declared outside all functions is **global**: visible everywhere and alive for the whole program. Globals make code hard to reason about, so use them sparingly.
lessons.example_note: The static variable climbs 1, 2, 3 while the ordinary local resets to 1 every call.
lessons.task: Write `void tick(void)` with a static counter that prints `tick 1`, `tick 2`, `tick 3` across three calls.
hints: A static local keeps its value between calls.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: Why does void swap(int a, int b) fail to swap the caller’s variables?
options: The parameters are copies of the arguments
questions.explain: C passes by value, so the function rearranges only its own copies. Passing addresses is the fix.

questions.q: What is a function prototype for?
options: Declaring a signature so the function can be called before it is defined
questions.explain: It lets the compiler check calls that appear before the definition, which is essential across multiple files.

questions.q: What does a static local variable do?
options: Keeps its value between calls while staying private to the function
questions.explain: It is initialised once and persists for the program’s lifetime, but its name is only visible inside the function.

questions.q: What must every recursive function have?
options: A base case that returns without recursing
questions.explain: Without a base case the recursion never terminates and eventually overflows the call stack.

questions.q: What does void mean as a parameter list, as in int main(void)?
questions.explain: In the parameter position void explicitly states that the function accepts no arguments.

lessons.title: A fixed run of values
lessons.subtitle: Declaring and indexing arrays
lessons.concept:
An **array** is a fixed-size sequence of same-typed values laid out contiguously in memory. `int nums[5];` reserves room for five ints, indexed `0` to `4`.

Initialise with a brace list: `int nums[] = {4, 8, 15};` lets the compiler count for you. A partial list zero-fills the rest.

C does **not** check bounds. Reading `nums[99]` compiles fine and hands you whatever happens to be in that memory. Staying inside the array is entirely your responsibility — this is the single most common source of serious C bugs.
lessons.example_note: int zeros[3] = {0}; is the idiomatic way to zero an entire array.
lessons.task: Declare an array of the five values 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Print the first, the third, the last, then change the second to 99 and print it.
hints: Indexing starts at zero, so the third element is nums[2].

lessons.title: How long is this array?
lessons.subtitle: The sizeof idiom
lessons.concept:
An array does **not** know its own length. The standard trick computes it:

`int n = sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]);`

Total bytes divided by bytes per element gives the count. Dividing by `arr[0]` rather than a hard-coded type keeps it correct if the type ever changes.

This works **only in the scope where the array was declared**. Passed to a function, an array decays to a pointer and `sizeof` gives the pointer size instead — which is why array functions always take the length as a separate parameter.
lessons.example_note: Always loop with i < n, never i <= n — the last valid index is n - 1.
lessons.task: Given `int scores[] = {67, 91, 42, 78, 57};` compute the length with sizeof, then print the count and the sum.
hints: Divide the total size by the size of one element.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Processing every element
lessons.subtitle: Aggregating over arrays
lessons.concept:
C has no built-in `sum` or `max`, so every aggregate is a loop you write yourself. The patterns match what you saw with plain loops:

- sum: accumulate from 0
- max/min: initialise from `arr[0]`, then compare
- count: increment when a test passes
- average: sum, then divide with a cast

Initialising max from `arr[0]` rather than 0 matters whenever the data might be negative.
lessons.example_note: One pass computes all four results — there is no reason to loop repeatedly.
lessons.task: Given `int values[] = {34, 91, 12, 78, 56};` print the count, the largest, the smallest, the sum and the average to two decimals.
hints: Initialise max and min from the first element.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Passing arrays to functions
lessons.subtitle: Decay and the length parameter
lessons.concept:
When an array is passed to a function it **decays** into a pointer to its first element. The function receives an address, not a copy, so:

1. It can modify the caller’s array — unlike ordinary pass-by-value.
2. `sizeof` inside the function gives the pointer size, so the length must be passed separately.

The signatures `int arr[]` and `int *arr` mean exactly the same thing in a parameter list. Adding `const` documents that the function will not modify the data.
lessons.example_note: double_all changed the caller’s array, because it received the address rather than a copy.
lessons.task: Write `int largest(const int arr[], int n)` and `void increment_all(int arr[], int n)`. Apply both to {5, 12, 3} and print the largest before and after incrementing.
hints: Both functions need the length as a second parameter.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Finding and ordering
lessons.subtitle: Linear search and simple sorts
lessons.concept:
Two operations you will write many times.

**Linear search** walks the array comparing each element, returning the index on a match and `-1` otherwise. `break` or an early `return` stops as soon as it succeeds.

**Bubble sort** repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs. Each pass settles one more value at the end, so the inner range shrinks. It is slow, but implementing it once makes sorting concrete.

Swapping in C needs a temporary variable, since there is no tuple assignment.
lessons.example_note: Returning -1 for "not found" is the universal C convention, mirroring strchr and friends.
lessons.task: Sort `{64, 25, 12, 22, 11}` ascending with bubble sort and print the values on one line, then print the index of the value 22.
hints: Sort first, then search the sorted array.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Arrays of arrays
lessons.subtitle: Two-dimensional arrays
lessons.concept:
`int grid[3][4];` declares three rows of four columns. Access with two indexes: `grid[row][col]`.

The memory is laid out **row by row**, contiguously. Iterating rows in the outer loop and columns in the inner one therefore walks memory in order, which is measurably faster on real hardware.

Initialise with nested braces. When passing to a function, all dimensions except the first must be specified: `void show(int grid[][4], int rows)`.
lessons.example_note: The nested braces make the row structure visible, though a flat list would also compile.
lessons.task: Build a 3x3 array where each cell holds row times column (zero-indexed), print each row on its own line with spaces, then print the total of all cells.
hints: Fill and total in one nested loop, then print in another.

questions.q: How do you get the element count of int arr[] = {1,2,3};?
questions.explain: Arrays carry no length, so total bytes must be divided by the size of one element — and only in the declaring scope.

questions.q: What happens when you read arr[99] on a 5-element array?
options: Undefined behaviour — you get whatever is in that memory
questions.explain: C performs no bounds checking. The read may appear to work, may crash, or may silently corrupt data.

questions.q: Why must array functions take the length as a parameter?
options: Because the array decays to a pointer, so sizeof no longer gives the array size
questions.explain: Inside the function the parameter is a pointer, so sizeof returns the pointer size rather than the array size.

questions.q: Can a function modify the caller’s array?
options: Yes, because it receives the address of the first element
questions.explain: Array decay means the function works on the original memory, which is why const documents read-only intent.

questions.q: How is int grid[3][4] laid out in memory?
questions.explain: C uses row-major order, so iterating rows outermost walks memory sequentially and is cache-friendly.

lessons.title: There is no string type
lessons.subtitle: char arrays and the null terminator
lessons.concept:
C has no string type. A string is an **array of char ending in a `\0` byte** — the null terminator — which is how every function knows where the text stops.

So `"hi"` occupies three bytes: `h`, `i`, `\0`. `char word[] = "hi";` creates an array of size 3.

This single design decision explains most of C’s string behaviour: `strlen` must scan to find the length, buffers must always leave room for the terminator, and forgetting it produces the classic runaway read.
lessons.example_note: strlen gives 2 but sizeof gives 3 — the difference is the invisible terminator.
lessons.task: Given `char word[] = "pointer";` print the string, its strlen, its sizeof, its first character and its last character.
hints: The last character is at index len - 1, not len.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: The string library
lessons.subtitle: strlen, strcpy, strcmp, strcat
lessons.concept:
`<string.h>` provides the core operations:

- `strlen(s)` length, excluding the terminator
- `strcpy(dst, src)` copy, including the terminator
- `strcmp(a, b)` returns **0 when equal**, negative if a sorts first, positive otherwise
- `strcat(dst, src)` append
- `strchr(s, c)` find a character, returning a pointer or NULL

Strings cannot be compared with `==`, which compares addresses instead of contents. And `strcpy`/`strcat` write as much as the source demands, so the destination must be large enough — the `strncpy`/`strncat` variants take a limit and are safer.
lessons.example_note: strcmp returning 0 for equal reads oddly, but it lets one function express all three orderings.
lessons.task: Declare `char buffer[40]`. Copy `"Hello"` into it, append `", world"`, print the result and its length, then print whether it equals `"Hello, world"`.
hints: Compare with strcmp(...) == 0, never with ==.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Walking a string
lessons.subtitle: Character-by-character processing
lessons.concept:
Since a string is an array, you process it with a loop. Two idioms:

`for (int i = 0; s[i] != '\0'; i++)` stops at the terminator without calling strlen.

`for (size_t i = 0; i < strlen(s); i++)` is clearer but re-scans the string on **every pass**, turning a linear loop into a quadratic one. Compute the length once beforehand instead.

`<ctype.h>` supplies the character tests: `isalpha`, `isdigit`, `isspace`, `toupper`, `tolower`.
lessons.example_note: text[i] alone works as the condition, since the terminator is zero and therefore false.
lessons.task: Given `char text[] = "programming in C";` count the vowels, count the spaces, and print the text with every character uppercased.
hints: Lowercase each character first so the vowel test needs only five comparisons.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Producing new strings
lessons.subtitle: Buffers, sprintf and safety
lessons.concept:
To build a string you need a **buffer** — a char array large enough for the result plus its terminator. Getting the size wrong is a buffer overflow, historically the most exploited bug class in software.

`sprintf(buffer, "format", ...)` works exactly like printf but writes into a buffer. `snprintf(buffer, size, ...)` takes the capacity and refuses to exceed it, which is why it is always the better choice.

When writing character by character, remember to terminate the result yourself.
lessons.example_note: sizeof(line) passes the capacity automatically, so the buffer size and the limit can never drift apart.
lessons.task: Using a 64-byte buffer and snprintf, build the line `item: coffee, price: 3.50` and print it plus its length. Then build and print the reverse of `"level"`.
hints: Do not forget to write the terminator after the reversal loop.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Many strings at once
lessons.subtitle: Arrays of strings
lessons.concept:
An array of strings is an **array of pointers to char**: `const char *names[] = {"ada", "bob"};`. Each element points at a string literal stored elsewhere.

String literals are read-only, which is why `const char *` is the correct type — attempting to modify one is undefined behaviour.

The alternative, `char names[3][20]`, allocates a fixed block per string and is writable, at the cost of wasting space and capping the length.
lessons.example_note: The sizeof idiom still works here, because names is a genuine array of pointers.

questions.q: What does strlen("hi") return?
questions.explain: strlen counts the characters before the null terminator, so 2 — even though the array occupies 3 bytes.

questions.q: Why can strings not be compared with ==?
questions.explain: A string is an address, so == asks whether both point at the same memory. strcmp compares the characters.

questions.q: What does strcmp return for two equal strings?
questions.explain: Zero means equal; negative and positive results express the ordering, which lets one function serve all three cases.

questions.q: Why is snprintf safer than sprintf?
options: It takes the buffer capacity and will not exceed it
questions.explain: sprintf writes as much as the format demands, overflowing the buffer; snprintf truncates at the limit you supply.

questions.q: What must you do after building a string character by character?
questions.explain: Without the terminator, every string function keeps reading past your data into whatever follows in memory.

lessons.title: Variables that hold addresses
lessons.subtitle: & and * explained
lessons.concept:
Every variable lives at a numbered location in memory. A **pointer** is a variable whose value *is* such a location.

Two operators do the work:
- `&x` gives the **address of** x
- `*p` **dereferences** p, reading or writing the value stored at that address

`int *p = &x;` declares p as "pointer to int" and aims it at x. Then `*p = 99;` changes x itself, because p refers to x’s actual storage.

The asterisk is doing two different jobs: in a declaration it means "is a pointer", in an expression it means "the value there". Keeping those apart is the key.
lessons.example_note: Writing through *p changed x, because both names refer to exactly the same memory.
lessons.task: Declare `int value = 10;` and a pointer to it. Print the value directly, the value through the pointer, then set it to 55 through the pointer and print the original variable.
hints: Assign &value to the pointer, then write through *p.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Letting a function change your variable
lessons.subtitle: Output parameters
lessons.concept:
Earlier you saw that C passes by value, so a function cannot modify its caller’s variables. Pointers are the solution: pass the **address**, and the function can reach back through it.

A parameter of type `int *` receives an address; `*param = newValue` writes to the caller’s variable. At the call site you must write `&variable`.

This is also how a function returns several results — fill in several output parameters rather than returning one value.
lessons.example_note: min_max returns two results by writing through two pointers — the standard C answer to multiple return values.
lessons.task: Write `void swap(int *a, int *b)` exchanging the two values it points at, then use it on variables holding 3 and 8, printing before and after.
hints: Swapping the pointers themselves does nothing — swap what they point at.

lessons.title: Moving a pointer along
lessons.subtitle: Pointer arithmetic and arrays
lessons.concept:
Adding to a pointer moves it by **whole elements**, not bytes. `p + 1` on an `int *` advances four bytes on a typical system, because that is one int.

This is why array indexing and pointers are the same thing: `arr[i]` is defined as `*(arr + i)`. An array name used in an expression *is* a pointer to its first element.

Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of elements between them, which is how you recover an index from a pointer.
lessons.example_note: The loop walks with a pointer rather than an index — idiomatic older C, and exactly equivalent.
lessons.task: Given `int nums[] = {5, 10, 15, 20, 25};` use a pointer to print the first element, the third via pointer arithmetic, and then every element using a pointer-based loop on one line.
hints: An array name decays to a pointer to its first element, so int *p = nums; needs no &.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Pointers to nothing
lessons.subtitle: NULL and dangling pointers
lessons.concept:
`NULL` is a pointer value guaranteed not to point at any object. It is the conventional "no result" return and the safe initial value for a pointer you have not aimed yet.

Dereferencing NULL crashes the program — which, perversely, is the good case. The dangerous alternatives are:

- an **uninitialised** pointer, holding garbage that may point anywhere
- a **dangling** pointer, still holding the address of memory that has been freed or has gone out of scope

Always initialise pointers, always check a pointer that might be NULL before dereferencing, and never return the address of a local variable.
lessons.example_note: The check before dereferencing is what makes the NULL return safe to use.
lessons.task: Write `int *first_even(int arr[], int n)` returning a pointer to the first even value or NULL. Test it on {3, 7, 8, 9} and on {1, 3, 5}, printing the value or `none`.

lessons.title: What exactly is constant?
lessons.subtitle: const with pointers
lessons.concept:
`const` and pointers combine in two distinct ways, and the position matters.

`const int *p` — pointer to constant int. You may move p, but not write through it. This is the standard way to say "this function reads your data but will not change it".

`int *const p` — constant pointer to int. You may write through p, but not repoint it.

Read the declaration right to left. The first form is what you will use ninety percent of the time, and putting it on function parameters documents intent and lets the compiler enforce it.

questions.q: In int *p = &x; what is *p?
questions.explain: & takes an address; * dereferences, giving the value living at that address.

questions.q: What does p + 1 advance by for an int *p?
questions.explain: Pointer arithmetic works in whole elements, which is exactly why arr[i] and *(arr + i) are equivalent.

questions.q: How does a function modify its caller’s variable?
options: By taking a pointer and writing through it
questions.explain: Passing an address lets the function reach the caller’s storage rather than a copy of the value.

questions.q: What does const int *p prevent?
options: Writing through p to the value
questions.explain: Read it right to left: pointer to const int. The pointer may move; the pointed-at value may not be written.

questions.q: Why is returning the address of a local variable a bug?
options: The local dies when the function returns, leaving a dangling pointer
questions.explain: The storage is reclaimed on return, so the caller holds an address to memory that is no longer valid.

lessons.title: Grouping related data
lessons.subtitle: struct and member access
lessons.concept:
A **struct** bundles several values into one type. Where an array holds many of the same thing, a struct holds a few different things that belong together — a point, a date, an employee record.

Declare the shape once, then create variables of that type. Access members with a dot: `p.x`.

Unlike arrays, structs **can** be assigned and passed by value — the whole thing is copied. For large structs that copy is wasteful, which is why pointers to structs are so common.
lessons.example_note: The assignment copied a into copy, so changing copy.x left a.x alone — structs really are copied.

lessons.title: Shorter type names
lessons.subtitle: typedef
lessons.concept:
Writing `struct Point` everywhere is tedious. `typedef` creates an alias so you can write just `Point`.

The common idiom combines the declaration and the alias:

`typedef struct { int x, y; } Point;`

This is what most real C code does. Note that a struct declared this way is anonymous — the only name for it is the typedef alias.

By convention typedef’d types are capitalised, which distinguishes them from variables at a glance.
lessons.example_note: A function can return a struct by value, which is a clean way to build one from parts.

lessons.title: Structs through pointers
lessons.subtitle: The arrow operator
lessons.concept:
When you have a pointer to a struct, `(*p).x` is awkward, so C provides the **arrow operator**: `p->x` means exactly the same thing.

Passing a pointer avoids copying the whole struct and lets the function modify the original — the same reasoning as with any other type.

The convention is clear: `const Thing *` for read-only access, `Thing *` when the function needs to modify. Passing by value is fine for small structs like a point.
lessons.example_note: p->score and (*p).score are identical; the arrow simply reads better.

lessons.title: Many records
lessons.subtitle: Arrays of structs
lessons.concept:
An array of structs is how C represents a table of records. `Student class[3];` gives three students, each with all their members.

Access combines both notations: `class[0].name`. Iterate with an ordinary loop.

This is the shape of most real data processing in C — read records into an array of structs, then loop to search, total or sort. Sorting works exactly as for integers, except you compare one member and swap whole structs.

lessons.title: Named constants
lessons.subtitle: enum
lessons.concept:
An `enum` defines a set of named integer constants. `enum Colour { RED, GREEN, BLUE };` makes RED 0, GREEN 1 and BLUE 2 automatically, or you can assign explicit values.

Enums make code self-documenting: `if (state == RUNNING)` is far clearer than `if (state == 2)`. They also pair naturally with `switch`, since the cases are named.

Underneath they are just ints, so C will not stop you assigning an out-of-range value — the benefit is readability, not safety.

lessons.title: Two kinds of memory
lessons.subtitle: The stack and the heap
lessons.concept:
Local variables live on the **stack**: created on entry to a block, destroyed on exit, with a size fixed at compile time. That automatic cleanup is convenient but means you cannot return a pointer to a local, and cannot decide the size at run time.

The **heap** is memory you request explicitly and keep until you release it. It survives function returns and can be any size computed at run time.

The trade is responsibility: every heap allocation must be freed exactly once. Never freeing is a **leak**; freeing twice or using after freeing is **undefined behaviour**.
lessons.example_note: A heap pointer is indexed exactly like an array, because that is all an array subscript ever was.
lessons.task: Allocate room for 5 ints on the heap, fill index i with the square of (i+1), print each on its own line, then free the memory and print `freed`.
hints: malloc(n * sizeof(int)) reserves room for n ints.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: The allocation functions
lessons.subtitle: malloc, calloc, realloc, free
lessons.concept:
Four functions from `<stdlib.h>` manage the heap.

`malloc(bytes)` reserves uninitialised memory — the contents are garbage. `calloc(count, size)` reserves and **zeroes** it, which is safer when you will read before writing.

`realloc(ptr, newBytes)` resizes an existing block, possibly moving it, and returns the new address. Always assign the result to a temporary first: if realloc fails it returns NULL, and overwriting your only pointer would leak the original block.

`free(ptr)` releases it. Setting the pointer to NULL afterwards prevents accidental reuse.
lessons.example_note: calloc gave three zeros; malloc would have given whatever was left in that memory.

lessons.title: Arrays sized at run time
lessons.subtitle: Growable buffers
lessons.concept:
The real reason to use the heap is a size you do not know until the program runs.

The growable-array pattern tracks three things: the pointer, the **count** of items used, and the **capacity** allocated. When count reaches capacity, realloc to a larger block — doubling is the standard choice, because it keeps the total cost of n insertions proportional to n.

This is precisely what a dynamic array in any higher-level language does internally.
lessons.example_note: Capacity doubled twice, from 2 to 4 to 8, so only two reallocations were needed for six items.
lessons.task: Build a growable array starting at capacity 2. Append the values 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50, doubling capacity when full and printing `grew to N` each time. Then print the contents and the final capacity, and free.

lessons.title: Strings on the heap
lessons.subtitle: Duplicating and building text
lessons.concept:
A heap string is a char buffer you allocate yourself. The size must be `strlen + 1` to leave room for the terminator — forgetting the `+ 1` is the most common buffer bug in C.

The standard idiom:

```
char *copy = malloc(strlen(src) + 1);
strcpy(copy, src);
```

This is what `strdup` does, and it lets a function return a string that outlives it — impossible with a local array. The caller then owns the memory and must free it.
lessons.example_note: join allocates the exact total plus one byte for the single terminator the result needs.

hints: Allocate len + 1 bytes and write the terminator yourself.

lessons.title: Who is responsible for freeing?
lessons.subtitle: Ownership discipline
lessons.concept:
C has no garbage collector, so every allocation needs a clear **owner** — the code responsible for freeing it. Since the language will not enforce this, it becomes a documented convention.

The rules that keep programs correct:

1. Whoever allocates, or receives ownership, must free exactly once.
2. A function returning heap memory transfers ownership to the caller — say so in a comment.
3. On an error path, free everything already allocated before returning.
4. Set pointers to NULL after freeing, so a mistaken reuse crashes immediately rather than corrupting data silently.

This discipline is what Rust later encoded into its type system.
lessons.example_note: free(NULL) is explicitly safe, which is why the error path can free both pointers unconditionally.

questions.q: What is the difference between malloc and calloc?
options: calloc zeroes the memory; malloc leaves it uninitialised
questions.explain: calloc takes a count and element size and guarantees zeroed memory, which malloc does not.

questions.q: Why assign realloc’s result to a temporary first?
options: Because realloc returns NULL on failure, and overwriting your pointer would leak the original block
questions.explain: On failure the original block is still valid, but you would have lost the only pointer to it.

questions.q: How many bytes does a heap copy of a string of length 5 need?
questions.explain: strlen + 1, because the null terminator needs a byte of its own.

questions.q: What happens if you never call free?
options: The memory leaks — unavailable until the program exits
questions.explain: Leaked memory accumulates, which matters greatly in long-running programs even though the OS reclaims it at exit.

questions.q: Is free(NULL) safe?
options: Yes — it is explicitly defined to do nothing
questions.explain: The standard guarantees free(NULL) is a no-op, which is what makes unconditional cleanup on error paths possible.

lessons.title: Functions as values
lessons.subtitle: Function pointers
lessons.concept:
A function has an address, so a pointer can hold it. The declaration mirrors the signature:

`int (*op)(int, int);`

Read the parentheses carefully — `int *op(int, int)` would be a function *returning* a pointer instead.

Assign with just the function name, and call through it exactly as you would call the function. This is how C achieves callbacks and pluggable behaviour: `qsort` takes a comparison function, and event loops take handlers. A `typedef` makes the syntax bearable.
lessons.example_note: apply takes behaviour as a parameter, which is the essence of a callback.

lessons.title: The library sort
lessons.subtitle: qsort and comparators
lessons.concept:
`qsort` from `<stdlib.h>` sorts any array, given four things: the base address, the element count, the size of one element, and a **comparison function**.

The comparator receives two `const void *` pointers and must return negative, zero or positive. Inside, you cast the void pointers back to the real type and compare.

Because the interface is untyped, you supply the type knowledge. That is C’s version of generics: `void *` plus an element size.
lessons.example_note: (x > y) - (x < y) avoids the overflow that x - y risks for large values.

hints: Reversing the comparator arguments reverses the sort order.

lessons.title: Packing data into bits
lessons.subtitle: Masks and flags
lessons.concept:
Bit manipulation lets a single integer carry many independent boolean flags, which is how file permissions, hardware registers and network protocols are represented.

The four operations to memorise:
- **set** bit n: `x |= (1 << n)`
- **clear** bit n: `x &= ~(1 << n)`
- **toggle** bit n: `x ^= (1 << n)`
- **test** bit n: `(x >> n) & 1`

Counting set bits is the other classic: repeatedly test the lowest bit and shift right.
lessons.example_note: 29 is 11101 in binary, so four bits are set.
lessons.task: Starting from 0, set bits 1 and 4, print the value, test bit 4 and bit 2, clear bit 1, print the value, then count the set bits in 255.
hints: Bit n has the value 1 << n, so bits 1 and 4 give 2 + 16 = 18.

lessons.title: Splitting a program up
lessons.subtitle: Headers and translation units
lessons.concept:
Real C programs span many files. Each `.c` file is a **translation unit** compiled separately, then linked together.

A `.h` header holds the declarations — prototypes, typedefs, macros — that other files need. The `.c` file holds the definitions. Every header needs an **include guard** so that including it twice does not redeclare everything:

```
#ifndef MYLIB_H
#define MYLIB_H
/* declarations */
#endif
```

`static` at file scope makes a function or variable private to its translation unit, which is how C expresses internal helpers.
lessons.example_note: factor is static, so no other file could call it even if it knew the name.
lessons.task: Write a single file with an include-guarded declaration block for `int cube(int)` and `int sum_to(int)`, a `static` helper, and definitions below. Print cube(4) and sum_to(10).
hints: The guard macro name conventionally matches the header filename.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline (\n).

lessons.title: Code before compilation
lessons.subtitle: Macros and conditional compilation
lessons.concept:
The **preprocessor** runs before the compiler, performing pure text substitution.

`#define MAX 100` replaces every MAX with 100. Function-like macros take arguments: `#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))`. Those inner parentheses are essential — without them `SQUARE(a + b)` expands to `a + b * a + b`.

A macro argument used twice is evaluated twice, so `MAX(i++, j)` increments i unpredictably. Prefer real functions unless you need the textual behaviour.

`#ifdef` / `#endif` compile code conditionally, which is how debug builds and platform differences are handled.
lessons.example_note: SQUARE(2 + 3) gives 25 only because of the inner parentheses; without them it would be 11.
lessons.task: Define macros `CUBE(x)`, `MIN(a,b)` and a constant `LIMIT` of 50, plus a DEBUG flag. Print CUBE(3), CUBE(1+2), MIN(9,4), LIMIT and a debug line.
hints: Wrap every macro parameter in its own parentheses.

lessons.title: Algorithms worth writing once
lessons.subtitle: Recursion, searching and merging
lessons.concept:
A closing tour of algorithms that exercise everything in this track.

**Binary search** halves the range each comparison, so a million sorted items need about twenty steps. It requires sorted input.

**Merge** walks two sorted arrays with two indexes, always taking the smaller head. It is the core of merge sort.

**Recursive traversal** suits problems whose structure is itself recursive; iterative versions are usually faster and use no stack.

Writing these by hand once makes the cost of each operation concrete in a way library calls never do.
lessons.example_note: low + (high - low) / 2 avoids the integer overflow that (low + high) / 2 can cause on huge arrays.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: advanced C
lessons.subtitle: Check what stuck before moving on
lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What does int (*op)(int, int) declare?
options: A pointer to a function taking two ints and returning an int
questions.explain: The parentheses around *op bind the pointer to the function; without them it would be a function returning int *.

questions.q: What must a qsort comparator return?
questions.explain: The sign of the result expresses the ordering, which is why (x > y) - (x < y) is the safe idiom.

questions.q: How do you clear bit n of x?
questions.explain: Anding with the inverted mask leaves every other bit untouched and forces bit n to zero.

questions.q: Why must macro parameters be parenthesised?
options: Because the substitution is textual, so surrounding operators can bind unexpectedly
questions.explain: SQUARE(a + b) without parentheses expands to a + b * a + b, which is not the square of anything.

questions.q: What does an include guard prevent?
options: The same header being processed twice in one translation unit
questions.explain: Without the guard, a header included via two paths would redeclare its contents and fail to compile.

lessons.title: Output with streams
lessons.subtitle: iostream, cout and <<
lessons.concept:
C++ starts from C but replaces printf with a **stream**. `std::cout` is the standard output stream, and `<<` pushes values into it.

There are no format specifiers. The compiler already knows each value’s type, so it selects the right formatting itself — which also means a type mismatch is impossible. That is a genuine safety improvement over printf.

`std::` is a **namespace** qualifier: cout lives in the standard library’s namespace, so its full name is `std::cout`. Writing it out is the unambiguous style.
lessons.example_note: 42 needs no %d — the stream works out that it is an int. That type safety is the whole point.
lessons.task: Print exactly `Hello, world!` using std::cout.
hints: The two less-than signs are the stream insertion operator, not a comparison.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Ending a line
lessons.subtitle: endl versus '\n'
lessons.concept:
Two ways to end a line. `'\n'` writes a newline character. `std::endl` writes a newline **and flushes the stream**, forcing the buffer out immediately.

Flushing costs time. In a loop printing thousands of lines, `endl` can be dramatically slower for no benefit. Prefer `'\n'` and reserve `endl` for the rare case where you need output to appear right now.

Note the single quotes: `'\n'` is a char, `"\n"` is a string. Both work, but the char is marginally cheaper.
lessons.example_note: The visible output is identical; the difference is only whether the buffer is flushed.
lessons.task: Print three lines: `first` using '\n', `second` using std::endl, and `third` using a newline inside the string literal.
hints: All three approaches produce the same visible result.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Where names live
lessons.subtitle: Namespaces and using
lessons.concept:
A **namespace** groups names so that libraries cannot collide. Everything in the standard library lives in `std`.

`using namespace std;` imports every name at once, letting you write `cout`. It is convenient in a tiny program and a genuine problem in a large one, because `std` contains hundreds of common words like `count`, `sort` and `data` that will collide with your own.

The measured position: qualify with `std::` in headers and real code; a targeted `using std::cout;` is an acceptable middle ground.
lessons.example_note: Both namespaces define area, and the qualification makes clear which one is meant.
lessons.task: Define a namespace `util` containing `int twice(int)`, call it as `util::twice(21)`, then use a targeted `using std::cout;` to print a second line.
hints: The namespace block goes above main.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: The shape of a C++ file
lessons.subtitle: Includes, comments and main
lessons.concept:
A C++ file has a predictable structure: includes first, then declarations, then definitions, with `main` as the entry point.

In C++, `int main()` needs no `void` in the parameter list — empty parentheses already mean "no parameters". The `return 0;` may be omitted entirely; the compiler supplies it.

Both C comment styles work. Header includes come in two forms: `<angle brackets>` for library headers, `"quotes"` for your own files.
lessons.example_note: Angle brackets search the system include paths; quotes search your project first.
lessons.task: Write a file with two includes, a commented helper `int halve(int)`, and a main that prints halve(84) and a message.
hints: Define the helper above main so it is known when called.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Controlling how numbers look
lessons.subtitle: iomanip and stream manipulators
lessons.concept:
Streams accept **manipulators** that change formatting from that point on.

From `<iomanip>`:
- `std::setprecision(n)` significant digits, or decimals when combined with `std::fixed`
- `std::setw(n)` minimum field width for the **next** item only
- `std::setfill(c)` the padding character
- `std::left` / `std::right` alignment

The important asymmetry: `setw` applies once, while `fixed` and `setprecision` persist until changed. That catches everyone the first time.
lessons.example_note: The alignment and precision settings stick; setw affects only the item immediately after it.

hints: std::fixed plus setprecision gives decimal places rather than significant digits.

questions.explain: Both emit a newline, but endl forces a buffer flush, which can be very costly inside a loop.

questions.q: Why is using namespace std; discouraged in large code?
options: std contains many common words that will collide with your own names
questions.explain: Names like count, sort and data are all in std, so wholesale importing invites ambiguity.

questions.q: How many items does std::setw affect?
questions.explain: setw is consumed by the next insertion, unlike fixed and setprecision which persist.

questions.q: What does std::fixed change about setprecision?
options: It makes the precision mean decimal places rather than significant digits
questions.explain: Without fixed, setprecision counts total significant digits; with it, the count applies after the decimal point.

lessons.title: Declaring variables
lessons.subtitle: Fundamental types and initialisation
lessons.concept:
C++ has C’s fundamental types — `int`, `double`, `char`, `bool` — with `bool` built into the language rather than bolted on by a header.

There are several initialisation syntaxes. `int x = 5;` is the familiar one. `int x{5};` is **brace initialisation**, which is stricter: it refuses narrowing conversions that would silently lose data, so `int x{3.7};` is a compile error where `int x = 3.7;` quietly truncates.

Preferring braces catches real bugs at compile time.
lessons.example_note: int truncated = 3.7; compiles and loses the fraction. int truncated{3.7}; would refuse to compile.
lessons.task: Declare `int items{7}` and `double price{2.5}`, compute the total, and print the three values, with the price and total to two decimals.
hints: int times double promotes to double automatically.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Letting the compiler name the type
lessons.subtitle: auto and type deduction
lessons.concept:
`auto` asks the compiler to deduce a variable’s type from its initialiser. The variable is still **statically typed** — you simply did not spell out something already obvious.

It earns its place with long types: `std::map<std::string, std::vector<int>>::iterator` becomes `auto`.

The rule of thumb: use `auto` when the type is obvious from the right-hand side or too long to be useful, and write the type explicitly when naming it documents intent. `auto` always requires an initialiser.
lessons.example_note: auto name = "ada"; would deduce const char *, not std::string — hence the explicit std::string on that line.
lessons.task: Using auto, declare an int, a double and a std::string, print all three, then loop over an auto-declared vector of three ints printing each.

lessons.title: Another name for a variable
lessons.subtitle: References
lessons.concept:
A **reference** (`int&`) is an alias for an existing variable. Unlike a pointer there is no address arithmetic, no null, and no dereferencing syntax — you use it exactly as you would the original.

A reference must be initialised when declared and can never be reseated afterwards.

The main use is function parameters. `void f(int& n)` lets the function modify the caller’s variable; `void f(const std::string& s)` passes a large object without copying it while promising not to change it. That `const&` form is the default choice for any non-trivial parameter.
lessons.example_note: Assigning through alias changed n, because they are two names for one object.
lessons.task: Write `void triple(int& n)` multiplying its argument by three in place, and `void describe(const std::string& s)` printing the text and its length. Use both.
hints: Inside triple just write n *= 3; the ampersand in the parameter does the rest.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Promising not to change
lessons.subtitle: const and constexpr
lessons.concept:
`const` marks a value as unmodifiable, and the compiler enforces it. Applied to parameters and member functions it documents intent in a way comments cannot.

`constexpr` goes further: the value must be computable **at compile time**, so it costs nothing at run time and can size arrays or appear in template arguments.

The habit worth forming is "const by default" — make everything const and remove it only where mutation is genuinely needed. It prevents accidental modification and helps the optimiser.
lessons.example_note: area was computed by the compiler, which is why it can size an array.
lessons.task: Declare `const double RATE = 0.2`, a `constexpr int DOZEN = 12`, and a constexpr function `cube(int)`. Print the rate, the dozen, cube(3) and cube(DOZEN).
hints: A constexpr function can also be called at run time with ordinary values.

lessons.title: Converting between types
lessons.subtitle: static_cast and integer division
lessons.concept:
C++ inherits C’s integer division trap: `7 / 2` is `3` when both operands are int. The fix is to convert one operand.

C++ prefers `static_cast<double>(a) / b` over the C-style `(double)a`. The named form is deliberately verbose so that casts are easy to find, and it performs only conversions the compiler considers sensible — a C-style cast will silently attempt almost anything.

There are four named casts; `static_cast` covers the ordinary numeric and class-hierarchy conversions you will actually need.
lessons.example_note: static_cast<int> truncates toward zero rather than rounding.

questions.q: What is the advantage of int x{3.7} over int x = 3.7?
options: It refuses the narrowing conversion at compile time
questions.explain: Brace initialisation rejects conversions that would lose data, turning a silent bug into a compile error.

questions.q: Is auto dynamically typed?
options: No — the type is deduced at compile time and then fixed
questions.explain: auto is pure convenience; the resulting variable has one static type just as if you had written it out.

questions.q: What is the main difference between a reference and a pointer?
options: A reference cannot be null or reseated, and needs no dereferencing syntax
questions.explain: A reference is an alias that must be bound at declaration, which makes it safer for parameters.

questions.q: Why pass a large object as const T& ?
options: To avoid copying it while promising not to change it
questions.explain: Passing by value copies the whole object; a const reference avoids that cost without granting write access.

questions.q: Why prefer static_cast<double>(a) over (double)a?
options: It is easy to search for and performs only sensible conversions
questions.explain: The named casts are deliberately visible and more restricted, so dangerous conversions cannot happen by accident.

lessons.title: Arithmetic and its traps
lessons.subtitle: The five operators
lessons.concept:
C++ has `+ - * / %`, behaving exactly as in C. There is no exponentiation operator — `std::pow` from `<cmath>` covers that.

The division trap persists: two ints divide as integers. `%` requires integers and gives the remainder.

The augmented forms `+= -= *= /= %=` update in place, and `++`/`--` come in prefix and postfix flavours. As a standalone statement they are identical; inside a larger expression, postfix yields the old value and prefix the new one.
lessons.example_note: std::pow returns a double, so pow(2, 10) prints 1024 rather than an int.
lessons.task: With `int a{23}` and `int b{4}`, print the sum, product, integer quotient, remainder, exact quotient to two decimals, and 2 to the power 8.
hints: Cast pow back to int to print a whole number.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Comparing and combining
lessons.subtitle: Relational and logical operators
lessons.concept:
The six comparisons produce a genuine `bool`, not an int as in C. Printing one shows `1` or `0` unless you add `std::boolalpha`.

`&&`, `||` and `!` combine conditions and **short-circuit**: `&&` stops at the first false, `||` at the first true. That guarantee makes `if (p != nullptr && p->value > 0)` safe.

C++ has no chained comparisons — `0 < x < 10` compiles but is nonsense, because it means `(0 < x) < 10`, comparing a bool with 10. Write `0 < x && x < 10`.
lessons.example_note: std::boolalpha makes the output read true/false, which is far clearer when debugging.

hints: The range test needs two comparisons joined by &&.
