lessons.title: Which operation binds tighter
lessons.subtitle: Precedence and associativity
lessons.concept:
Precedence, tightest first: unary operators and casts, then `* / %`, then `+ -`, then shifts, then comparisons, then `&`, `^`, `|`, then `&&`, then `||`, then assignment.

Two practical consequences. The bitwise operators bind **looser** than comparisons, so `a & 1 == 0` means `a & (1 == 0)` — almost never intended.

And because `<<` is a shift operator with middling precedence, `std::cout << a == b` parses as `(std::cout << a) == b`. Always parenthesise comparisons inside a stream insertion.
lessons.example_note: Without the parentheses, the last line would try to compare the stream itself with b.
lessons.task: Print `5 + 2 * 3`, `(5 + 2) * 3`, `20 / 4 / 5`, and whether `(12 & 10) == 8`, each on its own line.
hints: Division is left-associative, so 20 / 4 / 5 is (20 / 4) / 5.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Working with bits
lessons.subtitle: Bitwise operators
lessons.concept:
C++ inherits C’s bit operators: `&` and, `|` or, `^` xor, `~` not, `<<` and `>>` shift.

The four idioms:
- set bit n: `x |= (1u << n)`
- clear bit n: `x &= ~(1u << n)`
- toggle bit n: `x ^= (1u << n)`
- test bit n: `(x >> n) & 1u`

`<<` is overloaded for streams as well as shifting, which is why bit expressions inside `std::cout <<` need parentheses.

For readable flag work, `std::bitset` from `<bitset>` prints the binary form directly.
lessons.example_note: 12 is 00001100 and 10 is 00001010, so & gives 8 and | gives 14.
lessons.task: With `unsigned int flags{10}`, print the result of anding with 12, oring with 5, xoring with 15, and the 8-bit binary form using std::bitset.
hints: Parenthesise each bitwise expression inside the stream insertion.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Choosing inside an expression
lessons.subtitle: The conditional operator
lessons.concept:
The conditional operator is C++’s only ternary operator:

`condition ? value_if_true : value_if_false`

Because it is an expression it produces a value, so it can be assigned or inserted straight into a stream. Both branches must have compatible types, since the whole expression has one type.

It shines for small choices. Nesting several is legal but quickly unreadable — use `if` when there is real branching to express.
lessons.example_note: Conditional operators chain to the right, which is what makes the grade ladder work.

questions.q: Why does std::cout << a == b fail to do what you expect?
options: << binds tighter than ==, so it means (std::cout << a) == b
questions.explain: The shift operator has higher precedence than comparison, so comparisons inside an insertion need parentheses.

questions.q: What does 0 < x < 10 mean in C++?
questions.explain: C++ has no chained comparisons; the first comparison yields a bool which is then compared with 10.

questions.q: What does std::boolalpha do?
options: Makes bools print as true/false instead of 1/0

questions.q: How do you raise 2 to the power 10 in C++?
questions.explain: There is no exponentiation operator; ^ is bitwise xor. std::pow from <cmath> does the job.

questions.q: What does x &= ~(1u << n) accomplish?
questions.explain: Anding with the inverted mask forces bit n to zero while leaving every other bit unchanged.

lessons.title: Branching
lessons.subtitle: if, else and init-statements
lessons.concept:
`if` takes a condition in parentheses and a block in braces, exactly as in C. `else if` chains test in order, first match winning.

C++17 added a useful refinement: an **init-statement** inside the if, declaring a variable scoped to the if and its else.

`if (int remainder = n % 3; remainder == 0)`

The variable exists only where it is relevant, which keeps the surrounding scope clean — a small but genuine improvement over declaring it above.
lessons.example_note: remainder is visible in both branches of the if but nowhere afterwards.
lessons.task: With `int temp{5}`, print `freezing` below 0, `cold` below 10, `mild` below 25, otherwise `hot`. Then use an if with an init-statement to report whether temp is even.
hints: The init-statement is separated from the condition by a semicolon.

lessons.title: Matching against many values
lessons.subtitle: switch and fall-through
lessons.concept:
`switch` compares one integral value against `case` labels. Without a `break`, execution **falls through** into the next case, which is occasionally useful for grouping and otherwise a bug.

C++17 added `[[fallthrough]];` to mark deliberate fall-through, so compilers can warn about the accidental kind.

As in C, `switch` works only on integral types. For strings you need an `if` chain or a map of handlers.
lessons.example_note: Case 6 falls through into case 7 deliberately, grouping both weekend days.
lessons.task: With `char op{'*'}` and ints 6 and 7, use switch to print the result of the operation, handling +, -, * and / with a default of `unknown`.
hints: Each case needs its own break.

lessons.title: The three loop forms
lessons.subtitle: for, while and do-while
lessons.concept:
The counting `for` loop, the conditional `while`, and `do...while` which always runs its body once. All behave as in C.

The C++ convention is `++i` rather than `i++` in the step clause. For an int they are identical, but for a class type with an overloaded operator, postfix must construct and return a copy of the old value while prefix need not — so `++i` became the habit.

Declaring the counter inside the for scopes it to the loop.

lessons.title: Looping over a collection
lessons.subtitle: Range-based for
lessons.concept:
The **range-based for** walks any container directly, with no index to get wrong:

`for (int value : values) { ... }`

The loop variable declaration matters. `for (auto v : items)` **copies** each element. `for (const auto& v : items)` binds a read-only reference, avoiding the copy — the right default for anything larger than a number. `for (auto& v : items)` allows modification of the elements in place.

That three-way choice is worth internalising: `const auto&` to read, `auto&` to modify, plain `auto` only for cheap types.

lessons.title: Leaving early and skipping
lessons.subtitle: break, continue and nesting
lessons.concept:
`break` exits the innermost loop; `continue` skips to the next iteration. Both affect only the loop they sit in, so escaping two levels needs a flag or a restructure — often extracting the inner loop into a function and returning from it is cleanest.

Nested loops multiply work: an inner loop of ten inside an outer loop of ten runs its body a hundred times.

In a range-based for, `continue` simply moves to the next element.

questions.q: What is the difference between for (auto v : items) and for (const auto& v : items)?
options: The first copies each element; the second binds a read-only reference
questions.explain: Copying is wasteful for anything larger than a scalar, so const auto& is the right default for reading.

questions.q: Which range-for form lets you modify the elements?
questions.explain: A non-const reference binds to the element itself, so assignments through it change the container.

questions.q: Why does C++ convention prefer ++i over i++ in a for loop?
options: For class types, postfix must copy the old value while prefix need not
questions.explain: For an int they are identical, but the habit avoids an unnecessary copy when the counter is a class type such as an iterator.

questions.q: What does an if init-statement achieve?
options: Declares a variable scoped to the if and its else
questions.explain: It limits the variable’s lifetime to where it is relevant, keeping the enclosing scope uncluttered.

questions.q: Can switch test a std::string?
questions.explain: switch requires an integral expression, so string dispatch needs an if chain or a map of handlers.

lessons.title: Defining functions
lessons.subtitle: Parameters, returns and declarations
lessons.concept:
A C++ function declares its return type, name and parameter types, exactly as in C. `void` means it returns nothing; empty parentheses mean it takes nothing.

As in C, a function must be declared before use. A **declaration** (prototype) ends with a semicolon and lets you define the function later, which is how you put `main` at the top.

Parameters are passed by value by default, so the function receives copies — unless you use a reference.
lessons.example_note: Because square returns a value, results can be combined arithmetically.
lessons.task: Declare `int max_of(int, int)` above main, define it below, and print max_of(17, 42) and max_of(7, 3).
hints: The declaration ends with a semicolon; the definition follows main.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: One name, several versions
lessons.subtitle: Function overloading
lessons.concept:
C++ allows several functions to share a name as long as their **parameter lists differ**. The compiler picks the match from the argument types — this is **overload resolution**, decided entirely at compile time.

The return type alone is not enough to distinguish overloads, because the compiler cannot tell which you wanted from the call site.

Overloading is why `std::cout <<` works for every type, and why `std::max` accepts ints or doubles. Use it when the operations are conceptually the same; different names are clearer when the behaviour differs.
lessons.example_note: area(4) and area(2.0) call different functions, chosen by the argument type alone.
lessons.task: Overload `describe` for an int, a double and a std::string, each printing a distinguishing line, then call all three.
hints: Wrap the literal in std::string so the string overload is selected.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Optional parameters
lessons.subtitle: Default arguments
lessons.concept:
A parameter may have a **default value**, making it optional at the call site. Defaults must be the trailing parameters — you cannot skip one in the middle.

The default goes in the **declaration**, not the definition, when both exist. Repeating it in both is an error.

Defaults often replace a family of overloads: one function with two defaults covers what three overloads would. Where they differ, an overload can change behaviour entirely while a default only supplies a value.
lessons.example_note: You may omit any trailing arguments, but not one from the middle.
lessons.task: Write `int scaled(int value, int factor = 2, int offset = 0)` returning value * factor + offset, and call it with one, two and three arguments.
hints: Defaults must come after all required parameters.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: How to pass an argument
lessons.subtitle: Value, reference and const reference
lessons.concept:
Three ways to pass a parameter, and choosing correctly matters for both correctness and speed.

**By value** (`int n`) copies. Right for small cheap types: int, double, char, pointers.

**By reference** (`int& n`) aliases the caller’s object, so the function can modify it. Use when modification is the point.

**By const reference** (`const std::string& s`) avoids the copy and forbids modification. This is the default for any type larger than a machine word — strings, vectors, structs.

The guideline: cheap types by value, everything else by `const&` unless you must modify, in which case plain `&`.
lessons.example_note: by_const_ref inspected a thousand-element vector without copying a single one of them.
lessons.task: Write `void bump(int& n)` adding one, `int doubled(int n)` returning twice its argument, and `std::size_t length(const std::string& s)`. Demonstrate all three.
hints: Only the reference parameter changes the caller’s variable.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Functions defined where they are used
lessons.subtitle: Lambda expressions
lessons.concept:
A **lambda** is an anonymous function written inline:

`[capture](parameters) { body }`

The capture list is the distinctive part — it says which surrounding variables the lambda may use. `[]` captures nothing, `[x]` captures x by copy, `[&x]` by reference, `[=]` and `[&]` capture everything used by copy or reference respectively.

Lambdas exist so that a small piece of behaviour can be passed to an algorithm without the ceremony of a named function. Store one in `auto`, or accept one as a template parameter.
lessons.example_note: [&total] captured by reference so the lambda could accumulate into the outer variable.
lessons.task: Create a lambda squaring its argument, one capturing a `base` variable by copy and adding it, and one capturing a counter by reference to count calls. Demonstrate each.
hints: Use [base] for a copy and [&calls] for a reference.

lessons.title: Functions that call themselves
lessons.subtitle: Recursion
lessons.concept:
A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem, with a **base case** that returns without recursing. Without one it exhausts the stack.

Each call gets its own parameters and locals, stacked until the base case unwinds them.

Recursion suits naturally recursive structures — trees, nested data, divide-and-conquer. For plain counting a loop is faster and uses no stack. Naive recursive Fibonacci is the classic illustration: it recomputes the same values exponentially many times.

questions.q: What distinguishes two overloads of the same function name?
questions.explain: Overload resolution uses the argument types, so the return type alone cannot distinguish two overloads.

questions.q: Where do default arguments belong when a function is declared and defined separately?
questions.explain: The default goes in the declaration that callers see; repeating it in the definition is an error.

questions.q: What should you use to pass a large std::vector you only read?
questions.explain: A const reference avoids copying every element while guaranteeing the function will not modify it.

questions.q: What does [&total] in a lambda capture list mean?
options: A reference to total, so the lambda can modify it
questions.explain: The ampersand captures by reference, which is how a lambda accumulates into an enclosing variable.

questions.q: What must every recursive function have?
options: A base case that returns without recursing
questions.explain: Without a base case the recursion never terminates and eventually overflows the call stack.

lessons.title: Strings that manage themselves
lessons.subtitle: std::string
lessons.concept:
`std::string` from `<string>` is the antidote to C’s char arrays. It knows its own length, grows as needed, frees its own memory, and compares with `==` as you would expect.

No null terminator to manage, no buffer size to get wrong, no `strcpy` overflow. The class owns its storage and releases it when it goes out of scope.

Core members: `.size()` (or `.length()`, identical), `.empty()`, `[i]` for characters, and `+` to concatenate.
lessons.example_note: Comparing with == just works, unlike C where it would compare addresses.
lessons.task: Given `std::string lang{"C++"}`, print the string, its size, its first character, and the sentence `I am learning C++ today`.
lessons.expected_output:

3
C
I am learning C++ today
hints: Concatenation with + produces a new string.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: What a string can do
lessons.subtitle: substr, find, replace and more
lessons.concept:
`std::string` carries a large interface. The essentials:

- `.substr(pos, count)` a section, or from pos to the end if count is omitted
- `.find(text)` the index of the first match, or `std::string::npos` when absent
- `.replace(pos, count, text)` substitute in place
- `.append(text)` / `+=` add to the end
- `.insert(pos, text)`, `.erase(pos, count)`

The `npos` return is the one to remember: it is a huge unsigned value, so always compare against `std::string::npos` rather than testing for a negative result.
lessons.example_note: find returned 3 for "gram", and npos for the missing substring.
lessons.task: Given `std::string text{"the quick brown fox"}`, print the first three characters, everything from index 4, the index of `"brown"`, and whether it contains `"cat"`.
hints: Compare find’s result against std::string::npos.

lessons.title: Walking a string
lessons.subtitle: Loops and character tests
lessons.concept:
A `std::string` is a container, so a range-based for works: `for (char c : text)`.

Use `for (char& c : text)` to modify characters in place. `<cctype>` supplies `std::isalpha`, `std::isdigit`, `std::toupper` and `std::tolower`.

One subtlety carried over from C: those functions take an int and are undefined for negative values, so casting to `unsigned char` is the correct discipline. In practice you will see it in careful code and omitted elsewhere.
lessons.example_note: The char& loop modified upper in place; a plain char loop would only have changed copies.

lessons.title: Strings as streams
lessons.subtitle: stringstream for parsing and building
lessons.concept:
`<sstream>` lets you treat a string as a stream, which solves both parsing and formatting.

`std::istringstream` reads from a string: `>>` extracts whitespace-separated tokens with automatic type conversion, so pulling an int out of text takes one line. `std::getline(stream, piece, delim)` splits on any delimiter.

`std::ostringstream` builds a string with `<<`, giving you all the formatting manipulators and then `.str()` to retrieve the result.

This is the C++ answer to both `sscanf` and `sprintf`, with full type safety.

lessons.title: Between strings and numbers
lessons.subtitle: to_string and sto* functions
lessons.concept:
Two directions, both one-liners.

`std::to_string(value)` converts any arithmetic type to a string. Note it gives no control over precision — for formatted output use an ostringstream.

`std::stoi`, `std::stod`, `std::stol` parse a string into a number. They **throw** on failure: `std::invalid_argument` when there are no digits, `std::out_of_range` when the value will not fit. That is a real improvement over `atoi`, which silently returned 0 and left you unable to distinguish failure from a genuine zero.

lessons.title: The array that grows
lessons.subtitle: std::vector
lessons.concept:
`std::vector` is the container to reach for by default. It is a dynamic array that knows its size, grows on demand, and **frees its own memory** when it goes out of scope — no malloc, no free, no leak possible.

Core operations: `.push_back(x)` appends, `.size()` counts, `[i]` indexes, `.empty()` tests, `.clear()` empties, `.front()` and `.back()` reach the ends.

Compare this with the C module on malloc: the same capability, none of the bookkeeping. That is what a container buys you.
lessons.example_note: Note the difference: {3, 7} makes a two-element vector, while (3, 7) makes three copies of 7.
lessons.task: Build a vector of the squares of 1 to 5 with push_back, then print the size, each element on its own line, and the total.
hints: Fill the vector first, then print the size before the element loop.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Changing a vector
lessons.subtitle: insert, erase, resize
lessons.concept:
Beyond `push_back`, a vector supports:

- `.pop_back()` removes the last element
- `.insert(it, value)` inserts at an iterator position
- `.erase(it)` removes at a position; `.erase(first, last)` a range
- `.resize(n)` changes the size, default-filling any new elements
- `.assign(n, value)` replaces the contents

Insertion and removal in the **middle** must shift every following element, so they cost time proportional to the distance from the end. Appending and removing at the back are cheap. That asymmetry is the main thing to know when choosing a container.
lessons.example_note: resize filled the new slots with zero, since int default-initialises to 0 in a vector.

lessons.title: Positions within a container
lessons.subtitle: begin, end and iterators
lessons.concept:
An **iterator** is a generalised position in a container. `.begin()` is the first element and `.end()` is **one past the last** — a deliberately invalid position that marks the boundary.

That half-open convention `[begin, end)` is used everywhere in C++. It means `end() - begin()` is exactly the size, and an empty range is simply `begin() == end()`.

Dereference with `*it`, advance with `++it`. Every standard algorithm takes a pair of iterators rather than a container, which is why the same `std::sort` works on vectors, arrays and deques alike.
lessons.example_note: rbegin and rend are reverse iterators, so incrementing them walks backwards.

lessons.title: Vectors of vectors

A grid is a `std::vector<std::vector<int>>` — a vector whose elements are themselves vectors. Access with two subscripts: `grid[row][col]`.

Declare a fixed size with the fill constructor:

`std::vector<std::vector<int>> grid(3, std::vector<int>(4, 0));`

That reads as "three rows, each a vector of four zeros". Unlike a C two-dimensional array, the rows need not be the same length — each is independent, which makes ragged structures possible.

Iterate with nested range-for loops, using `const auto&` for the rows to avoid copying them.

lessons.title: Fixed size, modern interface
lessons.subtitle: std::array
lessons.concept:
`std::array<int, 5>` is a fixed-size array with a container interface. The size is part of the type, fixed at compile time.

Compared with a raw C array it gives you `.size()`, `.at()` with bounds checking, iterators, and normal copy semantics — while remaining exactly as fast, with no heap allocation.

Compared with a vector it cannot resize, but avoids the allocation entirely.

The choice: `std::array` when the size is known at compile time and never changes, `std::vector` otherwise. A raw `int[]` is rarely the right answer in modern C++.

options: It knows its size and frees its own memory

questions.q: What does v.end() point to?

questions.q: When should you prefer std::array over std::vector?

lessons.title: Key to value
lessons.subtitle: std::map
lessons.concept:
`std::map` stores sorted key/value pairs. Where a vector is indexed by position, a map is indexed by whatever key type you choose.

The behaviour to know: indexing with a key that does not exist **creates** it with a default value — zero for numbers, empty for strings. That makes counting a one-liner: `counts[word]++`.

It also means `if (m["key"] == 0)` silently inserts. Use `.count(key)` or `.find(key)` to test for presence without modifying, and `.at(key)` to read with an exception on failure.

Iterating a map always yields keys in **sorted** order.
lessons.example_note: The output is apple, banana, cherry — sorted by key, not by insertion order.

Peru: Lima
hints: Structured bindings unpack each pair into two names.

lessons.title: Counting with a map
lessons.subtitle: The counting idiom
lessons.concept:
Counting is the most common use of a map, and C++ makes it a single expression:

`counts[key]++`

Because `operator[]` default-constructs the value when the key is absent, an int starts at 0 and the increment leaves it at 1. No special case for the first occurrence.

This generalises: `totals[key] += amount` accumulates, and `groups[key].push_back(item)` builds a map of vectors, since the vector is default-constructed empty.
lessons.example_note: by_length[w.size()] created an empty vector on first use, so push_back always works.

lessons.title: Unique sorted values
lessons.subtitle: std::set
lessons.concept:
`std::set` stores unique values in sorted order. Inserting a duplicate is silently ignored, which makes it the natural deduplicator.

`.insert(x)` adds, `.count(x)` tests membership, `.erase(x)` removes, and iteration yields sorted values.

`.insert` returns a pair whose `.second` is a bool saying whether the insertion actually happened — useful when you need to know if a value was new.

Use a set when you need uniqueness or ordered membership testing; use `std::unordered_set` when you need neither ordering and want faster lookups.

lessons.title: Bundling two or more values
lessons.subtitle: std::pair and std::tuple
lessons.concept:
`std::pair<A, B>` holds exactly two values, accessed as `.first` and `.second`. It is what a map element is, and it is the simplest way for a function to return two things.

`std::tuple` generalises to any number, accessed with `std::get<0>(t)`.

Since C++17, **structured bindings** unpack either into named variables:

`auto [name, score] = get_result();`

That is far more readable than `.first` and `.second`, and it is why the map iteration in these lessons reads so cleanly. For anything with meaning beyond "two values", a small struct with named members is still better.

lessons.title: Hashing instead of sorting
lessons.subtitle: unordered_map and unordered_set
lessons.concept:
`std::unordered_map` and `std::unordered_set` are hash-based. They provide the same interface as their ordered siblings, with two differences: lookups are faster on average, and iteration order is **unspecified**.

The trade is exactly that. Choose `map` when you need sorted iteration or ordered queries; choose `unordered_map` when you only need fast key lookups.

Because the order is unpredictable, any program that must produce deterministic output has to collect the entries and sort them before printing — which is worth remembering when comparing the two.

lessons.title: Ordering a range
lessons.subtitle: std::sort and comparators
lessons.concept:
`std::sort(first, last)` orders a range in place. It takes **iterators**, not a container, which is why the same function works on vectors, arrays and any other random-access range.

A third argument supplies a custom comparison: a function or lambda returning `true` when the first argument must come **before** the second. `return a > b;` gives descending order.

The comparator must define a strict ordering — using `>=` instead of `>` is undefined behaviour, because the algorithm relies on the comparison being irreflexive.

`std::stable_sort` preserves the relative order of equal elements, at slightly higher cost.
lessons.example_note: The last sort ordered by length rather than alphabetically, purely by changing the comparator.

lessons.title: Searching a range
lessons.subtitle: find, count and their _if variants
lessons.concept:
The searching algorithms all return **iterators**, and signal failure by returning the end iterator — the same half-open convention as everywhere else.

- `std::find(first, last, value)` locates a value
- `std::find_if(first, last, pred)` locates the first element satisfying a predicate
- `std::count(first, last, value)` and `std::count_if(...)` tally matches
- `std::any_of`, `std::all_of`, `std::none_of` answer questions about the whole range

The `_if` suffix is the pattern: the plain version compares against a value, the `_if` version calls your predicate. Always compare a result against `end()` before dereferencing it.
lessons.example_note: Subtracting begin() from the found iterator converts it back to an index.

lessons.title: Mapping and reducing
lessons.subtitle: transform and accumulate
lessons.concept:
`std::transform` applies a function to every element of a range, writing the results to a destination. The destination may be the same range (transform in place) or a different one — use `std::back_inserter` to append to an empty vector.

`std::accumulate` from `<numeric>` reduces a range to one value. The third argument is the initial value, and it also determines the result **type**: passing `0` with doubles truncates every intermediate result, so pass `0.0`.

A fourth argument replaces addition with any binary operation, making it a general fold.
lessons.example_note: The last transform wrote back into nums itself, modifying it in place.

lessons.title: Extremes and rearrangement
lessons.subtitle: min_element, reverse, unique
lessons.concept:
A group of algorithms that operate on whole ranges:

- `std::min_element` / `std::max_element` return **iterators**, so dereference to get the value
- `std::minmax_element` returns both as a pair
- `std::reverse` reverses in place
- `std::rotate` shifts elements around
- `std::unique` removes **consecutive** duplicates and returns the new logical end

That last one has a famous quirk: `unique` does not shrink the container, it only moves the unwanted elements to the back. The idiom is `v.erase(std::unique(v.begin(), v.end()), v.end())`, and the range must be sorted first for it to remove all duplicates.
lessons.example_note: Sorting before unique is essential, since it only collapses runs of adjacent equal values.
lessons.task: For {8, 3, 91, 42, 17}, print the smallest, the largest, and the vector reversed. Then deduplicate {4, 1, 4, 2, 1} properly and print the result.

lessons.title: Searching sorted ranges
lessons.subtitle: binary_search and bounds
lessons.concept:
On a **sorted** range, the library offers logarithmic searches.

`std::binary_search` returns only a bool. When you need the position, use `std::lower_bound` — the first element **not less** than the value — or `std::upper_bound`, the first element **greater** than it.

Together they delimit the range of equal values, which `std::equal_range` returns as a pair. `lower_bound` is also exactly the correct insertion point to keep a vector sorted.

All of these are undefined on an unsorted range, and will silently give wrong answers rather than complaining.
lessons.example_note: lower_bound gave the correct insertion point, keeping the vector sorted after the insert.

hints: lower_bound gives the insertion point that preserves sorted order.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Chaining algorithms together
lessons.subtitle: Building real pipelines
lessons.concept:
Real work combines several algorithms. The typical pipeline is filter, transform, then reduce.

`std::copy_if` selects elements into a destination. `std::transform` maps them. `std::accumulate` reduces. Each step is a named operation with obvious intent, which is the argument for using them over hand-written loops.

`std::remove_if` deserves particular note: like `unique`, it does not shrink the container. It moves the unwanted elements to the back and returns the new logical end, so the erase-remove idiom is:

`v.erase(std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), pred), v.end())`

questions.q: Why do standard algorithms take iterators rather than containers?
options: So the same algorithm works on any range, including parts of a container
questions.explain: Iterator pairs decouple algorithms from containers, so std::sort works on vectors, arrays and sub-ranges alike.

questions.q: What does std::remove_if actually do?
options: Moves unwanted elements to the back and returns the new logical end
questions.explain: It cannot resize the container, which is why it must be wrapped in the erase-remove idiom.

questions.q: Why must a range be sorted before std::unique?
options: unique only collapses runs of adjacent equal elements
questions.explain: Non-adjacent duplicates are left untouched, so sorting first is what makes the deduplication complete.

questions.q: What does accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0) do with a vector of doubles?
options: Truncates each intermediate result because the accumulator is an int
questions.explain: The initial value fixes the accumulator type, so 0.0 must be passed for floating-point sums.

questions.q: What does std::lower_bound return?
options: The first element not less than the value — the sorted insertion point
questions.explain: That property makes it both a search and the correct place to insert while keeping the range sorted.

lessons.title: Defining your own types
lessons.subtitle: struct, class and access
lessons.concept:
A `struct` groups data; in C++ it can also hold **member functions** that operate on that data, which is what makes it an object rather than a bag of fields.

`class` is the same construct with one difference: members are **private** by default, whereas a struct’s are public.

The convention that follows: use `struct` for plain aggregates with no invariants, and `class` when the type maintains rules about its own state. `public:` and `private:` sections switch the access level for everything following.

Marking a member function `const` promises it will not modify the object, which lets it be called on const instances.
lessons.example_note: Counter’s value is private, so the only way to change it is through increment — that is encapsulation.
lessons.task: Define a `Rect` struct with width, height, and const member functions `area()` and `is_square()`. Create a 4x6 and a 5x5 and print both results for each.
hints: Mark both member functions const since neither modifies the object.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Setting up an object
lessons.subtitle: Constructors and initialiser lists
lessons.concept:
A **constructor** runs when an object is created. It has the class’s name and no return type.

The preferred way to set members is the **member initialiser list** — the `: name{value}` clause between the signature and the body. It initialises members directly, rather than default-constructing them and then assigning, which is both faster and required for const members and references.

Constructors can be overloaded, and a **default constructor** takes no arguments. If you declare any constructor, the compiler stops generating the default one for you.

Members are initialised in **declaration order**, regardless of the order you list them.
lessons.example_note: std::move avoids copying the string parameter into the member — a small but idiomatic touch.
lessons.task: Define a `Student` class with private name and score, a two-argument constructor using an initialiser list, and a const `describe()` printing `Ada scored 91`. Create two students and describe both.
hints: The initialiser list goes after the constructor signature, before the body.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Controlling access to state
lessons.subtitle: Encapsulation and validation
lessons.concept:
Making members private and exposing functions is not bureaucracy — it is where **invariants** live. A setter can reject impossible values, so the object can never hold nonsense.

The pattern: a `const` getter returning the value, and a setter that validates before assigning. Once the class guarantees its own consistency, no caller can break it.

Derived values need no storage at all: `area()` computes from width and height, so it can never disagree with them. Prefer computing over caching when the calculation is cheap.
lessons.example_note: The impossible temperature was refused, so the object still holds its last valid value.
lessons.task: Define an `Account` class with a private balance, a const `get_balance()`, a `deposit(amount)` rejecting non-positive amounts, and a `withdraw(amount)` refusing overdrafts. Both return bool. Demonstrate a valid deposit, a valid withdrawal and a refused withdrawal.
hints: Validate before assigning, and return false without changing anything on failure.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Making your type feel built in
lessons.subtitle: Operator overloading
lessons.concept:
C++ lets you define what the operators mean for your own types. `operator+` enables `a + b`, `operator==` enables comparison, and `operator<<` enables stream output.

The stream operator must be a **free function**, not a member, because the left operand is the stream rather than your object:

`std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Point& p)`

It returns the stream so insertions can chain.

The discipline: overload only when the meaning is genuinely obvious. `+` on two points is clear; `+` on two employees is not. Surprising operators are worse than named functions.
lessons.example_note: Because operator<< returns the stream, the whole expression chains in one statement.
lessons.task: Define a `Money` class holding cents, with `operator+`, `operator==` and a free `operator<<` printing it as `12.50`. Add two amounts and print the result and an equality test.
hints: operator<< must be a free function returning std::ostream&.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Cleanup that cannot be forgotten
lessons.subtitle: Destructors and RAII
lessons.concept:
A **destructor** (`~ClassName()`) runs automatically when an object goes out of scope. This is the foundation of **RAII** — Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation — the single most important idea in C++.

The principle: acquire a resource in the constructor, release it in the destructor. Then it is released **no matter how** the scope exits: normal return, early return, or an exception. There is no `free` to forget and no cleanup path to miss.

This is why `std::vector` and `std::string` cannot leak, and why C++ needs no garbage collector. Destruction happens in reverse order of construction.
lessons.example_note: inner was released at its closing brace, and outer when demo returned — reverse construction order, automatically.
lessons.task: Define a `Guard` class printing `open: name` in its constructor and `close: name` in its destructor. Create one in main and another inside a nested scope, printing a line between, to demonstrate the ordering.

open: outer
open: inner
working
close: inner
after
close: outer
hints: The destructor name is the class name with a leading tilde.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Data belonging to the class
lessons.subtitle: Static members
lessons.concept:
A **static** data member belongs to the class, not to any instance: one copy shared by all objects. It is the right tool for counters and shared constants.

A **static member function** likewise belongs to the class. It has no `this`, so it cannot touch instance members, and is called as `ClassName::function()`. Factory functions and utilities are the usual uses.

Since C++17, a static member can be declared `inline` and initialised inside the class; before that it required a separate definition outside.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: classes
lessons.subtitle: Check what stuck before moving on
lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What is the only difference between struct and class in C++?
options: Default access: struct members are public, class members are private
questions.explain: Both support member functions, constructors and inheritance; only the default access level differs.

questions.q: Why prefer a member initialiser list over assigning in the constructor body?
options: It initialises members directly instead of default-constructing then assigning, and is required for const members
It is required by the standard
questions.explain: Assignment in the body means the member is constructed twice over, and const members and references cannot be assigned at all.

questions.q: What does marking a member function const promise?
options: The function will not modify the object
questions.explain: A const member function can be called on const objects, and the compiler enforces that it makes no modifications.

questions.q: Why must operator<< be a free function?
options: The left operand is the stream, not your class
questions.explain: A member operator takes the object as its left operand, but here the stream is on the left, so it cannot be a member of your type.

questions.q: What is RAII?
options: Acquiring a resource in the constructor and releasing it in the destructor, so cleanup cannot be skipped
questions.explain: Because destructors run on every exit path including exceptions, RAII is what makes leaks structurally impossible.

lessons.title: One function, any type
lessons.subtitle: Function templates
lessons.concept:
A **template** is a pattern the compiler uses to generate code for whatever type you supply. `template <typename T>` introduces T as a placeholder.

When you call `larger(3, 7)`, the compiler **instantiates** a version for int; calling it with doubles generates a second version. Both are fully type-checked, and there is no run-time cost — this is compile-time polymorphism.

The type is usually deduced from the arguments, so you rarely write it explicitly. When you need to, `larger<double>(3, 7)` forces the choice.

This is how the entire standard library achieves generality.
lessons.example_note: One definition of larger served ints, doubles and strings, with each version type-checked separately.
lessons.task: Write a template `T triple(T value)` and a template `void print_pair(const T& a, const T& b)` printing both separated by a space. Use both with ints, doubles and strings.
hints: Using + rather than * makes triple work for strings as well as numbers.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Generic types
lessons.subtitle: Class templates
lessons.concept:
A class can be templated too. `std::vector<int>` and `std::vector<std::string>` are two distinct classes generated from one template.

Inside the class, T is used like any other type. Member functions defined in the class body are themselves templates, instantiated only when actually called.

A template can take several parameters, and they need not all be types — `template <typename T, std::size_t N>` takes a type and a compile-time integer, which is exactly how `std::array` works.

Since C++17 the class template argument is often deduced from the constructor, so `Pair p{1, 2.5}` works without spelling out the types.
lessons.example_note: Box<int> and Box<std::string> are entirely separate classes, each generated on demand.
lessons.task: Write a template `class Stack<T>` backed by a std::vector with `push`, `pop` returning the removed value, `size` and `empty`. Use it with ints and strings.
hints: Store the elements in a std::vector<T> member.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Templates that accept anything callable
lessons.subtitle: Generic algorithms
lessons.concept:
A template parameter can be a **callable** — a function, a lambda, or anything with `operator()`. This is how the standard algorithms accept your predicates without knowing their types.

`template <typename T, typename Predicate> int count_if(const std::vector<T>&, Predicate)` works with any lambda you pass, and the compiler generates a version specialised to that exact lambda type. That is why algorithm calls with lambdas are as fast as hand-written loops — the call is inlined, with no indirection.

This pattern, generic over both data and behaviour, is the heart of the standard library’s design.
lessons.example_note: The same count_matching worked on ints and strings with completely different predicates.
lessons.task: Write `template <typename T, typename Predicate> std::vector<T> filter(const std::vector<T>&, Predicate)` returning the matching elements. Use it to keep the values above 10 from a vector of ints, and the strings longer than two characters.
hints: The predicate parameter type is just another template parameter.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: A special case for one type
lessons.subtitle: Template specialisation
lessons.concept:
Sometimes the generic implementation is wrong for one particular type. **Full specialisation** provides a distinct definition for it:

`template <> std::string describe<bool>(bool value) { ... }`

The compiler prefers the specialisation when the type matches exactly, and falls back to the general template otherwise.

The classic real example is `std::vector<bool>`, specialised to pack booleans as bits — which is also a cautionary tale, since it behaves subtly differently from every other vector.

Use specialisation sparingly; overloading is usually simpler and clearer.
lessons.example_note: Without the specialisation, describe(true) would have printed "value 1".
lessons.task: Write a template `std::string label(T)` returning `number: N`, with a full specialisation for bool returning `flag: true` or `flag: false`. Call it with an int, a double and both bool values.
lessons.expected_output:

number: 1.500000
flag: true
flag: false
hints: The specialisation begins with an empty template <> and names the type explicitly.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Building on an existing class
lessons.subtitle: Inheritance and virtual functions
lessons.concept:
`class Dog : public Animal` makes Dog a subclass, inheriting everything Animal has.

The crucial keyword is `virtual`. Without it, calling a function through a base-class pointer or reference calls the **base** version, even when the object is really a Dog. Marking it `virtual` enables **dynamic dispatch**, so the correct override runs — which is what polymorphism means.

Two rules follow. Any class meant to be inherited from needs a `virtual` destructor, or deleting through a base pointer leaks the derived part. And `override` on the derived function makes the compiler verify that you really are overriding something.

A `virtual` function with `= 0` is **pure virtual**, making the class abstract — an interface that cannot be instantiated.
lessons.example_note: report() is defined only on Shape, yet each object’s own area() and name() are called — that is dynamic dispatch.

Tom says meow
hints: The derived constructors pass the name up to Animal in their initialiser lists.

questions.q: When is template code generated?
options: At compile time, once per set of types actually used
questions.explain: The compiler instantiates a separate version for each type combination, which is why templates cost nothing at run time.

questions.q: What happens if a base-class function is not virtual and you call it through a base reference?
options: The base version runs, because the static type decides
questions.explain: Without virtual there is no dynamic dispatch, so the type of the reference rather than the object selects the function.

questions.q: Why does a polymorphic base class need a virtual destructor?
options: So deleting through a base pointer also destroys the derived part
It is required for all classes
questions.explain: Without it only the base destructor runs, leaking whatever the derived class owned.

questions.q: What does = 0 on a virtual function mean?
options: It is pure virtual, making the class abstract
questions.explain: A pure virtual function has no base implementation, so the class cannot be instantiated and acts as an interface.

questions.q: What does the override keyword achieve?
options: It makes the compiler verify that the function really overrides a virtual base function
It creates a new virtual function
questions.explain: It catches subtle signature mismatches that would otherwise silently create an unrelated function.

lessons.title: Ownership without leaks
lessons.subtitle: unique_ptr and shared_ptr
lessons.concept:
Raw `new` and `delete` are almost never correct in modern C++, because any early return or exception between them leaks.

`std::unique_ptr<T>` owns a heap object exclusively and deletes it in its destructor. It cannot be copied — only **moved** — which encodes "exactly one owner" in the type system. Create one with `std::make_unique<T>(args)`.

`std::shared_ptr<T>` allows several owners by reference counting, deleting the object when the last one goes away. It is heavier, so reach for `unique_ptr` first.

This is RAII applied to memory: the resource is released automatically, on every exit path.
lessons.example_note: The count rose to 2 while the second owner existed, then fell back — and the object survived until the last one left.
lessons.task: Define a `Logger` class printing on construction and destruction. Create one in a unique_ptr inside a nested scope, then create a shared_ptr and print use_count before, during and after copying it in an inner scope.
lessons.expected_output:
start one
inside unique scope
stop one
start many
1
2
1
stop many
hints: make_unique and make_shared construct the object and the pointer together.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Transferring rather than copying
lessons.subtitle: Move semantics
lessons.concept:
Copying a large object duplicates all its data. **Moving** transfers ownership of the internals instead, leaving the source in a valid but unspecified state. For a vector of a million elements, a copy allocates and copies everything while a move just swaps a few pointers.

The compiler moves automatically when the source is a temporary — a function return value, for instance. `std::move(x)` asks for a move from a named variable, promising you will not rely on its value afterwards.

This is why returning a large vector by value is efficient in modern C++: the return is a move, not a copy.
lessons.example_note: After the move, source is valid but its contents are unspecified — never read it, only reassign it.
lessons.task: Write a function returning a vector of five ints. Call it and print the size. Then copy a string and print both sizes, move it into another string and print the destination and its size.
hints: Returning a local vector by value is a move, so it costs nothing.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Reporting failures
lessons.subtitle: try, catch and throw
lessons.concept:
An **exception** signals that a function cannot fulfil its contract. `throw` raises one and unwinds the stack until a matching `catch` is found, running every destructor along the way — which is precisely why RAII and exceptions work so well together.

Catch by `const&` to avoid copying, and catch specific types before general ones since the first match wins. The standard hierarchy has `std::logic_error` and `std::runtime_error` under `std::exception`, whose `.what()` returns the message.

Use exceptions for genuinely exceptional conditions, not ordinary control flow. A function that fails routinely should return an optional or a status instead.
lessons.example_note: The Guard destructor ran during the unwinding, before the catch — no cleanup was skipped.
lessons.task: Write `int withdraw(int balance, int amount)` throwing `std::invalid_argument` for a non-positive amount and `std::runtime_error` for insufficient funds. Call it three times inside try/catch blocks, printing the result or the message.
lessons.expected_output:
70
invalid: amount must be positive
failed: insufficient funds
hints: Catch the more specific type first, and catch by const reference.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: A value that might not be there
lessons.subtitle: std::optional
lessons.concept:
`std::optional<T>` from `<optional>` holds either a value or nothing. It replaces the old conventions of returning `-1`, a null pointer, or a bool plus an output parameter.

The advantage is that the absence is **in the type**, so the compiler reminds you it exists. Test with `.has_value()` or by using the optional directly as a bool, read with `*opt` or `.value()`, and supply a fallback with `.value_or(default)`.

Use it when failure is ordinary and expected — a lookup that finds nothing. Use an exception when failure means something has genuinely gone wrong.
lessons.example_note: value_or collapses the two cases into one expression when a sensible default exists.
lessons.task: Write `std::optional<int> safe_divide(int a, int b)` returning nullopt when b is zero. Call it with (10, 2) and (10, 0), printing has_value, the value via value_or(-1), and dereferencing only when present.
hints: Return std::nullopt for the empty case.
Match the expected output exactly, including every space and newline.

lessons.title: Putting it all together
lessons.subtitle: Realistic data processing
lessons.concept:
A closing tour combining the whole track: a class with encapsulated state, a vector of objects, algorithms with lambdas, and formatted output.

The shape of most real C++ data work is exactly this. Parse input into objects, store them in a container, then use algorithms to filter, sort and reduce. Each step reads as what it does rather than how it loops.

The habits worth carrying forward: `const` by default, `const&` for parameters, containers over raw arrays, algorithms over hand-written loops, and RAII for anything that needs cleaning up.

lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: Why can std::unique_ptr not be copied?
options: Because it encodes exclusive ownership — copying would create two owners of one object
questions.explain: Allowing a copy would mean two destructors deleting the same object, so only moving is permitted.

questions.q: What does std::move actually do?
options: Marks a value as movable so the move constructor is selected
questions.explain: It performs no work itself; it changes overload resolution so the move rather than the copy is chosen.

questions.q: Why do RAII and exceptions work well together?
options: Destructors run during stack unwinding, so cleanup cannot be skipped
questions.explain: Every automatic object between the throw and the catch is destroyed, which is why RAII types never leak on error paths.

questions.q: When should you prefer std::optional over throwing?
options: When absence is an ordinary expected outcome, such as a lookup finding nothing
questions.explain: Exceptions are for genuinely exceptional conditions; routine absence is better expressed in the return type.

questions.q: Why is returning a large std::vector by value efficient in modern C++?
options: The return is a move, transferring the buffer rather than copying it
questions.explain: Move semantics and copy elision mean the caller receives the same buffer, so nothing is duplicated.

lessons.title: Everything lives in a class
lessons.subtitle: The class wrapper and main
lessons.concept:
Java has one firm rule: all code lives inside a **class**. Even a one-line program needs a class to hold it.

Execution begins at a method with this exact signature:

`public static void main(String[] args)`

Every word matters. `public` means callable from outside, `static` means it belongs to the class rather than an instance, `void` means it returns nothing, and `String[] args` receives command-line arguments.

`System.out.println(...)` prints a line. Statements end with semicolons and blocks use braces. The ceremony looks heavy for one line, but it is the same structure a million-line codebase uses.
lessons.example_note: The class must be named Main here, because that is the filename the runner uses.
lessons.task: Print exactly `Hello, world!` from inside main.
hints: System.out.println("Hello, world!"); — note the semicolon.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: With or without a newline
lessons.subtitle: print, println and printf
lessons.concept:
Three output methods, each with a distinct purpose.

`println(x)` prints and adds a newline. `print(x)` prints without one, so the next output continues on the same line. `printf(format, args...)` uses format specifiers like C, and needs an explicit `%n` for the newline.

`println` with no argument prints just a blank line. Prefer `printf` when you need alignment or a fixed number of decimals; prefer `println` for everything else.
lessons.example_note: printf without %n leaves the cursor mid-line, which is a common surprise.
lessons.task: Using print and println, build the single line `red-green-blue`, then use printf to print `count: 7` and `price: 2.50`.
hints: Only the last piece of the joined line needs println.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Notes for humans
lessons.subtitle: Three comment styles
lessons.concept:
Java has three comment forms. `//` runs to the end of the line. `/* ... */` spans multiple lines. `/** ... */` is a **Javadoc** comment, which tooling extracts into API documentation.

Javadoc is the distinctive one: placed above a class or method, it uses tags like `@param` and `@return` and becomes the official documentation. The entire Java standard library reference is generated this way.
lessons.example_note: Comments are stripped before compilation, so they can never affect behaviour.
lessons.task: Print `well documented` and `and clear` on two lines, including a Javadoc comment above the class and a line comment inside main.
hints: The Javadoc comment starts with /** and sits above the class declaration.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Special characters
lessons.subtitle: Escape sequences
lessons.concept:
Awkward characters inside a string literal need escaping:

- `\n` newline
- `\t` tab
- `\\` a literal backslash
- `\"` a literal double quote

Since `println` already adds a newline, `\n` is used to create additional line breaks inside one string. A single `println` containing two `\n` characters therefore produces three lines.
lessons.example_note: The backslash is an instruction to the compiler, so it never appears in the output.
lessons.task:
Produce these three tab-separated lines using exactly two println calls:

`lang	year`
`Java	1995`
`Rust	2015`
hints: Put the \n inside the second string to get two lines from one call.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Formatted output
lessons.subtitle: printf specifiers and widths
lessons.concept:
`printf` takes a format string with **specifiers** filled by the following arguments:

- `%s` any object, via its toString
- `%d` integer
- `%f` floating point, `%.2f` for two decimals
- `%b` boolean
- `%n` platform newline

A width before the type sets a minimum field: `%10s` right-aligns in ten columns, `%-10s` left-aligns. That is how tables are produced without counting spaces.

Unlike C, a mismatch throws an exception at run time rather than producing garbage.
lessons.example_note: The minus sign left-aligns; without it the text is pushed right within the field.
lessons.task: Print a table with names left-aligned in 8 columns and scores right-aligned in 4, for ada/91, bob/7 and cy/100.
hints: Use %-8s for the name and %4d for the number.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: How Java runs
lessons.subtitle: Bytecode and the JVM
lessons.concept:
Java compiles in two stages. `javac` turns source into **bytecode** — a portable instruction set stored in `.class` files. The **JVM** then executes that bytecode, compiling the hot parts to native code as the program runs.

That is what "write once, run anywhere" means: the bytecode is identical on every platform, and only the JVM differs.

One practical consequence: a public class must live in a file matching its name, so `public class Main` belongs in `Main.java`. Another is that Java catches type errors at compile time, like C++, rather than at run time like Python.
lessons.example_note: System.getProperty reads JVM properties — evidence that the program is running inside a managed runtime.

questions.q: Why must main be declared static?
options: So the JVM can call it without creating an instance of the class
questions.explain: static members belong to the class itself, so the JVM can invoke main before any object exists.

questions.q: What is the difference between print and println?

questions.q: What does printf need that println does not?

questions.q: What does javac produce?
options: Bytecode in .class files, executed by the JVM
questions.explain: The portable bytecode is what makes the same compiled program run on any platform with a JVM.

questions.q: What must be true of a file containing public class Main?

It must have a main method

lessons.title: The eight primitive types
lessons.subtitle: Declaring variables
lessons.concept:
Java has exactly eight **primitive** types, and every variable’s type is fixed at declaration.

The ones you need first:
- `int` — whole number, 32 bits
- `double` — floating point, 64 bits
- `boolean` — `true` or `false`, a real type unlike in C
- `char` — a single character in single quotes

The others are `byte`, `short`, `long` and `float`. A `long` literal needs an `L` suffix and a `float` literal an `f`, because the defaults are `int` and `double`.

Unlike a local variable in C, Java refuses to compile if you read a local before assigning it — a genuinely useful restriction.
lessons.example_note: Without the L suffix, 9000000000 would be an int literal and would not fit, causing a compile error.
lessons.task: Declare an int of 7, a double of 2.5, a boolean of true and a char of `Z`, then print each on its own line.
hints: Char literals use single quotes; strings use double quotes.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: String is not a primitive
lessons.subtitle: Objects and references
lessons.concept:
`String` starts with a capital letter because it is a **class**, not a primitive. A String variable holds a **reference** to an object rather than the value itself.

That distinction has one immediate consequence: comparing Strings with `==` compares references, asking "are these the same object". Use `.equals()` to compare the characters. This is the single most common Java beginner bug.

Strings are also **immutable** — every method returns a new String rather than modifying the original.

String concatenation with `+` converts the other operand automatically, evaluating strictly left to right: `1 + 2 + "x"` is `3x`, but `"x" + 1 + 2` is `x12`.
lessons.example_note: toUpperCase returned a new String; name itself was unchanged, as the last print of name shows.
lessons.task: Declare `String word = "java"`. Print it, its length, its uppercase form, the original again to show immutability, and whether it equals `"java"`.
hints: Compare with .equals(), never with ==.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Letting the compiler infer
lessons.subtitle: The var keyword
lessons.concept:
Since Java 10, `var` lets the compiler deduce a local variable’s type from its initialiser. The variable is still **statically typed** — you simply avoided repeating something obvious.

`var names = new ArrayList<String>();` is much better than writing the type twice.

The limits: `var` works only for local variables with an initialiser, never for fields, parameters or return types. And it cannot be `null` on its own, since there would be nothing to infer from.

Use it when the type is obvious from the right-hand side; write the type out when naming it documents intent.
lessons.example_note: var items avoided writing ArrayList<String> twice on one line, which is its clearest use.
lessons.task: Using var, declare an int, a double, a String and an ArrayList<String> with two elements added. Print all four.
hints: var always needs an initialiser to infer from.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Converting between types
lessons.subtitle: Widening, narrowing and integer division
lessons.concept:
Java converts **widening** types automatically — an int becomes a double without asking, since nothing is lost. **Narrowing** requires an explicit cast, because data may be lost: `(int) 3.9` gives `3`, truncating rather than rounding.

The integer division trap is present as ever: `7 / 2` is `3` when both operands are int. Cast one to double to get `3.5`.

For strings, `Integer.parseInt("42")` and `Double.parseDouble("2.5")` parse text into numbers and **throw** `NumberFormatException` on failure. `String.valueOf(n)` or concatenating with `""` goes the other way.
lessons.example_note: Widening from int to double needed no cast; narrowing from double to int did.
lessons.task: With `int total = 47` and `int people = 6`, print the truncating division, the exact average via a cast, that average truncated back to an int, and the result of parsing `"250"` plus one.
hints: Casting one operand is enough; the other is promoted automatically.

lessons.title: Objects wrapping primitives
lessons.subtitle: Wrapper classes and autoboxing
lessons.concept:
Every primitive has a matching **wrapper class**: `Integer` for int, `Double` for double, `Boolean` for boolean, `Character` for char.

Wrappers are needed because collections hold objects, not primitives — `ArrayList<int>` is illegal, so you write `ArrayList<Integer>`. Java converts between the two automatically, which is called **autoboxing** and **unboxing**.

Wrappers also carry useful statics: `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, `Integer.parseInt`, `Double.parseDouble`.

The trap: `==` on two Integer objects compares references. Small values are cached so it sometimes appears to work, which makes the bug worse. Always use `.equals()` or compare the unboxed `intValue()`.
lessons.example_note: a == b was false despite equal values, because the two Integer objects are distinct. That is why .equals matters.
lessons.task: Declare an Integer holding 100 and unbox it into an int, printing both. Print Integer.MAX_VALUE. Add two Integers to an ArrayList<Integer> and print it. Then compare two Integers holding 500 with both == and .equals().
hints: Autoboxing means you can add an int literal directly to an ArrayList<Integer>.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Values that must not change
lessons.subtitle: final
lessons.concept:
`final` on a variable means it can be assigned exactly once. Attempting to reassign it is a compile error.

Constants are conventionally `static final` fields in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, declared at class level. `static` means one shared copy, `final` means unchangeable.

One subtlety worth understanding: `final` on a reference prevents **repointing**, not modification. A `final List` cannot be reassigned to a different list, but items can still be added to it. Immutability of the object is a separate concern from finality of the reference.
lessons.example_note: The final StringBuilder could still be appended to — final locked the reference, not the object.

hints: Class-level constants go outside main but inside the class.

lessons.title: Arithmetic operators
lessons.subtitle: Five operators and integer division
lessons.concept:
Java has `+ - * / %`. There is no exponentiation operator — `Math.pow(base, exp)` covers that, returning a double.

The division rule depends on the operand types: two ints divide as integers, truncating, while any double operand gives floating-point division. `%` works on both, and on doubles gives a fractional remainder.

Integer overflow **wraps silently** rather than throwing, so `Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1` becomes the minimum value. Use `long` when values may grow large, or `Math.addExact` which throws on overflow.
lessons.example_note: The overflow wrapped to the minimum int without any warning — a genuine hazard.
lessons.task: With `int a = 23` and `int b = 4`, print the sum, product, integer quotient, remainder, exact quotient to two decimals, and 2 to the power 8 as an int.
hints: Math.pow returns a double, so cast it to print a whole number.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Updating a value
lessons.subtitle: Increment and compound assignment
lessons.concept:
`i++` and `++i` both add one, but they **evaluate** differently. Postfix yields the old value, prefix the new one. As a standalone statement they are identical.

The compound operators `+= -= *= /= %=` update in place. They have a hidden feature: they perform an **implicit cast** back to the target type. So `int i = 5; i += 2.7;` compiles and gives 7, whereas `i = i + 2.7;` would refuse to compile because the result is a double.

That asymmetry is worth knowing, since it can silently truncate.
lessons.example_note: truncated became 7, not 7.7 — the compound operator cast the double result back to int.
lessons.task: Start `int n = 8`. Print n, then n++, then n, then ++n, then n. Then start at 100 and apply -=20, /=2 and %=7, printing after each.
hints: Postfix reports the old value, prefix the new one.

lessons.title: Comparing and combining
lessons.subtitle: Relational and logical operators
lessons.concept:
The six comparisons produce a genuine `boolean`, so `if (x = 5)` is a **compile error** rather than a silent bug as in C.

`&&`, `||` and `!` combine booleans and **short-circuit**: `&&` stops at the first false, `||` at the first true. That guarantee is what makes `if (s != null && s.length() > 0)` safe.

Java also has `&` and `|` for booleans, which do **not** short-circuit and always evaluate both sides. They are rarely what you want.

Java has no chained comparisons, so `0 < x < 10` will not compile.
lessons.example_note: The last line is safe because && never evaluates length() when s is null.
lessons.task: With `int n = 15`, print whether it equals 15, is under 10, lies strictly between 10 and 20, and is not 20. Then with a null String, safely print whether it is non-null and non-empty.
hints: The range test needs two comparisons joined by &&.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Working with bits
lessons.subtitle: Bitwise and shift operators
lessons.concept:
Java has `& | ^ ~` and the shifts `<< >>`, plus one operator C lacks: `>>>`, the **unsigned right shift**.

The distinction matters because Java has no unsigned integer types. `>>` preserves the sign bit, so `-8 >> 1` is `-4`. `>>>` fills with zeros, so `-8 >>> 1` becomes a large positive number.

The standard idioms are the same as in C: set with `|=`, clear with `&= ~`, toggle with `^=`, test with `(x >> n) & 1`.

`Integer.toBinaryString(n)` prints the bits, which makes experimenting far easier.
lessons.example_note: -8 >> 1 gave -4 while -8 >>> 28 gave a positive value, because the sign bit was not preserved.
lessons.task: With `int flags = 10`, print the result of anding with 12, oring with 5, xoring with 15, shifting left once, the binary string, and Integer.bitCount of 255.
hints: Integer.bitCount counts the set bits directly.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Order of evaluation and choices
lessons.subtitle: Precedence and the conditional operator
lessons.concept:
Precedence, tightest first: unary operators and casts, then `* / %`, then `+ -`, then shifts, then comparisons, then `& ^ |`, then `&&`, then `||`, then `?:`, then assignment.

As in C, the bitwise operators bind looser than comparisons, so `a & 1 == 0` means `a & (1 == 0)` — which in Java is a compile error rather than a silent bug, since you cannot bitwise-and an int with a boolean. Java’s type system catches this one for you.

The conditional operator `?:` is the only ternary operator. It produces a value, so it fits inside expressions where an `if` statement cannot.
lessons.example_note: Conditional operators chain to the right, which is what makes the grade ladder work.

questions.q: Why is if (x = 5) a compile error in Java but not in C?
options: Java requires a boolean condition, and an int assignment is not one
It is an error in both
questions.explain: Because boolean is a distinct type, an int expression cannot be used as a condition — the type system catches the typo.

questions.q: What does i += 2.7 do when i is an int holding 5?
options: Sets i to 7, casting the double result back to int
questions.explain: Compound operators perform an implicit narrowing cast, which is why this compiles while i = i + 2.7 does not.

questions.q: What is the difference between >> and >>> ?
options: >> preserves the sign bit, >>> fills with zeros
questions.explain: Java has no unsigned types, so >>> exists to provide a logical shift that ignores the sign.

questions.q: What happens on integer overflow in Java?
options: It wraps silently to the opposite end of the range
questions.explain: Overflow is silent, which is why long or Math.addExact is needed when values may grow large.

questions.q: How do you raise 2 to the power 10?
questions.explain: Java has no exponentiation operator, and ^ is bitwise xor. Math.pow returns a double.

lessons.title: Branching
lessons.subtitle: if, else if, else
lessons.concept:
`if` takes a **boolean** condition in parentheses and a block in braces. Unlike C, the condition must genuinely be a boolean — an int will not do.

`else if` chains test in order, and the first match wins. Order therefore matters with overlapping thresholds.

Braces are optional for a single statement but should always be used: adding a second line later would silently leave it outside the if, a mistake that has caused real security bugs.
lessons.example_note: 74 fails the first two tests and passes the third. Reversing the order would print C for 95 as well.
lessons.task: With `int temp = 5`, print `freezing` below 0, `cold` below 10, `mild` below 25, otherwise `hot`. Then print `even` or `odd` for the same value.
hints: Ascending thresholds mean each else if only sees what fell through.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Matching one value
lessons.subtitle: switch, fall-through and arrow labels
lessons.concept:
Java’s classic `switch` compares one value against `case` labels, with **fall-through** if you omit `break`. Unlike C, it works on `String` as well as integral types and enums.

Java 14 added the **arrow form**, which does not fall through and can group labels with commas:

`case "sat", "sun" -> System.out.println("weekend");`

That is now the preferred style, since the commonest bug in the old form was a forgotten break. A `switch` can also be an **expression** that yields a value with `yield` or an arrow.
lessons.example_note: The second switch is an expression producing a value, which the old form could not do.
lessons.task: With `char op = '*'` and ints 6 and 7, use an arrow switch to print the result of +, -, * or / with a default of `unknown`. Then use a switch expression to store the number of days in month 4 and print it.
hints: The arrow form needs no break statements.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: The three loop forms
lessons.subtitle: for, while and do-while
lessons.concept:
The counting `for` packs initialisation, condition and step into one line. `while` tests before each pass. `do...while` tests **after** the body, so it always runs at least once, and needs a trailing semicolon.

Declaring the counter inside the for scopes it to the loop, which is the standard style.

As always, a `while` loop needs something inside the body to move the condition toward false, or it never ends.
lessons.example_note: The do-while body executed before the condition was ever tested.
lessons.task: Print the first five multiples of 3 one per line, then their sum. Then use a while loop to count how many times 1000 can be halved before reaching 1.
hints: Declare the accumulator before the loop so it survives afterwards.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Looping over a collection
lessons.subtitle: The enhanced for loop
lessons.concept:
The **enhanced for** (or for-each) walks an array or any `Iterable` without an index:

`for (int value : values) { ... }`

There is no index to get wrong and no off-by-one possible. Use it whenever you need the elements rather than their positions.

One important limitation: assigning to the loop variable changes only the local copy, so it **cannot** modify the array. To write back you need an indexed loop.

For strings, `text.toCharArray()` produces something the enhanced for can walk.
lessons.example_note: Setting n to 0 changed nothing, because n is a copy — nums[0] is still 4.
lessons.task: Given an int array of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, print each element with an enhanced for, then the total, then double each element using an indexed loop and print the array total again.
hints: Only an indexed loop can write back into the array.
