questions.q: What can a Java switch test that a C switch cannot?
questions.explain: Java supports String and enum switches in addition to the integral types C allows.

questions.q: What is the advantage of the arrow form case x -> ... ?
options: It does not fall through, so no break is needed
questions.explain: The commonest classic switch bug was a forgotten break, which the arrow form eliminates entirely.

questions.q: Can an enhanced for loop modify the array it walks?
options: No — the loop variable is a copy
questions.explain: Assigning to the loop variable changes only the copy, so writing back requires an indexed loop.

questions.q: What does break outer; do?
options: Exits the loop labelled outer, escaping several levels at once
questions.explain: Labelled break is Java’s alternative to the flag variable that C requires for the same job.

questions.q: What is unique about do-while?
options: The body always executes at least once
questions.explain: The condition is tested after the body, which suits prompt-then-validate patterns.

lessons.title: Functions inside a class
lessons.subtitle: Static methods
lessons.concept:
A function inside a class is called a **method**. To call one from `main` without creating an object, mark it `static` — static members belong to the class itself.

The signature is `modifiers returnType name(parameters)`. Use `void` when nothing is returned.

Unlike C, Java does not care about declaration order: methods can be defined in any order and call each other freely, because the compiler reads the whole class before resolving anything.
lessons.example_note: square is defined above main here, but it could equally be below — order does not matter.
lessons.task: Write a static `int maxOf(int, int)` returning the larger value, and a static `void line()` printing five dashes. Print maxOf(17, 42) and maxOf(7, 3) between two lines.
hints: Both methods go inside the class, alongside main.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: One name, several versions
lessons.subtitle: Method overloading
lessons.concept:
Several methods may share a name provided their **parameter lists differ** in number or type. The compiler selects the match from the argument types — this is resolved entirely at compile time.

The return type alone cannot distinguish overloads, since the compiler has no way to know which you wanted.

This is why `System.out.println` accepts every type: it is dozens of overloads. Use overloading when the operations are conceptually the same; different names are clearer when the behaviour differs.
lessons.example_note: area(4) and area(2.0) call different methods, chosen purely by the argument type.
lessons.task: Overload a static `describe` method for an int, a double and a String, each returning a distinguishing string, then print all three results.
hints: The parameter type distinguishes each overload.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Any number of arguments
lessons.subtitle: Varargs
lessons.concept:
A parameter declared `int... numbers` accepts any number of arguments, arriving inside the method as an **array**.

There can be at most one varargs parameter and it must come **last**. You may also pass an array directly where varargs is expected.

This is how `String.format` and `System.out.printf` accept a variable argument list. Calling with no arguments gives an empty array, so `numbers.length` is 0 rather than null.
lessons.example_note: An existing array can be passed straight to a varargs parameter, as the fourth call shows.
lessons.task: Write a static `int largest(int... numbers)` returning the biggest value, or 0 for no arguments. Call it with three values, five values and an existing array.
hints: Check numbers.length before reading the first element.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: What a method receives
lessons.subtitle: Pass by value, always
lessons.concept:
Java passes **everything by value**. For a primitive that means a copy of the number, so reassigning the parameter cannot affect the caller.

For an object it means a copy of the **reference**. That has two consequences worth separating carefully:

1. The method **can** modify the object the reference points to — adding to a passed list is visible to the caller.
2. The method **cannot** make the caller’s variable point somewhere else — reassigning the parameter changes only the local copy.

Understanding that distinction removes most confusion about Java’s argument semantics.
lessons.example_note: addItem modified the object; reassign only repointed its local copy, so the caller saw no change.
lessons.task: Write a static method that tries to change an int parameter, one that adds an element to a passed ArrayList, and one that reassigns its list parameter. Demonstrate all three, printing the caller’s state each time.
hints: The list keeps the element added by append but is unaffected by replace.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Methods that call themselves
lessons.subtitle: Recursion
lessons.concept:
A recursive method calls itself on a smaller problem, with a **base case** that returns without recursing. Without one it exhausts the stack and throws `StackOverflowError`.

Each call gets its own parameters and locals, stacked until the base case unwinds them.

Recursion suits naturally recursive structures. For plain counting a loop is faster. Naive recursive Fibonacci is the classic warning: it recomputes the same values exponentially often, which is why memoisation exists.
lessons.example_note: gcd fits on one line because the conditional operator supplies both the base case and the recursive step.
lessons.task: Write recursive static methods `power(int base, int exp)` and `int fib(int n)`. Print power(2, 10), power(5, 3) and the first ten Fibonacci numbers on one line.
hints: Anything to the power zero is 1, and n < 2 covers both Fibonacci base cases.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

questions.q: What distinguishes two overloads of a method?
questions.explain: Overload resolution uses the argument types, so the return type alone cannot distinguish two methods.

questions.q: Where must a varargs parameter appear?
options: Last, and there can only be one
It must be the only parameter
questions.explain: Since it absorbs all remaining arguments, it must come last and cannot be repeated.

questions.q: Can a method modify the object a reference parameter points to?
options: Yes — the reference is copied, but it points at the same object
questions.explain: Java copies the reference, not the object, so mutations to the object are visible to the caller.

questions.q: Can a method make the caller’s variable point at a different object?
options: No — reassigning the parameter changes only the local copy
questions.explain: This is the other half of pass-by-value: the reference itself is a copy, so repointing it is invisible outside.

questions.q: What happens when a recursion has no base case?
questions.explain: Each call consumes stack space, so unbounded recursion eventually exhausts it and throws.

lessons.title: What a String can do
lessons.subtitle: The core methods
lessons.concept:
`String` carries a large interface, and because Strings are **immutable** every method returns a new String rather than modifying the original.

The essentials:
- `.length()`, `.charAt(i)`, `.substring(from, to)`
- `.indexOf(text)` returning `-1` when absent, `.contains(text)`
- `.toUpperCase()`, `.toLowerCase()`, `.trim()` / `.strip()`
- `.replace(old, new)`, `.startsWith()`, `.endsWith()`
- `.isEmpty()`, `.isBlank()`, `.repeat(n)`

Note `substring(from, to)` excludes the end index, matching the half-open convention used everywhere.
lessons.example_note: The second print of clean shows it unchanged — replace returned a new String.
lessons.task: Given `String raw = "  Data Science Rocks  "`, print the stripped text, its length, its uppercase form, the index of `"Science"`, whether it contains `"Rocks"`, and the original stripped value again to show immutability.

18
DATA SCIENCE ROCKS
5
true
Data Science Rocks
hints: Store the stripped version once and reuse it.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Why Strings never change
lessons.subtitle: Immutability and the string pool
lessons.concept:
A String’s characters can never be modified. Every apparent change produces a new object, which is why `text.toUpperCase();` on its own accomplishes nothing — you must assign the result.

Immutability brings real benefits: Strings are safe to share between threads, safe to use as map keys, and can be **interned**. Identical literals share one object in the **string pool**, which is why `"abc" == "abc"` happens to be true while `new String("abc") == "abc"` is false.

That inconsistency is precisely why `.equals()` is the only correct comparison.
lessons.example_note: The two literals shared one pooled object; the explicitly constructed String did not. Only .equals gave the right answer both times.
lessons.task: Show that calling toUpperCase without assigning changes nothing, then assign it and print the result. Then compare two identical literals with ==, a literal against a new String with ==, and the same pair with .equals().
hints: The result of a String method must be assigned to be kept.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Building strings efficiently
lessons.subtitle: StringBuilder
lessons.concept:
Because Strings are immutable, `result += piece` inside a loop creates a **new String every iteration**, copying everything each time. For a thousand appends that is a thousand allocations and quadratic total work.

`StringBuilder` is the mutable alternative. `.append()` modifies the buffer in place, and `.toString()` produces the final String once at the end. It also offers `.insert()`, `.reverse()`, `.deleteCharAt()` and `.setCharAt()`.

The rule: for a handful of concatenations use `+`, since the compiler optimises simple cases. Inside a loop, always use StringBuilder.
lessons.example_note: Every operation modified the same buffer — no intermediate Strings were created at all.

lessons.title: Between text and arrays
lessons.subtitle: split, join and formatting
lessons.concept:
`.split(regex)` breaks a String into an array. The argument is a **regular expression**, so characters like `.` and `|` must be escaped: splitting on a literal dot needs `"\\."`.

`String.join(separator, parts)` is the inverse, accepting an array, a list or varargs.

`String.format(pattern, args...)` builds a formatted String using the same specifiers as printf, returning it rather than printing. That is the right tool whenever you need formatted text in a variable.
lessons.example_note: Splitting on a dot required escaping it, because an unescaped dot matches any character in a regex.

lessons.title: Working character by character
lessons.subtitle: char loops and Character methods
lessons.concept:
To examine every character, either index with `charAt(i)` or walk `toCharArray()` with an enhanced for.

The `Character` class supplies the tests: `Character.isLetter`, `isDigit`, `isWhitespace`, `isUpperCase`, `toUpperCase`, `toLowerCase`.

A `char` is also a 16-bit number, so arithmetic works: `c - '0'` converts a digit character to its value, and `(char)(c + 1)` gives the next letter. Casting back to `char` is required, since the arithmetic promotes to int.

questions.q: What does text.toUpperCase(); on its own accomplish?
options: Nothing — the result must be assigned
questions.explain: Strings are immutable, so every method returns a new String and the original is untouched.

questions.q: Why is "abc" == "abc" true but new String("abc") == "abc" false?
options: Identical literals share one pooled object, while new always creates a distinct one
questions.explain: The string pool interns literals, which is exactly why relying on == for text comparison is unreliable.

questions.q: Why use StringBuilder inside a loop?
options: String += creates a new object each iteration, giving quadratic work
questions.explain: A mutable buffer avoids copying the entire accumulated string on every append.

questions.q: What does split take as its argument?
options: A regular expression, so characters like . must be escaped
questions.explain: An unescaped dot matches any character, which is why splitting on a literal dot needs "\\.".

questions.q: What does '7' - '0' evaluate to?
questions.explain: Digit character codes are consecutive, so subtracting the code of zero converts a digit character to its value.

lessons.title: A fixed run of values
lessons.subtitle: Declaring and indexing arrays
lessons.concept:
An array holds a fixed number of same-typed values. Two ways to create one:

`int[] nums = new int[5];` allocates five slots, **zero-filled** — unlike C, Java always initialises them. Objects default to `null`, booleans to `false`.

`int[] nums = {4, 8, 15};` uses a literal and infers the length.

Unlike C, a Java array **knows its length**, exposed as the field `.length` — no parentheses, because it is a field rather than a method. And unlike C, going out of bounds throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of silently corrupting memory.
lessons.example_note: The out-of-bounds access threw an exception rather than returning rubbish — a major safety improvement over C.
lessons.task: Create an int array of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Print its length, the first element, the last element, then set the second to 99 and print it. Also create a String array of size 2 and print its first element.
hints: nums.length has no parentheses because it is a field.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Processing every element
lessons.subtitle: Indexed and enhanced loops
lessons.concept:
Two ways to walk an array. The **indexed** loop gives you the position and allows writing back. The **enhanced** loop is cleaner when you only need the values.

The key limitation returns: the enhanced loop variable is a copy, so it cannot modify the array. Use an indexed loop to write.

The aggregate patterns are the familiar ones: accumulate a sum from 0, track a maximum starting from the **first element** rather than 0, and count with a conditional increment.
lessons.example_note: max started from nums[0], not 0 — essential here since every value could have been negative.

hints: Initialise max and min from the first element.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: The Arrays helper class
lessons.subtitle: toString, sort, fill, copyOf
lessons.concept:
Printing an array directly gives something useless like `[I@1b6d3586` — the type and hash. `Arrays.toString(arr)` produces the readable `[1, 2, 3]` form.

The rest of `java.util.Arrays`:
- `Arrays.sort(arr)` sorts in place
- `Arrays.fill(arr, value)` sets every element
- `Arrays.copyOf(arr, newLength)` copies, padding or truncating
- `Arrays.equals(a, b)` compares contents, since `==` compares references
- `Arrays.binarySearch(arr, value)` searches a **sorted** array
- `Arrays.stream(arr).sum()` for aggregates

Remember to `import java.util.Arrays;`.
lessons.example_note: The first print showed the useless default form; every subsequent one used Arrays.toString.
lessons.task: Given {45, 12, 78, 23}, print the array with Arrays.toString, sort it and print again, print the sum with Arrays.stream, create a copy extended to length 6 and print it, and print whether two identical literal arrays are equal.
hints: Arrays.equals compares contents; == would compare references.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Finding and ordering by hand
lessons.subtitle: Linear search and bubble sort
lessons.concept:
Two algorithms worth writing once, even though `Arrays.sort` exists.

**Linear search** walks the array comparing each element, returning the index on a match and `-1` otherwise. It works on unsorted data and costs time proportional to the length.

**Bubble sort** repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs, with the inner range shrinking each pass as values settle at the end.

Swapping needs a temporary, since Java has no tuple assignment. In production always use `Arrays.sort`, which uses a far better algorithm — the point here is understanding the cost.
lessons.example_note: Returning -1 for "not found" mirrors String.indexOf, which is the standard Java convention.
lessons.task: Sort {64, 25, 12, 22, 11} with bubble sort and print it with Arrays.toString. Then write a linear search method and print the index of 22 and the result of searching for 99.
hints: The inner range shrinks each pass because the largest values settle at the end.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Arrays of arrays
lessons.subtitle: Two-dimensional and ragged arrays
lessons.concept:
`int[][] grid = new int[3][4];` creates three rows of four columns, accessed as `grid[row][col]`.

Java’s two-dimensional arrays are genuinely **arrays of arrays**, so each row is a separate object with its own length. That means rows can differ in size — a **ragged** array — which a C two-dimensional array cannot do.

`grid.length` gives the row count and `grid[r].length` the length of that row. Always use the latter in the inner loop, since it may vary.

`Arrays.deepToString` prints a nested array readably, where `Arrays.toString` would show the inner references.
lessons.example_note: The ragged array shows the rows are independent objects, each with its own length.

questions.q: How do you get the size of a Java array?
questions.explain: For arrays it is the field arr.length with no parentheses; collections use the method .size() instead.

questions.q: What happens when you read arr[99] on a 5-element array?
questions.explain: Java bounds-checks every access, which turns C’s silent memory corruption into an immediate, diagnosable exception.

questions.q: What does new int[3] contain?
questions.explain: Java always initialises arrays: numbers to zero, booleans to false, and object references to null.

questions.q: Why use Arrays.toString(arr)?
options: Printing an array directly shows its type and hash rather than the contents
questions.explain: An array has no useful toString of its own, so the helper is needed to see the elements.

questions.q: How do Java 2D arrays differ from C ones?
options: They are arrays of arrays, so rows can have different lengths
questions.explain: Each row is an independent object with its own length, which makes ragged arrays possible.

lessons.title: The list that grows
lessons.subtitle: ArrayList
lessons.concept:
When the size is not known in advance, use `ArrayList` from `java.util`. The angle brackets specify the element type: `ArrayList<String>`.

Because collections hold objects rather than primitives, `ArrayList<int>` is illegal — write `ArrayList<Integer>` and let autoboxing handle the conversion.

Core methods: `.add(x)`, `.get(i)`, `.set(i, x)`, `.size()`, `.remove(i)`, `.contains(x)`, `.indexOf(x)`, `.isEmpty()`, `.clear()`.

One subtlety with `ArrayList<Integer>`: `.remove(2)` removes the element **at index 2**, while `.remove(Integer.valueOf(2))` removes the value 2. Overload resolution picks the int version.
lessons.example_note: Printing an ArrayList shows its contents directly, unlike an array — it has a useful toString.
lessons.task: Build an ArrayList<Integer> of the squares of 1 to 5. Print the list, its size, the first element, whether it contains 16, then remove the element at index 0 and print the list again.
hints: Autoboxing lets you add an int literal to an ArrayList<Integer>.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Programming to the interface
lessons.subtitle: List, ArrayList and LinkedList
lessons.concept:
`List` is an **interface**; `ArrayList` and `LinkedList` are implementations. The convention is to declare the variable as the interface and choose the implementation only at construction:

`List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();`

That way the rest of your code depends only on the contract, and swapping implementations touches one line.

The practical difference: `ArrayList` gives fast indexed access but shifts elements on insertion in the middle, while `LinkedList` inserts cheaply at the ends but must walk to reach an index. ArrayList is the right default.

`List.of(...)` creates an **immutable** list, useful for fixed data.
lessons.example_note: total accepted both implementations, because it depends only on the List interface.
lessons.task: Declare a `List<String>` backed by an ArrayList with three names, print it and its size. Then create an immutable `List.of` with two elements, print it, and catch the exception from trying to add to it.
hints: Declare the variable as List and construct an ArrayList.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Key to value
lessons.subtitle: HashMap
lessons.concept:
`HashMap<K, V>` stores key/value pairs with fast lookup. `.put(k, v)` stores, `.get(k)` retrieves and returns **null** when absent, and `.containsKey(k)` tests presence.

That null return is a common source of `NullPointerException` when the result is unboxed into an int. `.getOrDefault(k, fallback)` avoids it entirely and is almost always the better choice.

For counting, `.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum)` or `map.put(k, map.getOrDefault(k, 0) + 1)` are the idioms.

Iterate with `.entrySet()` for pairs, `.keySet()` for keys, or `.values()`. A HashMap has **no defined order**, so sort the keys when deterministic output matters.
lessons.example_note: TreeMap was used for the counts so the output order is sorted and predictable.
lessons.task: Build a Map<String, String> of three capital cities. Print the size, the capital of Japan, a missing key with getOrDefault, and whether France is a key. Then count the words in `"a b a c b a"` into a TreeMap and print each entry in sorted order.

hints: merge(key, 1, Integer::sum) is the concise counting idiom.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Unique values
lessons.subtitle: HashSet and TreeSet
lessons.concept:
`Set` holds unique elements. `.add(x)` returns `false` when the value was already present, which is a neat way to detect duplicates as you insert.

`HashSet` is fast but unordered. `TreeSet` keeps the elements sorted, at a small cost. `LinkedHashSet` preserves insertion order.

Constructing a set from a list deduplicates it in one step: `new HashSet<>(list)`.

Sets also support the bulk operations `.retainAll` (intersection), `.removeAll` (difference) and `.addAll` (union), each modifying the receiver.
lessons.example_note: TreeSet was used throughout so every printed set has a predictable sorted order.
lessons.task: From the list {5, 3, 8, 3, 1, 5, 8}, build a TreeSet and print the original and unique sizes plus the sorted set. Then compute the intersection and difference of {1,2,3,4} and {3,4,5} as TreeSets, and show that adding a duplicate to a HashSet returns false.
hints: retainAll and removeAll modify the receiver, so copy the set first.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Sorting and searching collections
lessons.subtitle: Collections and Comparator
lessons.concept:
`java.util.Collections` provides the helpers: `.sort(list)`, `.reverse(list)`, `.shuffle(list)`, `.max(list)`, `.min(list)`, `.frequency(list, value)`.

`Collections.sort(list)` uses the elements’ natural ordering. To sort differently, pass a **Comparator**. The clean way to build one is `Comparator.comparing`:

`list.sort(Comparator.comparing(String::length).reversed())`

A comparator can be chained with `.thenComparing(...)` for multi-level sorts, which is far more readable than a hand-written compare method.

`list.sort(...)` is the modern equivalent of `Collections.sort(list, ...)`.
lessons.example_note: The last sort ordered by length and then alphabetically within each length — two criteria in one readable expression.
lessons.task: Build a List<String> of four words. Sort alphabetically and print, sort by length and print, sort by length descending and print, then print the maximum and the frequency of a repeated value in a List<Integer>.

[be, fig, delta, charlie]
[charlie, delta, fig, be]
7
2
hints: Comparator.comparing takes a method reference to the field to sort by.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: Why is ArrayList<int> illegal?
options: Generics require reference types, so Integer must be used
questions.explain: Collections store objects, which is exactly why the wrapper classes and autoboxing exist.

questions.q: What does map.get(key) return for an absent key?
questions.explain: The null return causes NullPointerException when unboxed, which is why getOrDefault is usually preferable.

questions.q: Why declare a variable as List rather than ArrayList?
options: So the code depends only on the interface and the implementation can be swapped
questions.explain: Programming to the interface localises the choice of implementation to a single line.

questions.q: What does Set.add return when the value is already present?
questions.explain: The boolean result makes add a convenient duplicate detector as you insert.

questions.q: Why use a TreeMap instead of a HashMap for printed output?
options: A HashMap has no defined iteration order, so output would be unpredictable
questions.explain: TreeMap keeps keys sorted, which makes the output deterministic without a separate sorting step.

lessons.title: Defining your own type
lessons.subtitle: Fields, instances and new
lessons.concept:
A class describes a kind of thing: its **fields** (data) and **methods** (behaviour). `new ClassName()` creates an **instance** with its own copy of every field.

Fields declared without a value get defaults — 0, false or null — unlike local variables, which must be assigned before use.

A file may contain several classes, but only one can be `public`, and it must match the filename. Helper classes are declared without `public` alongside it.

This is where `static` finally earns its meaning: instance methods operate on one object and need no `static`, because they are called through an instance.
lessons.example_note: b got the field defaults — null and 0 — because nothing was assigned to it.
lessons.task: Define a `Rect` class with width and height fields and methods `area()` and `isSquare()`. Create a 4x6 and a 5x5 instance and print both results for each.

Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Setting up an object
lessons.subtitle: Constructors and this
lessons.concept:
A **constructor** runs when an object is created. It has the class’s name and **no return type**.

Inside it, `this.name = name;` distinguishes the field from the same-named parameter — the parameter shadows the field, so `this.` is required.

Constructors can be overloaded, and one can delegate to another with `this(...)`, which avoids duplicating setup.

If you declare **any** constructor, the compiler stops providing the no-argument default. That is deliberate: a class requiring arguments should not be creatable without them.
lessons.example_note: The one-argument constructor delegated to the two-argument one with this(name, 0).

lessons.title: Controlling access
lessons.subtitle: private fields, getters and setters
lessons.concept:
Making fields `private` and exposing methods is where **invariants** live. A setter can validate before assigning, so the object can never hold nonsense.

The four access levels, from most to least restrictive: `private` (this class only), package-private (no keyword — same package), `protected` (same package plus subclasses), `public` (everywhere).

The habit worth forming: fields private by default, methods public only when they are part of the intended interface.

Derived values need no field at all — compute them in a method so they can never disagree with the underlying data.
lessons.example_note: The overdraft was refused and the balance left untouched — the class guarantees its own consistency.

lessons.title: Methods every class inherits
lessons.subtitle: toString, equals and hashCode
lessons.concept:
Every class implicitly extends `Object`, inheriting `toString()`, `equals()` and `hashCode()`.

The defaults are rarely useful. `toString()` returns something like `Book@1b6d3586`; overriding it defines how the object prints, and `println` calls it automatically.

`equals()` defaults to reference comparison. Overriding it lets two distinct objects with the same contents compare equal — which is what you almost always want.

The rule that catches people: **if you override equals you must override hashCode**, because hash-based collections use hashCode to find the bucket. Two equal objects with different hash codes will silently misbehave in a HashMap or HashSet.
lessons.example_note: equals was true while == was false, and the hash codes matched — exactly the behaviour collections require.

Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Data belonging to the class
lessons.subtitle: static fields and methods
lessons.concept:
A `static` field belongs to the class, not to any instance: one copy shared by every object. That makes it right for counters and shared constants.

A `static` method likewise belongs to the class. It has no `this`, so it cannot touch instance fields, and is called as `ClassName.method()`. `Math.max` and `Integer.parseInt` are static methods.

Constants are conventionally `static final` in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.

This finally explains `public static void main`: it must be static so the JVM can call it before any object exists.
lessons.example_note: issued() was callable before any Ticket existed, because it belongs to the class.

lessons.title: Data classes without the boilerplate
lessons.subtitle: record
lessons.concept:
Java 16 introduced `record`, which generates the whole boilerplate of an immutable data class:

`record Point(int x, int y) {}`

That single line gives you private final fields, a constructor, accessor methods named `x()` and `y()`, plus `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode` — all correct.

Records are **immutable** by design: there are no setters and the fields are final. You can still add methods, and a **compact constructor** allows validation.

Use a record whenever a type is simply a carrier of data. Use a class when it has behaviour or mutable state.

questions.q: What is the purpose of this.name = name in a constructor?
options: To distinguish the field from the parameter that shadows it
questions.explain: The parameter hides the field inside the constructor, so this. is needed to reach the instance field.

questions.q: What happens when you declare any constructor?
options: The compiler stops providing the no-argument default
questions.explain: This is deliberate: a class that requires arguments should not be constructible without them.

questions.q: Why must you override hashCode when you override equals?
options: Hash-based collections use hashCode to find the bucket, so equal objects must hash alike
questions.explain: Two equal objects with different hash codes land in different buckets and a HashSet will keep both.

questions.q: What does a record generate for you?
options: Fields, constructor, accessors, toString, equals and hashCode
questions.explain: That is the point of records: an immutable data carrier with all the boilerplate written correctly.

questions.q: Why can a static method not access instance fields?
options: It has no this, because it belongs to the class rather than any object
questions.explain: With no particular instance in scope there is nothing for an instance field reference to refer to.

lessons.title: Building on an existing class
lessons.subtitle: extends and super
lessons.concept:
`class Dog extends Animal` makes Dog a **subclass**, inheriting every accessible member of Animal.

`super(...)` calls the parent constructor and must be the **first statement** in the subclass constructor. If you omit it, Java inserts an implicit `super()`, which fails to compile when the parent has no no-argument constructor.

`super.method()` calls the parent’s version of an overridden method, which is how a subclass extends behaviour rather than replacing it.

Java allows only **single inheritance** of classes — one parent each — which avoids the ambiguities of multiple inheritance. Interfaces provide the multiple-type flexibility instead.
lessons.example_note: Dog.describe called super.describe() and added to it, extending rather than discarding the parent behaviour.
lessons.task: Define a `Vehicle` class with a wheels field, a constructor and a `describe()` method. Define `Car extends Vehicle` adding a brand, calling super, and overriding describe to append the brand. Print both descriptions.
hints: super(...) must be the first statement in the subclass constructor.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: One reference, many types
lessons.subtitle: Overriding and dynamic dispatch
lessons.concept:
A subclass instance can be held in a parent-typed variable: `Animal a = new Dog(...)`. When you call an overridden method through it, Java runs the **subclass** version.

That is **dynamic dispatch**, and unlike C++ it is the default — there is no `virtual` keyword because every method is virtual unless marked `final`, `static` or `private`.

The consequence is powerful: a loop over `List<Animal>` calls each object’s own behaviour without knowing the concrete types.

The `@Override` annotation is optional but valuable: it makes the compiler verify that you really are overriding something, catching signature typos that would otherwise create an unrelated method.
lessons.example_note: report is defined only on Shape, yet each object’s own area and name were used inside it.
lessons.task: Define an `Animal` class with a `speak()` returning `"..."` and a `describe()` printing `name says sound`. Derive Dog and Cat overriding speak. Put all three in a List<Animal> and describe each in one loop.
lessons.expected_output:

Rex says woof
Tom says meow
hints: The loop never needs to know which subclass each object is.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: A class that cannot be instantiated
lessons.subtitle: abstract classes and methods
lessons.concept:
An `abstract` class cannot be instantiated — it exists to be extended. It may contain both **abstract methods** (declared without a body) and concrete ones.

An abstract method forces every concrete subclass to provide an implementation, which the compiler enforces. That is stronger than a default implementation returning nothing, because forgetting to override becomes an error rather than a silent bug.

The pattern this enables is the **template method**: a concrete method in the abstract class defines the overall algorithm and calls abstract methods for the parts that vary.

Use an abstract class when subclasses share state and partial behaviour; use an interface when they share only a contract.
lessons.example_note: payslip is the template method: it defines the format once and delegates the varying calculation.
lessons.task: Define an abstract `Shape` class with a name field, an abstract `area()` and a concrete `report()` printing the name and area to two decimals. Derive Square and Rect, put both in a list and report each.
hints: The abstract method has no body, just a semicolon.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: A contract without implementation
lessons.subtitle: interface and implements
lessons.concept:
An `interface` declares methods a class promises to provide. Unlike a class, a type can `implements` **several** interfaces, which is how Java gets the flexibility of multiple inheritance without its ambiguities.

Interface methods are implicitly public and abstract. Since Java 8 an interface may also have `default` methods with a body, allowing new methods to be added without breaking existing implementors, and `static` helper methods.

The distinction from an abstract class: an interface describes what a type **can do**, an abstract class describes what a type **is**. A class extends one thing and implements many.
lessons.example_note: Square implements two interfaces at once, and inherited describe() from the default method without writing it.
lessons.task: Define an interface `Payable` with `double amount()` and a default `summary()` returning `owed: N`. Define two classes implementing it differently, put them in a List<Payable> and print each summary.
hints: Interface implementations must be declared public.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Making your type sortable
lessons.subtitle: Comparable and Comparator
lessons.concept:
Implementing `Comparable<T>` gives your class a **natural ordering**, so `Collections.sort` and `TreeSet` work on it without extra arguments.

`compareTo(other)` must return a negative number when this comes first, zero when equal, and positive otherwise. `Integer.compare(a, b)` produces exactly that, and avoids the overflow that `a - b` risks.

A `Comparator` is the alternative: an **external** ordering, so you can sort the same type several different ways. Use Comparable for the one obvious ordering and Comparators for everything else.
lessons.example_note: Collections.sort needed no comparator because Student has a natural ordering; the second sort supplied a different one.
lessons.task: Define a `Book` class implementing Comparable<Book> ordered by pages, with a toString. Sort a list naturally and print it, then sort by title with a Comparator and print again, then print the maximum.
hints: Integer.compare avoids the overflow risk of subtraction.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Checking and narrowing types
lessons.subtitle: instanceof and pattern matching
lessons.concept:
Assigning a subclass to a parent-typed variable is **upcasting** and always safe. Going the other way is **downcasting** and needs a check, or it throws `ClassCastException`.

`instanceof` tests the actual type. Java 16 added **pattern matching**, which combines the test and the cast:

`if (shape instanceof Square sq) { ... sq.getSide() ... }`

The variable is in scope only where the test succeeded, so the cast can never be wrong.

A design note: frequent `instanceof` chains usually mean the behaviour belongs on the classes as an overridden method instead. Polymorphism is the better tool when you can use it.
lessons.example_note: The pattern variable sq exists only inside the successful branch, so no separate cast statement is needed.

hints: The pattern variable is declared inside the instanceof test.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: Does Java need a virtual keyword for dynamic dispatch?
options: No — every method is virtual unless final, static or private
questions.explain: Unlike C++, overriding works by default, which is why forgetting a keyword cannot silently break polymorphism.

questions.q: Where must super(...) appear in a subclass constructor?
options: It is optional and never needed
questions.explain: The parent must be initialised before the subclass adds to it, so the call has to come first.

questions.q: What is the key difference between an abstract class and an interface?
options: A class extends one abstract class but can implement many interfaces
questions.explain: An abstract class describes what a type is and can hold state; interfaces describe what a type can do and are multiply implementable.

questions.q: What must compareTo return when this object should sort first?
questions.explain: The sign carries the meaning, which is why Integer.compare is preferred over subtraction that could overflow.

questions.q: What does if (o instanceof String s) achieve?
options: Tests the type and declares s as the cast value, scoped to that branch
questions.explain: Pattern matching binds the variable only where the test succeeded, so the cast can never fail.

lessons.title: When things go wrong
lessons.subtitle: try, catch and finally
lessons.concept:
An **exception** signals that an operation cannot proceed. Left unhandled it terminates the program with a stack trace.

`try` wraps the risky code, `catch` handles a specific type, and `finally` **always** runs — on success, on failure, even on an early return — which makes it the right place for cleanup.

Catch specific types before general ones, since the first matching block wins. `catch (Exception e)` at the top would swallow everything below it.

Every exception carries `.getMessage()`, and `e.getClass().getSimpleName()` names the type.
lessons.example_note: The finally block ran on both the successful and the failing call, even though the first returned normally.
lessons.task: Write a static `safeParse(String)` returning the parsed int or -1 on failure, printing `done` in a finally block. Call it with `"42"`, `"3.5"` and `"abc"`.
hints: Integer.parseInt throws NumberFormatException for "3.5" as well as "abc".
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Two kinds of exception
lessons.subtitle: Checked, unchecked and throws
lessons.concept:
Java uniquely divides exceptions into two categories.

**Unchecked** exceptions extend `RuntimeException` — `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`, `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. They represent programming errors and need no declaration.

**Checked** exceptions extend `Exception` directly — `IOException`, `ParseException`. The compiler **forces** you either to catch them or to declare `throws` on the method. They represent conditions a correct program must anticipate.

The guidance: throw unchecked for programmer mistakes such as invalid arguments, and checked for genuinely external failures. `throw` raises one; `throws` declares that a method may propagate one.
lessons.example_note: validate needed no throws clause because IllegalArgumentException is unchecked; mightFail required one.
lessons.task: Write `withdraw(int balance, int amount)` throwing IllegalArgumentException for a non-positive amount and IllegalStateException for insufficient funds. Call it three times in try/catch blocks printing the result or the message.
lessons.expected_output:
70
invalid: amount must be positive
failed: insufficient funds
hints: Both exception types here are unchecked, so no throws clause is needed.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Your own exception types
lessons.subtitle: Extending Exception
lessons.concept:
A custom exception is a class extending `RuntimeException` (unchecked) or `Exception` (checked). The body can be nothing more than a constructor forwarding the message with `super(message)`.

The value is precision: callers can catch exactly your error rather than a generic type, and the class name documents the failure at the throw site.

Custom exceptions can carry extra data as fields — a failing account number, a rejected value — which a plain message string cannot express in a machine-readable way.

Name them ending in `Exception`, and prefer unchecked unless callers can realistically recover.
lessons.example_note: The exception carried the shortfall as a field, which the caller could use programmatically.
lessons.task: Define `InvalidAgeException extends RuntimeException` carrying the rejected value as a field. Write a validate method throwing it for negatives, then call it with a valid and an invalid value, printing the message and the stored value.
hints: Forward the message to super and store the extra data in a field.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: One method, any type
lessons.subtitle: Generic methods
lessons.concept:
A **generic method** declares a type parameter before its return type:

`static <T> T first(List<T> items)`

The `<T>` introduces T as a placeholder, and the compiler infers it from the arguments at each call. The result is type-safe: `first(listOfStrings)` returns a String, with no cast and no possibility of a ClassCastException.

Before generics, collections held `Object` and every retrieval needed a cast that could fail at run time. Generics moved that check to compile time.

A **bounded** parameter constrains what T can be: `<T extends Comparable<T>>` guarantees T can be compared, which is what a generic max function needs.
lessons.example_note: largest required the Comparable bound; without it the compiler would reject the compareTo call.
lessons.task: Write a generic `<T> int count(List<T>)`, a generic `<T> T lastOf(List<T>)`, and a bounded `<T extends Comparable<T>> T smallest(List<T>)`. Use all three with a List<Integer> and a List<String>.
hints: The type parameter goes before the return type, after any modifiers.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Generic types of your own
lessons.subtitle: Generic classes
lessons.concept:
A class can take type parameters: `class Box<T>`. Inside, T is used like any other type, and `Box<String>` and `Box<Integer>` become distinct, fully checked types.

A class may take several parameters, as `Map<K, V>` does.

One limitation worth knowing: Java implements generics by **erasure**, meaning the type argument is discarded after compilation. So `new T()` is impossible, primitive arguments are not allowed, and `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are the same class at run time. Erasure kept generics backward compatible with older code, at the cost of these restrictions.
lessons.example_note: b.get() returned a String, so toUpperCase compiled with no cast — that is the safety generics provide.
lessons.task: Define a generic `Stack<T>` backed by an ArrayList with push, pop, size and isEmpty. Use it with Integers and Strings, printing sizes and popped values.

lessons.title: Accepting related types
lessons.subtitle: Wildcards
lessons.concept:
Generics are **invariant**: a `List<Integer>` is *not* a `List<Number>`, even though Integer is a Number. That surprises everyone at first, but it is necessary — if it were allowed you could add a Double to a list of Integers.

Wildcards restore the flexibility safely.

`List<?>` is a list of unknown type. You can read from it as Object and check its size, but not add anything.

`List<? extends Number>` accepts a List of Number or any subtype, and is **read-only** for the same reason. `List<? super Integer>` accepts Integer or any supertype and is safe to **write** to.

lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What is the difference between a checked and an unchecked exception?
options: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared with throws; unchecked need not be
questions.explain: The compiler enforces handling of checked exceptions, which represent anticipated external failures rather than programming bugs.

questions.q: When does a finally block run?
questions.explain: finally executes on every exit path, which makes it the right place for cleanup that must not be skipped.

questions.q: Why is List<Integer> not a List<Number>?
options: Because you could then add a Double to a list of Integers
questions.explain: Generic invariance prevents that unsound write, and wildcards restore the flexibility safely.

questions.q: What does <T extends Comparable<T>> guarantee?
options: T has a compareTo method, so it can be ordered
questions.explain: A bound tells the compiler which operations are available on T, which is what a generic max function needs.

questions.q: What does type erasure mean for generics?
options: Type arguments are discarded after compilation, so new T() is impossible
Generics are checked at run time
questions.explain: Erasure kept generics backward compatible, at the cost of restrictions like no primitive arguments and no runtime type information.

lessons.title: Behaviour as a value
lessons.subtitle: Lambda expressions
lessons.concept:
A **lambda** is an anonymous function written inline: `n -> n * 2`. Parameter types are inferred, and a single-expression body needs no `return` or braces.

A lambda can be assigned to any **functional interface** — an interface with exactly one abstract method. The built-in ones live in `java.util.function`:

- `Predicate<T>` takes T, returns boolean
- `Function<T, R>` takes T, returns R
- `Consumer<T>` takes T, returns nothing
- `Supplier<T>` takes nothing, returns T

Before lambdas this required an anonymous inner class, six lines of ceremony for one expression. `@FunctionalInterface` documents and enforces the single-method rule.
lessons.example_note: andThen composed two functions, so 3 was squared to 9 and then incremented to 10.

hints: Each functional interface has its own method name: test, apply, accept, get.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Naming an existing method
lessons.subtitle: Method references
lessons.concept:
When a lambda does nothing but call an existing method, a **method reference** says so more directly. `s -> s.length()` becomes `String::length`.

Four forms:
- `ClassName::staticMethod` — `Integer::parseInt`
- `ClassName::instanceMethod` — `String::length`, where the first argument becomes the receiver
- `object::instanceMethod` — `System.out::println`
- `ClassName::new` — a constructor reference

They are exactly equivalent to the lambda, so use whichever reads better. `Comparator.comparing(Book::getPages)` is far clearer than the lambda form.
lessons.example_note: words.forEach(System.out::println) is an object method reference — the receiver is System.out.
lessons.task: Use `String::length` as a Function, `Integer::parseInt` as a Function, `System.out::println` with forEach on a list, and `Comparator.comparing(String::length)` to sort a list. Print each result.
hints: String::length works as a Function<String, Integer> because the receiver becomes the argument.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Declarative data processing
lessons.subtitle: Streams: filter, map, collect
lessons.concept:
A **stream** is a pipeline over a sequence. `.stream()` starts one, **intermediate** operations transform it lazily, and a **terminal** operation produces a result.

The core three:
- `.filter(predicate)` keeps matching elements
- `.map(function)` transforms each element
- `.collect(Collectors.toList())` gathers the result

Nothing runs until the terminal operation, which lets the pipeline be optimised as a whole. A stream is single-use: consuming it twice throws.

The value is readability — the code states what you want rather than how to loop.
lessons.example_note: Collectors.joining produced a single delimited String directly, with no manual StringBuilder.
lessons.task: From a list of five words, print the uppercase forms of those longer than four letters, a list of their lengths, the count starting with a given letter, and the first three sorted words joined by commas.
hints: Chain the intermediate operations, then finish with a terminal one.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Collapsing a stream to one value
lessons.subtitle: reduce, sum and statistics
lessons.concept:
**Reduction** collapses a stream to a single value.

`.reduce(identity, accumulator)` is the general form: `reduce(0, Integer::sum)`. The identity is both the starting value and the result when the stream is empty.

For numbers, `.mapToInt(...)` converts to an `IntStream`, which offers `.sum()`, `.average()`, `.max()` and `.summaryStatistics()` directly. That avoids the boxing overhead of `Stream<Integer>` and gives cleaner code.

`.average()` and `.max()` return an `OptionalDouble` or `OptionalInt`, because an empty stream has neither — which is a genuinely useful reminder to handle that case.
lessons.example_note: The empty stream returned the identity 0 rather than failing — that is what the identity is for.

hints: mapToInt avoids boxing and gives the numeric terminal operations directly.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Gathering results
lessons.subtitle: Collectors and grouping
lessons.concept:
`Collectors` provides the terminal operations that build collections and summaries.

- `toList()`, `toSet()`, `toMap(keyFn, valueFn)`
- `joining(delimiter)` builds a String
- `counting()`, `summingInt(fn)`, `averagingInt(fn)`
- `groupingBy(classifier)` builds a `Map<K, List<T>>`
- `partitioningBy(predicate)` splits into true and false groups

`groupingBy` is the standout: grouping words by length, or orders by customer, becomes one line where a manual loop would need several. It also takes a **downstream** collector, so you can group and count in a single expression.
lessons.example_note: TreeMap::new was supplied so the grouped output has a predictable sorted order.

hints: groupingBy takes a classifier, an optional map factory and a downstream collector.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: A value that might be absent
lessons.subtitle: Optional
lessons.concept:
`Optional<T>` holds either a value or nothing, replacing the convention of returning `null`. The benefit is that the absence is **in the type**, so the compiler reminds you it exists.

`Optional.of(v)` wraps a value, `Optional.empty()` is the absent case, and `Optional.ofNullable(v)` handles either.

Read with `.isPresent()`, `.orElse(default)`, `.orElseGet(supplier)` or `.ifPresent(consumer)`. `.map(fn)` transforms the value only when present, so chains stay null-safe.

Use Optional as a **return type** for a lookup that may find nothing. Do not use it for fields or parameters — that is not what it is for.
lessons.example_note: map on the empty Optional produced another empty one, so orElse supplied 0 without any null check.
lessons.task: Write a method returning `Optional<Integer>` for the first value above 10 in a list. Call it on two lists, printing isPresent, orElse(-1), and the result of mapping the value to its double via orElse.
hints: Optional.empty() represents the absent case.
Match the expected output exactly. println adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Putting it all together
lessons.subtitle: A realistic data pipeline
lessons.concept:
A closing tour combining the whole track: records for the data, streams for the processing, comparators for the ordering, and collectors for the summaries.

The shape of most real Java data work is exactly this. Model the rows as records, hold them in a `List`, then use a stream pipeline to filter, sort, group and reduce.

The habits worth carrying forward: records for data carriers, `List` and `Map` interfaces in declarations, streams when the intent is a transformation, ordinary loops when it is genuinely imperative, and `Optional` rather than null for a lookup that may fail.
lessons.example_note: groupingBy with summingDouble totalled each region in one expression, where a loop would need a map and manual accumulation.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: advanced Java
lessons.subtitle: Check what stuck before moving on
lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What can a lambda be assigned to?
options: A functional interface — one with exactly one abstract method
questions.explain: The single abstract method gives the lambda its signature, which is why the rule exists.

questions.q: When does a stream pipeline actually execute?
questions.explain: Intermediate operations are lazy, so the whole pipeline can be optimised and short-circuited.

questions.q: What does Collectors.groupingBy produce?
options: A Map from the classifier result to a List of elements
questions.explain: It builds a Map<K, List<T>> by default, and a downstream collector can change what each group becomes.

questions.q: Why does .average() return an OptionalDouble?
options: Because an empty stream has no average
questions.explain: Encoding the empty case in the type forces the caller to decide what should happen, rather than returning a misleading zero.

questions.q: Where is Optional intended to be used?

lessons.title: fn main and a macro
lessons.subtitle: Your first Rust program
lessons.concept:
Rust programs start at `fn main()`. `fn` declares a function; `main` takes no arguments and returns nothing.

`println!` has an exclamation mark because it is a **macro**, not a function. It is expanded at compile time, which is how it can verify your format string against your arguments before the program ever runs — a mismatch is a compile error, not garbage output.

Inside the string, `{}` is a placeholder filled by the arguments that follow, in order. Statements end with semicolons.
lessons.example_note: If the number of {} does not match the number of arguments, the code will not compile. That check is only possible because println! is a macro.
lessons.task: Print exactly `Hello, world!`, then a second line using two placeholders to show that 6 times 7 is 42.
hints: Do not forget the ! after println.

lessons.title: Controlling how values print
lessons.subtitle: Format specifiers
lessons.concept:
Rust’s formatting syntax is rich and all checked at compile time.

- `{}` uses the `Display` trait, for human-readable output
- `{:?}` uses `Debug`, which is what collections and structs need
- `{:.2}` two decimal places
- `{:>8}` right-align in 8 columns, `{:<8}` left, `{:^8}` centre
- `{:08.2}` zero-padded to 8 wide with 2 decimals
- `{name}` interpolates a variable of that name directly

The `{:?}` distinction matters: a `Vec` has no `Display` implementation because there is no single obvious way to show it, so `{:?}` is required.
lessons.example_note: The last line mixes named interpolation with a positional placeholder, which is idiomatic modern Rust.
lessons.task: Print 2.718281828 to two and five decimals, the word `total` right-aligned in 10 columns between pipes, a vector of three numbers with debug formatting, and a line using named interpolation.
hints: A Vec needs {:?} because it has no Display implementation.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Notes and documentation
lessons.subtitle: Comment styles
lessons.concept:
Rust has `//` line comments and `/* */` block comments, plus two documentation forms.

`///` documents the **following** item and supports Markdown. `//!` documents the **enclosing** item, used at the top of a file or module.

Doc comments are more than convention: `cargo doc` generates HTML from them, and code blocks inside them are compiled and **run as tests** by `cargo test`. That means documented examples cannot silently rot.
lessons.example_note: The example inside the doc comment would be compiled and executed by cargo test, keeping it honest.
lessons.task: Write a documented `triple` function with a `///` doc comment, a `//!` comment at the top of the file, and a line comment inside main. Print triple(14).
hints: The //! comment must be the first thing in the file.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Why the exclamation mark
lessons.subtitle: Common macros
lessons.concept:
A macro operates on **syntax** at compile time, which lets it do things a function cannot — such as accepting a variable number of typed arguments and checking them.

The macros you meet first:
- `println!` / `print!` / `eprintln!` output
- `format!` builds a `String` instead of printing
- `vec!` constructs a `Vec`
- `panic!` aborts with a message
- `assert!` / `assert_eq!` check conditions

`format!` is particularly useful: it takes the same arguments as `println!` but returns the text, which is how you build formatted strings.
lessons.example_note: assert_eq! prints both values when it fails, which makes it far more useful than a bare assert!.

lessons.title: Immutable by default
lessons.subtitle: let and mut
lessons.concept:
`let x = 5;` creates a binding that **cannot be changed**. That is the default, and it is deliberate: most values never need to change, and the compiler can reason far better about ones that do not.

When you genuinely need mutation, opt in with `let mut x = 5;`.

This inverts the convention of most languages, where mutability is free and immutability requires a keyword. Rust’s choice means every mutable value is visibly marked, so you can see at a glance what might change.

Attempting to reassign an immutable binding is a compile error, not a warning.
lessons.example_note: Writing fixed = 6; would refuse to compile, with a message telling you to add mut.
lessons.task: Create an immutable binding holding 42 and print it. Create a mutable counter starting at 0, increment it three times, and print it. Create a mutable String, append to it, and print the result.
hints: Only bindings you actually modify need mut.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: What kind of value is this
lessons.subtitle: Scalar types and annotations
lessons.concept:
Rust’s scalar types are precise about size:

- integers: `i8` to `i128` signed, `u8` to `u128` unsigned, plus `isize`/`usize`
- floats: `f32` and `f64`
- `bool` and `char` — note that `char` is a full Unicode scalar, four bytes, not one

The defaults are `i32` and `f64`, chosen as the fastest sensible options.

Types are usually **inferred**, but an annotation is required when the compiler cannot decide — most often when parsing a string. Suffixes work too: `5u8`, `2.5f32`.
lessons.example_note: The parse call needed the annotation on parsed, because parse can produce many different numeric types.
lessons.task: Declare an i8, a u32, an f32, a bool and a char with explicit annotations and print all five. Then print i32::MAX, u8::MAX, and the result of parsing `"250"` into an i32 plus one.
hints: Underscores inside numeric literals are ignored and aid readability.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Reusing a name
lessons.subtitle: Shadowing versus mut
lessons.concept:
Declaring a binding again with `let` **shadows** the previous one. The old value is not modified — a new binding simply takes over the name.

This differs from `mut` in two important ways. Shadowing can **change the type**, and the result can still be immutable. That makes it ideal for converting a value while keeping one clear name:

```
let input = "42";
let input: i32 = input.parse().unwrap();
```

With `mut` the second line would be a type error. Shadowing also respects scope: a binding shadowed inside a block reverts when the block ends.
lessons.example_note: The inner x was a separate binding, so the outer one was unchanged when the block ended.
lessons.task: Shadow a binding to convert the string `"75"` into an integer and then double it, printing the result. Then shadow a string of four spaces into its length. Finally show a shadowed binding inside a block reverting afterwards.
hints: Each let creates a new binding, so the type may change.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Converting between numeric types
lessons.subtitle: The as keyword
lessons.concept:
Rust performs **no implicit numeric conversions** at all. Adding an `i32` to an `f64` is a compile error, where C and Java would silently promote. That strictness prevents a whole family of subtle bugs.

Convert explicitly with `as`: `x as f64`, `y as u8`.

Be aware `as` **truncates** rather than failing. `3.9 as i32` gives 3, and `300 as u8` wraps to 44. For a conversion that reports failure instead, use `try_into()`, which returns a `Result`.

Integer division still truncates, so cast before dividing when you want a real answer.
lessons.example_note: 300 as u8 wrapped silently to 44, while try_into reported the failure — which is why try_into exists.
lessons.task: With `let total = 47` and `let people = 6`, print the truncating division, the exact average to three decimals using `as f64`, and the average truncated back to an integer. Then show that `try_into` to a u8 fails for 1000.
hints: Both operands need casting, since Rust will not mix types at all.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Values fixed at compile time
lessons.subtitle: const and static
lessons.concept:
`const` declares a compile-time constant. It **requires** a type annotation, is inlined wherever used, and may be declared at any scope including module level. Names are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE by convention.

`static` also lives for the whole program but has a fixed memory address rather than being inlined. For ordinary constants, `const` is the right choice.

The difference from an immutable `let`: a `const` must be computable at compile time, so it can appear in array sizes and match patterns, and it can exist outside any function.
lessons.example_note: SIZE could size the array precisely because a const is known at compile time; a let binding could not.
lessons.task: Declare a module-level `const MINUTES_PER_HOUR: u32 = 60` and a `static NAME: &str`, plus a local const inside main. Print all three, the product of the constant with 7, and use a const to size an array whose length you print.
hints: A const always needs an explicit type annotation.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Bundling values together
lessons.subtitle: Tuples and destructuring
lessons.concept:
A **tuple** groups a fixed number of values, which may be of different types: `(3, "three", 3.0)`.

Access by position with dot notation — `t.0`, `t.1` — or **destructure** into named bindings: `let (a, b) = pair;`. Destructuring is the idiomatic approach and reads far better.

Tuples are how a Rust function returns several values, since there is no separate mechanism for it.

The empty tuple `()` is called the **unit type** and represents "no value". A function with no return type actually returns `()`.
lessons.example_note: min_max returned two values as a tuple, which the caller destructured into two names in one line.

hints: The tuple return type is written as (i32, usize).

questions.q: What happens if you reassign a binding declared without mut?
questions.explain: Immutability is the default and the compiler enforces it, so mutation must be opted into with mut.

questions.q: What can shadowing do that mut cannot?
options: Change the type of the value bound to the name
questions.explain: Each let creates a new binding, so a shadowed name may hold a different type while staying immutable.

questions.q: What does Rust do when you add an i32 to an f64?
options: Refuses to compile — there are no implicit numeric conversions
questions.explain: Every conversion must be written explicitly with as or try_into, which prevents a family of silent bugs.

questions.q: What does 300 as u8 produce?
questions.explain: as truncates the bits without checking, which is why try_into exists for conversions that must report failure.

questions.q: How does a Rust function return two values?
questions.explain: A tuple bundles the values and the caller destructures them, which is why tuples appear so often in signatures.

lessons.title: Arithmetic operators
lessons.subtitle: Five operators and overflow
lessons.concept:
Rust has `+ - * / %`. There is no exponentiation operator — use `.pow(n)` on integers or `.powi(n)` / `.powf(n)` on floats.

Integer division truncates, and `%` gives the remainder.

The distinctive part is **overflow**. In a debug build, `i32::MAX + 1` **panics** rather than wrapping silently as it does in C and Java. In release builds it wraps for speed, so Rust provides explicit methods to make the intent clear: `checked_add` returns an `Option`, `saturating_add` clamps to the limit, and `wrapping_add` wraps deliberately.
lessons.example_note: checked_add returned None, saturating_add clamped, and wrapping_add wrapped — three explicit choices instead of one silent default.
lessons.task: With `let a = 23` and `let b = 4`, print the sum, product, integer quotient, remainder, exact quotient to two decimals, and 2 to the power 8. Then show checked_add and saturating_add on i32::MAX.
hints: The pow method needs a typed receiver, so write 2i32.pow(8).
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Comparing and combining
lessons.subtitle: Relational and logical operators
lessons.concept:
The six comparisons produce a `bool`. Rust has **no truthiness** at all: a condition must be exactly a `bool`, so `if 1` is a compile error and `if x = 5` is impossible since assignment yields `()`.

`&&`, `||` and `!` combine booleans and **short-circuit**. The bitwise `&` and `|` also work on bools but always evaluate both sides.

Comparison requires matching types — comparing an `i32` with an `i64` will not compile without a cast, which is consistent with Rust’s refusal to convert implicitly.

There are no chained comparisons, so write `0 < x && x < 10`.
lessons.example_note: String comparison works because &str implements Ord, comparing lexicographically.
lessons.task: With `let n = 15`, print whether it equals 15, is under 10, lies strictly between 10 and 20, and is not 20. Then compare two string slices alphabetically.
hints: The range test needs two comparisons joined by &&.

lessons.title: Almost everything is an expression
lessons.subtitle: Blocks that produce values
lessons.concept:
This is one of Rust’s defining traits. A **block** `{ ... }` is an expression whose value is its final expression — provided that expression has **no semicolon**.

```
let x = { let a = 5; a * 2 };
```

Adding a semicolon after `a * 2` would make the block produce `()` instead, which is the single most common early confusion. The rule is precise: a semicolon turns an expression into a statement, discarding its value.

The same rule explains why a function’s last line needs no `return` and no semicolon.
lessons.example_note: The second block ended with a semicolon, so its value is the unit type () rather than 25.
lessons.task: Use a block expression to compute the square of 6 into a binding and print it. Write a function returning its argument tripled without using `return`. Then use an if expression to assign and print a label.
hints: Omit the semicolon on the final expression of the block and the function.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Working with bits
lessons.subtitle: Bitwise operators
lessons.concept:
Rust has `& | ^ !` and the shifts `<< >>`. Note that **`!` is the bitwise not**, not `~` as in C — the same symbol serves as logical not for bools, chosen by the operand type.

Because Rust has genuine unsigned types, `>>` behaves correctly for each: it is arithmetic for signed and logical for unsigned, so no separate `>>>` is needed.

The idioms match C: set with `|=`, clear with `&= !mask`, toggle with `^=`, test with `(x >> n) & 1`.

`count_ones()`, `leading_zeros()` and `{:b}` formatting make bit work far more readable than in C.
lessons.example_note: !a on a u32 flipped all 32 bits, giving a large number — the same symbol means logical not only for bools.
lessons.task: With `let flags: u32 = 10`, print the result of anding with 12, oring with 5, xoring with 15, shifting left once, the 8-bit binary form, and count_ones of 255.
hints: The {:08b} spec prints eight binary digits with leading zeros.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Order of evaluation
lessons.subtitle: Precedence and clarity
lessons.concept:
Rust’s precedence follows the familiar pattern: unary operators and casts, then `* / %`, then `+ -`, then shifts, then `&`, `^`, `|`, then comparisons, then `&&`, then `||`.

One genuine improvement over C: the bitwise operators bind **tighter** than comparisons in Rust, so `a & 1 == 0` means `(a & 1) == 0` — what you almost certainly intended. The classic C trap does not exist here.

Rust also **requires** parentheses in some ambiguous cases rather than silently choosing, and `as` binds tighter than arithmetic, so `a as f64 / b as f64` works as written.
lessons.example_note: The two bitwise lines agree in Rust, unlike C where the first would compare 1 with 0 first.

questions.q: What happens on integer overflow in a Rust debug build?
questions.explain: Debug builds panic to surface the bug, and the checked_, saturating_ and wrapping_ methods make the intended behaviour explicit.

questions.q: Why is if 1 { } a compile error in Rust?
options: A condition must be exactly a bool — Rust has no truthiness
questions.explain: Requiring a bool eliminates the accidental-assignment and truthiness bugs common in C.

questions.q: What does a block ending with a semicolon evaluate to?
questions.explain: A semicolon turns the expression into a statement, discarding its value — the commonest early Rust confusion.

questions.q: Which operator is bitwise not in Rust?
questions.explain: Rust reuses ! for both bitwise and logical not, choosing by the operand type.

questions.q: How does a & 1 == 0 parse in Rust?
questions.explain: Rust deliberately fixed C’s precedence trap, so the expression means what it appears to mean.

lessons.title: if is an expression
lessons.subtitle: Conditions that produce values
lessons.concept:
In Rust, `if` is an **expression**: it evaluates to a value, so it can be assigned directly. There is no ternary operator because `if` already does the job.

The condition needs no parentheses but the braces are **mandatory**, even for a single statement — which eliminates the dangling-else class of bug entirely.

Both branches must produce the same type. If one branch has a value and the other does not, the type is `()` and the whole thing cannot be assigned.

Note the missing semicolon on the final expression of each branch: that is what makes it the branch’s value.
lessons.example_note: No semicolon follows "even" inside the braces — adding one would make the block yield () and break the assignment.
lessons.task: With `let temp = 5`, use an if/else if chain as an expression to assign `freezing` below 0, `cold` below 10, `mild` below 25, otherwise `hot`, then print it. Also print `even` or `odd` for the same value using an if expression.
hints: Every branch must yield the same type, and none takes a trailing semicolon.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Three kinds of loop
lessons.subtitle: loop, while and for
lessons.concept:
Rust has three looping constructs.

`for x in iterable` is the one you will use almost always. `1..6` is an exclusive range and `1..=5` inclusive.

`while condition` repeats while the condition holds.

`loop` runs forever until you `break`. Uniquely, **`break value` returns a value out of the loop**, so a `loop` can be an expression — which is the clean way to express "keep trying until something works".

There is no C-style `for (i = 0; ...)` at all; ranges and iterators replace it.
lessons.example_note: break candidate returned a value from the loop, so found is 8 — no mutable variable outside was needed.
lessons.task: Print the first five multiples of 3 one per line using a for loop over an inclusive range, then their sum. Then use a `loop` with `break value` to find the first number whose cube exceeds 500.
hints: 1..=5 is the inclusive range giving 1 through 5.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Iterating over things
lessons.subtitle: Ranges, collections and enumerate
lessons.concept:
A `for` loop consumes an **iterator**, and many things produce one.

`0..n` counts up; `.rev()` reverses; `.step_by(k)` skips. To iterate a collection without consuming it, use `&collection` or `.iter()`.

`.enumerate()` yields `(index, item)` pairs, and destructuring in the pattern gives both names at once: `for (i, item) in items.iter().enumerate()`.

`.zip(other)` pairs two iterators, stopping at the shorter. These adaptors replace the manual index arithmetic that C requires, and they compile down to equally fast code.
lessons.example_note: Iterating &items borrows the vector, so it remains usable afterwards — iterating items directly would consume it.

lessons.title: Leaving early and skipping
lessons.subtitle: break, continue and labels
lessons.concept:
`break` exits the innermost loop and `continue` skips to the next iteration.

Rust supports **loop labels** written with a leading apostrophe: `'outer: for ...`. Then `break 'outer` escapes several levels at once, and `continue 'outer` jumps to the next outer iteration. That removes the flag variable C requires.

A labelled `break` can also carry a value out of a labelled `loop`, combining both features.

Because `loop` with `break value` is an expression, many searches that would need a mutable accumulator in other languages become a single binding here.
lessons.example_note: break 'outer left both loops at once, which an unlabelled break could not do.
lessons.task: Loop from 1 to 30, skipping multiples of 3 with continue and breaking once the value exceeds 12. Then use a labelled break to stop a nested 4x4 loop as soon as the product exceeds 6, printing the pair.
hints: A loop label starts with an apostrophe and is followed by a colon.

lessons.title: Matching against patterns
lessons.subtitle: match
lessons.concept:
`match` compares a value against patterns and is **exhaustive** — you must cover every possibility or the code will not compile. That guarantee is one of Rust’s most valuable features, since it makes forgotten cases impossible.

Each arm is `pattern => expression`. Patterns can be literals, ranges (`1..=9`), several alternatives with `|`, or `_` as the catch-all.

An arm can carry a **guard**: `n if n < 0 => ...` adds a condition to the pattern.

Like `if`, `match` is an expression, so its value can be assigned directly. That is usually clearer than a chain of if/else.
lessons.example_note: Removing the final _ arm would be a compile error, because the compiler cannot prove every integer is covered.
