questions.q: Why does Rust need no ternary operator?
options: Because if is an expression that produces a value
questions.explain: let x = if c { 1 } else { 2 }; already does the job, so a separate operator would be redundant.

questions.q: What makes match exhaustive?
options: The compiler requires every possible value to be covered
It stops at the first match
questions.explain: Exhaustiveness checking makes forgotten cases a compile error rather than a silent bug.

questions.q: What is unique about Rust’s loop construct?
options: break value returns a value out of the loop, making it an expression
questions.explain: That lets a search assign its result directly, with no mutable variable declared outside.

questions.q: What does 1..5 produce?
questions.explain: The two-dot form is exclusive of the end; 1..=5 is the inclusive version.

questions.q: Why iterate &items rather than items?
options: Iterating items consumes the collection, while &items borrows it
questions.explain: A plain for over a Vec takes ownership, so the collection cannot be used afterwards.

lessons.title: Declaring functions
lessons.subtitle: Parameters and return types
lessons.concept:
A Rust function declares every parameter type and its return type after `->`:

`fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }`

Type annotations on parameters are **mandatory** — there is no inference across function boundaries, which keeps signatures self-documenting and error messages precise.

The final expression is the return value, with **no `return` keyword and no semicolon**. `return` exists for early exits.

A function with no `->` returns the unit type `()`. Functions may be defined in any order.
lessons.example_note: classify uses early returns for two cases and the bare final expression for the third — both forms are idiomatic.
lessons.task: Write `fn max_of(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32` returning the larger value, and `fn line()` printing five dashes. Print max_of(17, 42) and max_of(7, 3) between two lines.
hints: The if expression can be the function body with no return needed.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: How arguments are passed
lessons.subtitle: By value, by reference and mutably
lessons.concept:
Three parameter forms, and the choice is visible at both the definition and the call site.

`fn f(n: i32)` takes a **copy** for simple types, so changes are local.

`fn f(s: &String)` **borrows** immutably: the function can read but not modify, and the caller retains ownership. The call is `f(&value)`.

`fn f(s: &mut String)` borrows **mutably**, so the function can modify the caller’s value. The call is `f(&mut value)`.

Because borrowing is explicit at the call site, you can see from the calling code whether a value might be modified — something no other mainstream language shows you.
lessons.example_note: The &mut at the call site makes it obvious that modifies may change message.
lessons.task: Write `fn bump(n: &mut i32)` adding one, `fn describe(text: &String) -> usize` returning the length, and a function taking an i32 by value that fails to change the caller. Demonstrate all three.
hints: Inside bump you must dereference with *n to reach the value.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Returning several values
lessons.subtitle: Tuples and destructuring
lessons.concept:
Rust returns several values as a **tuple**, which the caller destructures:

`fn min_max(v: &[i32]) -> (i32, i32)`

That is the whole mechanism — there are no output parameters and no multiple return values.

For more than two or three values, a **struct** with named fields is clearer, since `result.count` documents itself where `result.2` does not.

A slice parameter `&[i32]` is worth noting: it accepts a reference to an array, a Vec, or part of either, which makes it the most flexible way to take a sequence.
lessons.example_note: min_max accepted both a Vec and an array, because a slice parameter borrows from either.
lessons.task: Write `fn sum_and_count(values: &[i32]) -> (i32, usize)` and `fn min_max(values: &[i32]) -> (i32, i32)`. Call both on a vector, destructure the results, and print the sum, count, average to two decimals, minimum and maximum.

lessons.title: Functions defined inline
lessons.subtitle: Closures
lessons.concept:
A **closure** is an anonymous function written with pipes around its parameters: `|x| x * 2`. Types are usually inferred, and a single-expression body needs no braces.

What distinguishes a closure from a function is that it can **capture** its environment. It borrows what it uses by default, or takes ownership when you write `move`.

Three traits describe what a closure does with its captures: `Fn` borrows immutably, `FnMut` borrows mutably, and `FnOnce` consumes. The compiler infers the right one, so you rarely name them except in signatures.

A closure taken as a parameter is written `impl Fn(i32) -> i32`.
lessons.example_note: tally had to be declared mut because it mutably borrows count — that is the FnMut case.
lessons.task: Create a closure squaring its argument, one capturing a `base` variable and adding it, and a mutable closure incrementing a counter three times. Then write a function taking `impl Fn(i32) -> i32` and call it with a closure.
hints: A closure that mutates a captured variable must itself be declared mut.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Functions that call themselves
lessons.subtitle: Recursion
lessons.concept:
A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem, with a **base case** that returns without recursing. Without one it overflows the stack.

Rust does **not** guarantee tail-call optimisation, so deep recursion can overflow where a loop would not. For simple counting a loop is both faster and safer.

Recursion earns its place with genuinely recursive structures — trees, nested data, divide and conquer.

Because a recursive function’s return type is declared explicitly, the compiler checks every branch returns the right type, which catches a common class of mistake.
lessons.example_note: gcd fits on one line because the if expression supplies both the base case and the recursive step.

questions.q: Why does the last line of a Rust function need no return?
options: The final expression is the return value, provided it has no semicolon
questions.explain: A function body is a block, and a block evaluates to its final expression — a semicolon would discard it.

questions.q: Are parameter type annotations optional in Rust?
options: No — they are mandatory on every function parameter
questions.explain: Rust deliberately does not infer across function boundaries, which keeps signatures self-documenting.

questions.q: What does &mut at a call site tell the reader?
options: That the function may modify the value being passed
questions.explain: Explicit borrowing at the call site makes possible mutation visible in the calling code, unlike most languages.

questions.q: What distinguishes a closure from a function?
options: A closure can capture variables from its enclosing scope
questions.explain: Capturing the environment is the defining feature, and the Fn traits describe how the captures are used.

questions.q: Why must a closure that mutates a capture be declared mut?
options: Because calling it mutably borrows the closure itself
questions.explain: Such a closure implements FnMut, and invoking it requires a mutable borrow of the closure value.

lessons.title: Two string types
lessons.subtitle: String and &str
lessons.concept:
Rust has two string types, and understanding the split is essential.

`String` is **owned**, heap-allocated and growable. `&str` is a **borrowed** view into string data, immutable and fixed in size. A literal like `"hello"` is a `&'static str` baked into the binary.

The guideline is simple: use `&str` for function **parameters** so callers can pass either, and `String` for **owned data** you need to store or modify.

Convert with `String::from(s)` or `s.to_string()` one way, and `&owned` or `owned.as_str()` the other. A `&String` coerces to `&str` automatically, which is why a `&str` parameter accepts both.
lessons.example_note: length_of accepted a literal, a &String and a converted String — that flexibility is why &str is the right parameter type.
lessons.task: Write `fn describe(text: &str) -> usize` returning the length, and call it with a literal, a String and a to_string conversion. Then build a String with new, push_str and push, printing it and its length.
hints: A &String coerces to &str automatically at the call site.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: What a string can do
lessons.subtitle: Core string methods
lessons.concept:
Both `String` and `&str` share a large set of methods, all returning new values since strings are immutable through a shared reference.

- `.len()` gives the length in **bytes**, not characters
- `.is_empty()`, `.trim()`, `.to_uppercase()`, `.to_lowercase()`
- `.contains(p)`, `.starts_with(p)`, `.ends_with(p)`
- `.find(p)` returns `Option<usize>` — not `-1`, which is a genuine improvement
- `.replace(old, new)`, `.repeat(n)`
- `.split(p)` and `.split_whitespace()` return iterators

The `Option` return from `.find` is the pattern to notice: absence is in the type, so you cannot forget to handle it.
lessons.example_note: find returned Some(12) for the present substring and None for the absent one, rather than a magic -1.
lessons.task: Given `let raw = "  Data Science Rocks  "`, print the trimmed text, its byte length, its uppercase form, whether it contains `"Science"`, the debug form of finding `"Rocks"` and of finding `"Python"`, and the word count.
lessons.expected_output:
Data Science Rocks
18
DATA SCIENCE ROCKS
true

hints: find returns an Option, so print it with {:?}.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Bytes, characters and why it matters
lessons.subtitle: chars, bytes and UTF-8
lessons.concept:
Rust strings are guaranteed **UTF-8**, which has a consequence that surprises everyone: `.len()` returns **bytes**, and one character may take up to four of them.

So `"héllo".len()` is 6, not 5. And you **cannot** index a string with `s[0]` — Rust refuses, because a byte index might land in the middle of a character.

Instead:
- `.chars()` iterates characters, and `.chars().count()` gives the true character count
- `.bytes()` iterates raw bytes
- `.chars().nth(i)` reaches the i-th character, returning an `Option`

This strictness is deliberate: languages that allow byte indexing simply produce corrupted text for non-ASCII input.
lessons.example_note: len() gave 6 while chars().count() gave 5, because the accented character occupies two bytes.
lessons.task: For the text `"héllo"`, print its byte length and its character count. Print each character on one line separated by spaces, the debug form of the second character, and the reversed ASCII string `"abc"` collected into a String.

6
5
h é l l o

cba
hints: collect::<String>() gathers an iterator of chars back into a String.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Between strings and numbers
lessons.subtitle: parse and Result
lessons.concept:
`.parse()` converts a string to another type, and returns a **`Result`** rather than throwing or returning a sentinel. The target type must be known, either from an annotation or a turbofish: `"42".parse::<i32>()`.

Handle the Result with:
- `.unwrap()` — panics on failure, fine for known-good input
- `.unwrap_or(default)` — supplies a fallback
- `match` or `if let` — full control

Going the other way, `.to_string()` or `format!` produce a String.
Because failure is in the return type, it is impossible to forget — which is the same idea as `Option` from `.find`.
lessons.example_note: unwrap_or(-1) turned the failure into a default in one expression, with no exception handling needed.

lessons.title: Breaking text apart
lessons.subtitle: split, join and collect
lessons.concept:
`.split(pattern)` returns an **iterator**, not a collection — lazily, so nothing is allocated until you consume it. `.collect::<Vec<&str>>()` gathers the pieces.

`.split_whitespace()` handles any run of whitespace and skips empties, which is what you want for words. `.lines()` splits on newlines.

Joining goes the other way: `parts.join("-")` on a slice of strings.

Because the results are `&str` slices borrowing from the original, splitting allocates nothing at all — a genuine performance advantage over languages that copy each piece.
lessons.example_note: split_whitespace collapsed the double space, where split(' ') would have produced an empty piece.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: strings
lessons.subtitle: Check what stuck before moving on
lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What is the difference between String and &str?
options: String is owned and growable; &str is a borrowed, fixed view
questions.explain: Use &str for parameters so callers can pass either, and String when you need to own or grow the data.

questions.q: Why does "héllo".len() return 6?
options: len counts UTF-8 bytes, and the accented character takes two
questions.explain: Rust strings are UTF-8, so chars().count() is needed for the character count.

questions.q: Why can you not write s[0] on a string?
options: A byte index could land inside a multi-byte character
questions.explain: Rust refuses rather than risking corrupted output, which is what byte indexing produces for non-ASCII text.

questions.q: What does .find() return?
questions.explain: Putting absence in the type means the empty case cannot be forgotten, unlike a magic -1.

questions.q: What does .parse() return?
options: A Result, so failure must be handled
questions.explain: The Result forces a decision: unwrap, unwrap_or, or a full match.

lessons.title: The growable list
lessons.subtitle: Vec
lessons.concept:
`Vec<T>` is Rust’s growable array, heap-allocated and owning its elements. Create one with `vec![1, 2, 3]` or `Vec::new()` plus `.push(x)`.

It must be `mut` to push into, which makes growth visible in the code.

Core operations: `.push(x)`, `.pop()` returning an `Option`, `.len()`, `.is_empty()`, `.clear()`, and indexing with `v[i]`.

Two access styles matter: `v[i]` **panics** if out of range, while `v.get(i)` returns an `Option`. Use `get` whenever the index might be invalid — the Option makes the failure impossible to ignore.
lessons.example_note: nums.get(99) returned None rather than panicking, which is why get is the safe choice for uncertain indices.
lessons.task: Build a Vec of the squares of 1 to 5 with push. Print the debug form, the length, the first element by index, the debug of get(0) and get(99), then pop once and print the Vec again.
hints: The Vec must be declared mut to push into it.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Three ways to iterate
lessons.subtitle: iter, iter_mut and into_iter
lessons.concept:
How you iterate a `Vec` decides what happens to it, and this is where ownership first becomes visible in everyday code.

`for x in &v` (or `v.iter()`) **borrows** each element. The Vec stays usable afterwards.

`for x in &mut v` (or `v.iter_mut()`) borrows mutably, so you can modify elements in place — note you must dereference with `*x` to assign.

`for x in v` (or `v.into_iter()`) **consumes** the Vec. It cannot be used afterwards, and the compiler enforces that.

The rule of thumb: `&v` to read, `&mut v` to modify, plain `v` only when you are finished with it.
lessons.example_note: nums was still printable after the iter().sum() because iter borrows; consumed could not be used again.
lessons.task: Given a Vec of 2, 4, 6, 8, print each element by borrowing, then double every element with a mutable borrow and print the Vec, then print the sum using iter and show the Vec is still usable.
hints: Inside a &mut loop you must write *n to reach the value.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Transforming sequences
lessons.subtitle: map, filter and collect
lessons.concept:
Rust’s iterator adaptors are **lazy**: `map` and `filter` build a description of the work, and nothing runs until a consuming operation such as `collect`, `sum` or `count`.

- `.map(|x| ...)` transforms each element
- `.filter(|x| ...)` keeps matching elements — note the closure receives a **reference**
- `.collect()` gathers into a collection, needing a type annotation
- `.sum()`, `.count()`, `.min()`, `.max()`

Because the adaptors compile down to the same machine code as a hand-written loop, this style costs nothing — which is why it is called a zero-cost abstraction.
lessons.example_note: The filter closure took &&n because iter() yields references and filter passes another reference on top.
lessons.task: From a Vec of 1 to 6, collect the cubes into a Vec and print it, collect the values above 3 into a Vec and print it, then print the sum, the count of even values, and the debug of the maximum.
hints: Use .copied() after filter to turn references back into values for collect.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Putting a Vec in order
lessons.subtitle: sort, sort_by and dedup
lessons.concept:
`.sort()` orders a Vec in place and requires the elements to implement `Ord`. That excludes floats, because `NaN` makes a total ordering impossible — so floats need `.sort_by(...)` with `partial_cmp`.

`.sort_by(|a, b| ...)` takes a comparison returning an `Ordering`. `.sort_by_key(|x| ...)` is simpler when you sort by a derived value.

`.reverse()` reverses in place, and `b.cmp(a)` inside sort_by gives descending order.

`.dedup()` removes **consecutive** duplicates, so sort first to remove all of them — the same caveat as C++’s unique.
lessons.example_note: The floats needed partial_cmp because f64 implements only PartialOrd, not Ord.
lessons.task: Sort a Vec of five integers ascending and print it, then descending with sort_by and print it. Sort a Vec of three words by length with sort_by_key. Then sort and dedup a Vec containing duplicates.
hints: b.cmp(a) reverses the comparison for descending order.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Views into a sequence
lessons.subtitle: Slices
lessons.concept:
A **slice** `&[T]` is a borrowed view into part of a contiguous sequence. `&v[1..4]` borrows three elements without copying any of them.

A slice parameter is the most flexible way to accept a sequence: `fn total(values: &[i32])` works with a `Vec`, an array, or part of either.

Slices carry their length, so `.len()`, `.iter()`, `.first()`, `.last()` and `.windows(n)` all work. `.first()` and `.last()` return `Option`, since the slice may be empty.

Because a slice borrows, the compiler prevents the original from being modified while the slice lives — which is how it guarantees the view can never dangle.
lessons.example_note: The same total function served a Vec, an array and a sub-slice, because all three coerce to &[i32].
lessons.task: Write `fn total(values: &[i32]) -> i32` and call it with a Vec, an array and a sub-slice. Then print a middle slice with its length, the debug of its first and last elements, and the first element of an empty slice.
hints: A &[i32] parameter accepts a reference to a Vec, an array or a range of either.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Fixed-size sequences
lessons.subtitle: Arrays
lessons.concept:
An array `[i32; 5]` has its **length in the type**, fixed at compile time and stored on the stack with no allocation.

`[0; 5]` creates five zeros. Unlike C, the length is known so `.len()` works, and out-of-bounds access **panics** rather than corrupting memory.

Arrays are `Copy` when their elements are, so assigning one duplicates it rather than moving — different from a `Vec`, which moves.

The choice: an array when the size is known and small, a `Vec` when it varies. Both coerce to slices, so functions taking `&[T]` accept either.
lessons.example_note: nums was still usable after `let copy = nums` because arrays of Copy types are themselves Copy.
lessons.task: Create a `[i32; 4]` array of 10, 20, 30, 40. Print it with debug, its length, its sum, the debug of get(99), and show that copying it leaves the original usable. Then build a 2x3 array of zeros, set one cell, and print it.
hints: The array length is part of its type, written as [i32; 4].
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

questions.q: What is the difference between v[i] and v.get(i)?
options: v[i] panics if out of range while get returns an Option
questions.explain: Returning an Option puts the possible failure in the type, so it cannot be silently ignored.

questions.q: What happens to a Vec when you write for x in v?
options: It is consumed and cannot be used afterwards
questions.explain: A plain for takes ownership. Use &v to borrow instead, which leaves the Vec usable.

questions.q: When does a map or filter chain actually run?
options: When a consuming operation such as collect or sum is called
questions.explain: Adaptors are lazy, which lets the whole chain compile down to a single efficient loop.

questions.q: Why do floats need sort_by with partial_cmp?
options: f64 implements only PartialOrd, because NaN has no total ordering
questions.explain: sort requires Ord, and NaN being unordered means floats cannot provide it.

questions.q: What is the advantage of a &[T] parameter?
options: It accepts a Vec, an array, or part of either
questions.explain: Slices decouple the function from how the sequence was allocated, which makes it maximally reusable.

lessons.title: Who owns this value
lessons.subtitle: Moves and the ownership rule
lessons.concept:
This is the idea that makes Rust Rust. Every value has exactly **one owner**, and when the owner goes out of scope the value is freed. No garbage collector, no manual free, and no way to free twice.

Assigning a heap-owning value like a `String` **moves** it. The original binding becomes invalid, and using it is a compile error — which is precisely how use-after-free is prevented.

The move itself is free: nothing is copied, ownership of the existing buffer is simply transferred.

Simple types like `i32` implement `Copy`, so they are duplicated instead of moved and both bindings stay usable.
lessons.example_note: Printing a after `let b = a;` would refuse to compile, with a message saying the value was moved.
lessons.task: Create a String, clone it into a second binding, and print both plus the length of the original. Then show that an i32 copied into another binding leaves both usable.
hints: clone() makes an explicit deep copy; a plain assignment would move.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Passing ownership to a function
lessons.subtitle: Moves across calls
lessons.concept:
Passing a value to a function moves it, exactly as assignment does. The function becomes the owner, and the caller can no longer use the value.

A function can hand ownership back by returning the value, but that is clumsy. The better answer is to **borrow**, which the next lesson covers.

Recognising the problem first makes borrowing feel like a solution rather than an arbitrary complication. The compiler error is explicit: "value borrowed here after move" tells you exactly what happened and where.
lessons.example_note: n was still usable after copies(n) because i32 is Copy; a was not usable after consume(a).
lessons.task: Write a function consuming a String and returning its length, and another taking a String and returning it so the caller can keep using it. Demonstrate both, plus an i32 function showing the value survives.
hints: Rebind with `let b = ...` to receive the returned ownership.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Borrowing instead of taking
lessons.subtitle: References and &mut
lessons.concept:
Cloning everything would be wasteful. Instead you **borrow** with `&`, creating a reference that reads a value without taking ownership.

The rule the borrow checker enforces: at any moment you may have **either** any number of immutable references (`&T`) **or** exactly one mutable reference (`&mut T`) — never both.

That single rule eliminates data races at compile time. It also prevents subtler bugs, such as modifying a collection while iterating it.

Because borrowing is explicit at the call site (`&x` or `&mut x`), you can see from the calling code whether a value might change.
lessons.example_note: Two immutable references coexisted happily; the mutable one was created only after they were no longer used.
lessons.task: Write `fn add_suffix(s: &mut String)` appending ` (edited)` and `fn size(s: &String) -> usize`. Create a mutable String, print its size, modify it and print it again. Then show two immutable references coexisting.
hints: Through a &mut reference you can call mutating methods directly.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: How long a reference lives
lessons.subtitle: Scopes and dangling prevention
lessons.concept:
A reference must never outlive the value it points at. The compiler tracks this and rejects any code that would leave a **dangling** reference — the bug that causes so many crashes and vulnerabilities in C.

Most of the time this is invisible: the compiler infers the relationships. When a function returns a reference derived from its parameters, an explicit **lifetime annotation** may be needed:

`fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str`

That says the returned reference lives at least as long as both inputs. The annotation describes a relationship; it does not change how long anything lives.
lessons.example_note: first_word needed no annotation because there is only one input reference, so the compiler infers the relationship.
lessons.task: Write `fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str` returning the longer string, and `fn first_word(text: &str) -> &str`. Demonstrate both, then clone a value out of an inner scope so it survives.

questions.q: What happens to `a` after `let b = a;` when a is a String?
options: a is moved into b and can no longer be used
questions.explain: String owns heap data, so assignment transfers ownership — which is how use-after-free is prevented at compile time.

questions.q: How many mutable references to a value may exist at once?
options: Exactly one, and no immutable ones simultaneously
questions.explain: That single rule is what eliminates data races and iterator-invalidation bugs at compile time.

questions.q: Why is an i32 still usable after being passed to a function?
options: i32 implements Copy, so it is duplicated rather than moved
questions.explain: Copy types are cheap to duplicate, so Rust copies them instead of moving.

questions.q: What does a lifetime annotation do?
options: Extends how long a value lives
Describes a relationship between reference lifetimes so the compiler can verify it
Nothing at run time or compile time
questions.explain: It is purely descriptive: it tells the compiler which references must outlive which, and changes nothing at run time.

questions.q: What prevents a dangling reference in Rust?
options: The compiler rejects any reference that could outlive its value
questions.explain: The borrow checker proves at compile time that every reference is valid for its entire use.

lessons.title: A value that might be absent
lessons.subtitle: Option and match
lessons.concept:
Rust has **no null**. A value that might be absent has type `Option<T>`, which is either `Some(value)` or `None`.

Because it is a distinct type, the compiler forces you to handle the empty case — null-pointer bugs simply do not exist.

Handle an Option with `match` for full control, `if let` for the present case only, or the helpers: `.unwrap_or(default)`, `.unwrap_or_else(f)`, `.map(f)`, `.is_some()`.

`.unwrap()` panics on `None`. It is fine for values you have already proved present, and a code smell elsewhere.
lessons.example_note: match forced both cases to be handled; if let is the shorthand when only the present case matters.
lessons.task: Write `fn first_big(values: &[i32]) -> Option<i32>` returning the first value above 10. Call it on two slices, printing the debug form, a match result, an unwrap_or(-1), and a mapped value.
hints: Return Some(v) on success and None at the end.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: An operation that might fail
lessons.subtitle: Result and error handling
lessons.concept:
`Result<T, E>` is either `Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`. Where `Option` says "maybe nothing", `Result` says "maybe failed, and here is why".

Every fallible standard-library operation returns one: `.parse()`, file access, network calls. Because the failure is in the type, ignoring it is impossible.

Handle it with `match`, or the helpers `.unwrap_or(default)`, `.is_ok()`, `.ok()` to discard the error into an Option.

The `?` operator is the workhorse: inside a function returning `Result`, `value?` unwraps on success or returns the error immediately. That turns nested error handling into linear code.
lessons.example_note: The ? operator did the error propagation in one character, where a match would have taken four lines.

lessons.title: Your own sum types
lessons.subtitle: Enums with data
lessons.concept:
A Rust `enum` is far more powerful than in C or Java: each **variant can carry its own data**, of different shapes.

```
enum Shape {
    Circle(f64),
    Rect { w: f64, h: f64 },
    Empty,
}
```

That is a **sum type**: a value is exactly one variant, and `match` destructures the data as it selects the branch. The exhaustiveness check means adding a variant makes every incomplete match a compile error — the compiler shows you every place needing an update.

`Option` and `Result` are themselves ordinary enums defined this way.
lessons.example_note: Each variant carried a different shape of data, and match destructured it in the same expression that selected the branch.
lessons.task: Define an enum `Command` with variants `Quit`, `Move { x: i32, y: i32 }` and `Write(String)`. Write a function returning a description for each, and call it on all three variants.
hints: Struct-like variants are destructured with braces, tuple variants with parentheses.
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Types with behaviour
lessons.subtitle: Structs and impl blocks
lessons.concept:
A `struct` groups named fields. Methods go in a separate `impl` block, which keeps the data definition clean.

The first parameter decides what the method can do:
- `&self` borrows immutably — a read-only method
- `&mut self` borrows mutably — modifies the instance
- `self` consumes it — rare, used for conversions

A function in an `impl` block **without** a self parameter is an **associated function**, called with `::`. `new` is the conventional constructor, though Rust has no special constructor syntax.

`#[derive(Debug)]` generates a Debug implementation so the struct can be printed with `{:?}`.
lessons.example_note: Rect { width, height } used field-init shorthand, since the parameter names match the field names.
lessons.task: Define a `Counter` struct with a count field, an associated `new()`, a `&self` method returning the value, a `&mut self` method incrementing it, and derive Debug. Create one, increment three times, and print the value and the debug form.
hints: An associated function has no self parameter and is called with Counter::new().
Match the expected output exactly. println! adds the newline for you.

lessons.title: Shared behaviour
lessons.subtitle: Traits
lessons.concept:
A **trait** defines behaviour that types can implement — Rust’s equivalent of an interface. `impl Trait for Type` provides it.

A trait may supply **default** method bodies, which implementors inherit unless they override them.

Traits are used two ways. As a **bound**, `fn show<T: Describe>(item: &T)` accepts any implementing type and is resolved at compile time with no indirection. As a **trait object**, `&dyn Describe` or `Box<dyn Describe>` allows a collection of mixed concrete types, dispatched at run time.

`#[derive(...)]` implements common traits automatically: `Debug`, `Clone`, `PartialEq`, `Default`.
lessons.example_note: Dog inherited the default describe while Cat overrode it, and the Box<dyn Describe> vector held both types.
lessons.task: Define a trait `Priced` with `fn amount(&self) -> f64` and a default `summary()` returning `costs N`. Implement it for two structs, one overriding summary. Call a generic function on both, then collect them into a Vec<Box<dyn Priced>> and print each amount.

lessons.title: Key to value
lessons.subtitle: HashMap
lessons.concept:
`HashMap<K, V>` from `std::collections` stores key/value pairs. `.insert(k, v)` stores, and `.get(&k)` returns an **`Option<&V>`** — absence is in the type, so there is no null and no default-insertion surprise.

The counting idiom is `*counts.entry(key).or_insert(0) += 1`: `entry` looks up the key, `or_insert` supplies a default if missing, and the `*` dereferences the returned mutable reference.

A HashMap has **no defined order**, so collect the entries into a Vec and sort them when the output must be deterministic. `BTreeMap` is the sorted alternative.
lessons.example_note: The entries were collected into a Vec and sorted, because HashMap iteration order is unspecified.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: enums, structs and traits
lessons.subtitle: Check what stuck before moving on
lessons.concept: A short checkpoint. Every answer follows from the lessons in this module — nothing new is being tested. You can retry as many times as you like.
lessons.task: Answer every question, then check your answers.

questions.q: What does Option<T> replace?
questions.explain: Rust has no null; absence is represented by None inside Option, and match forces the empty case to be handled.

questions.q: What is the difference between Option and Result?
options: Option says maybe nothing; Result says maybe failed, with an error value
questions.explain: Result carries the reason for failure in its Err variant, which Option cannot express.

questions.q: What does the ? operator do?
options: Unwraps on success or returns the error immediately from the enclosing function
questions.explain: It turns nested error handling into linear code, and requires the function to return a Result.

questions.q: What makes a Rust enum more powerful than a C one?
options: Each variant can carry its own data of different shapes
questions.explain: That makes it a sum type, and match destructures the data in the same expression that selects the branch.

questions.q: What is the difference between &self and &mut self in a method?
options: &self borrows for reading; &mut self allows modifying the instance
questions.explain: The receiver type declares exactly what the method may do, which the borrow checker then enforces.
